tardigrade.funFact: They aren't indestructible. In 2019, dried tardigrades crash-landed on the Moon aboard Israel's Beresheet lander; lab tests firing them from a gun later showed they die above about 900 m/s, so researchers think they very likely didn't survive. The confirmed revival record isn't a century, either — it is about 30 years, from Antarctic moss kept frozen since 1983.

image.alt: Grey scanning electron micrograph of a plump tardigrade on a plain pale background, showing its wrinkled, segmented body and stubby clawed legs.

facts.fact1: Usually up to about 0.5 mm long; the largest species reach about 1.3 mm.
facts.fact2: About 1,500 known species, first described in 1773.
facts.fact3: Can tolerate radiation doses around a thousand times what would kill a human.
facts.fact4: Dried tardigrades survived 10 days exposed to open space on FOTON-M3 in 2007.

blue_whale.name: Blue Whale
blue_whale.tagline: The largest animal known to have ever lived — built on a diet of krill.
blue_whale.body: Blue whales can reach about 30 metres and up to roughly 190 tonnes, making them the heaviest animal known to science, living or extinct. They grow that big on krill, shrimp-like crustaceans just a few centimetres long, filtered from seawater through baleen plates by the tonne. Their deep, low-frequency calls can carry for hundreds of kilometres through the ocean. Twentieth-century whaling killed hundreds of thousands of them; hunting was banned in 1966, and they are recovering only slowly.
blue_whale.narrative: A typical 25-metre adult is as long as about fifteen people lying head to toe — and a big one is longer than a basketball court.
blue_whale.massNarrative: A large blue whale outweighs about 30 elephants, and its newborn calf already weighs as much as a small elephant.
blue_whale.funFact: Its heart is huge, but not car-sized: the one preserved by Canada's Royal Ontario Museum weighs about 180 kg and stands roughly 1.5 m tall. And no, a child couldn't swim through its arteries — the aorta is only about as wide as a dinner plate.

image.alt: A blue whale seen from above, its long blue-grey back breaking the surface of dark ocean water in a trail of white spray.

facts.fact1: Longest reliably measured: 29.9 m.
facts.fact2: Heart: about 180 kg — the largest known in any animal.
facts.fact3: On deep dives its heart rate can drop to 2 beats per minute.
facts.fact4: Protected worldwide since 1966, but still listed as Endangered.

mount_everest.name: Mount Everest
mount_everest.tagline: The highest point above sea level — but not the tallest mountain, nor the closest to the stars.
mount_everest.body: Mount Everest rises 8,848.86 metres above sea level, a figure fixed by a joint China–Nepal survey in 2020. It exists because India has been ploughing into Asia for some 50 million years, crumpling the crust into the Himalaya — and it is still rising by roughly 2 mm a year. Measured from base to peak, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller, at over 10,000 m, most of it underwater. And because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo sits about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's.
mount_everest.narrative: Shrink Earth to a 30 cm desk globe and Everest becomes a bump just 0.2 mm high — about the thickness of two sheets of paper.
mount_everest.funFact: The rock at the very top of the world is marine limestone, packed with fragments of trilobites, crinoids and other sea creatures that lived on an ocean floor around 450 million years ago.

image.alt: The snowy Everest massif at dusk, the summits of Everest and its neighbour Nuptse glowing orange in the last sunlight under a purple sky.

facts.fact1: Height: 8,848.86 m (China–Nepal survey, 2020).
facts.fact2: First summited on 29 May 1953 by Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary.
facts.fact3: Air pressure at the summit is only about a third of that at sea level.
facts.fact4: Average summit temperature in January: around −36 °C.

gravity.name: Gravity
gravity.seoTitle: What Is Gravity? From Newton to Curved Spacetime
gravity.tagline: The weakest force in nature — and the one that builds the cosmos.
gravity.body: Between two protons, gravity is about 10³⁶ times weaker than the electric force. Yet it never cancels out and reaches across any distance, so at large scales it wins: it rounds planets, ignites stars and herds galaxies into clusters. Newton described it in 1687 as a force between masses; Einstein's general relativity (1915) recast it as the curvature of spacetime itself. What gravity looks like at the quantum level is still unknown — its proposed particle, the graviton, has never been detected.
gravity.narrative: Gravity has no size of its own: its reach is unlimited, fading with the square of distance but never quite reaching zero. The same pull that keeps your feet on the floor shapes structures hundreds of millions of light-years across.
gravity.funFact: A small fridge magnet can lift a paperclip off the table — out-pulling the gravity of the entire Earth, all 6 × 10²⁴ kg of it. That's how feeble gravity is, until you gather a planet's worth of mass.

image.alt: NASA artwork of Earth sitting in a deep well in a grid of spacetime, with the Gravity Probe B satellite orbiting above it.

facts.fact1: About 10³⁶ times weaker than electromagnetism between two protons.
facts.fact2: Surface gravity on Earth: about 9.81 m/s².
facts.fact3: Newton's law of gravitation: 1687; Einstein's general relativity: 1915.
facts.fact4: No confirmed quantum theory of gravity — the graviton remains hypothetical.

gravity.metaDescription: Newton saw gravity as a force; Einstein showed it is the curvature of spacetime. How it shapes falling apples, orbits and black holes.

time_dilation.name: Time Dilation
time_dilation.seoTitle: What Is Time Dilation? Clocks, Speed and Gravity
time_dilation.tagline: Time runs at different speeds — and your phone has to correct for it.
time_dilation.body: Relativity says there is no universal clock. A clock that moves fast runs slow (special relativity), and a clock deep in a gravity well runs slow too (general relativity). The effect has been measured again and again: in 1971 Hafele and Keating flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners and saw them disagree by hundreds of nanoseconds. Muons created high in the atmosphere should decay long before reaching the ground — yet they arrive in large numbers, because their clocks tick slowly at nearly the speed of light.
time_dilation.narrative: Time dilation has no size — it's a difference in the rate of time itself. It is measurable across a whole planet's orbit and, with today's best atomic clocks, across a height difference of a few centimetres.
time_dilation.funFact: GPS satellites' clocks gain about 38 microseconds a day relative to the ground — losing 7 to their speed but gaining 45 from weaker gravity. Uncorrected, your position fix would drift by roughly 10 km every day.

image.alt: Artwork of a GPS satellite with two blue solar panels orbiting high above Earth; its atomic clocks must be corrected for time dilation.

facts.fact1: GPS clocks: −7 µs/day from speed, +45 µs/day from gravity, net ≈ +38 µs/day.
facts.fact2: Hafele–Keating (1971): airborne atomic clocks confirmed relativity's predictions.
facts.fact3: Six months on the ISS leaves an astronaut about 0.005 s younger.
facts.fact4: In 2010, optical clocks detected the effect over a 33 cm height difference.

time_dilation.metaDescription: Moving clocks and clocks deep in gravity tick slower. Time dilation is measured every day: GPS satellites would drift 38 µs a day without it.

gravitational_waves.name: Gravitational Waves
gravitational_waves.seoTitle: What Are Gravitational Waves? Ripples in Spacetime
gravitational_waves.tagline: Ripples in spacetime itself — heard for the first time in 2015.
gravitational_waves.body: When massive objects accelerate, they send ripples through spacetime that stretch and squeeze everything they pass. Einstein predicted them in 1916 but doubted they could ever be measured. On 14 September 2015, LIGO caught one: two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging 1.3 billion light-years away. In 2017, a neutron-star collision was seen in both gravitational waves and light, and in 2023 pulsar timing arrays found evidence of a slow background hum from across the cosmos.
gravitational_waves.narrative: A gravitational wave has no fixed size — its wavelength can range from kilometres to light-years. By the time one reaches Earth, it changes LIGO's 4 km arms by about 1/10,000 the width of a proton.
gravitational_waves.funFact: In its final fraction of a second, the 2015 merger turned about three Suns' worth of mass into gravitational waves — briefly radiating more power than all the stars in the observable universe combined. Yet none of it was light.

image.alt: A simulation of two black holes about to merge, their gravity warping the starry background into rings around them.

facts.fact1: First detection: GW150914, 14 September 2015, by LIGO.
facts.fact2: LIGO senses arm-length changes of ~1/10,000 the width of a proton.
facts.fact3: 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics: Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne.
facts.fact4: GW170817 (2017): first neutron-star merger seen in both waves and light.

gravitational_waves.metaDescription: Ripples in spacetime predicted by Einstein in 1916 and first detected by LIGO in 2015, from two black holes merging over a billion light-years away.

wormhole.name: Wormhole
wormhole.seoTitle: What Is a Wormhole? Could They Really Exist?
wormhole.tagline: A shortcut through spacetime that the equations allow — and nature may not.
wormhole.body: In 1935 Einstein and Nathan Rosen found that general relativity permits a 'bridge' linking two distant regions of spacetime. That original bridge pinches shut too fast for anything — even light — to cross. In 1988 Michael Morris and Kip Thorne showed a traversable wormhole is possible on paper, but only if propped open by exotic matter with negative energy, something never found in usable amounts. No wormhole has ever been observed; more recently, the ER = EPR conjecture has proposed that quantum entanglement and wormholes may be two faces of the same thing.
wormhole.narrative: A wormhole has no set size: the equations allow throats of any width, from subatomic to galactic. What they can't supply is the negative energy needed to keep one open.
wormhole.funFact: The modern physics of traversable wormholes began with a novelist's question. Carl Sagan asked his friend Kip Thorne for a scientifically plausible way to send his heroine across the galaxy in 'Contact' — and Thorne's answer became the 1988 Morris–Thorne paper. Decades later, Thorne helped shape the wormhole in 'Interstellar'.

image.alt: NASA concept art of a ring-shaped spacecraft flying into a wormhole, colourful light streaking past and a distant galaxy visible through the tunnel's dark mouth.

facts.fact1: Einstein–Rosen bridge first described in 1935.
facts.fact2: The name 'wormhole' was coined by John Wheeler in 1957.
facts.fact3: Traversable designs need negative-energy 'exotic matter'.
facts.fact4: No wormhole has ever been observed.

wormhole.metaDescription: General relativity allows shortcuts through spacetime, but keeping one open needs exotic matter that may not exist. What physics really says.

big_bang.name: The Big Bang
big_bang.seoTitle: What Was the Big Bang? Evidence and Certainty
big_bang.tagline: Not an explosion in space — the beginning of space stretching.
big_bang.body: About 13.8 billion years ago, the universe was extremely hot and dense, and it has been expanding and cooling ever since. The Big Bang didn't happen at a point in space; space itself has been stretching everywhere at once. Within minutes the first light nuclei formed, and after about 380,000 years the universe cooled enough for atoms to form and light to travel freely. That light still fills the sky as the cosmic microwave background, discovered by accident in 1965.
big_bang.narrative: The Big Bang has no size because it had no outside — it happened everywhere, including the patch of space you occupy now. Today that same expansion stretches across the observable universe, about 93 billion light-years wide.
big_bang.funFact: When Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found a stubborn hiss in their horn antenna in 1964, they first blamed the pigeons nesting inside it — and cleaned out their droppings. The hiss stayed: it was the afterglow of the Big Bang, and it won them the 1978 Nobel Prize. About 1% of the static on an old analogue TV came from that same glow.

image.alt: The Planck satellite's map of the cosmic microwave background, the Big Bang's afterglow: an oval of mottled blue, yellow and orange temperature ripples.

facts.fact1: Age of the universe: about 13.8 billion years.
facts.fact2: Cosmic microwave background: 2.725 K, discovered in 1965.
facts.fact3: First atoms formed about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
facts.fact4: The name was coined in 1949 by Fred Hoyle — a sceptic of the idea.

big_bang.metaDescription: The Big Bang wasn't an explosion in space but space itself expanding from a hot, dense state 13.8 billion years ago. The evidence, explained.

multiverse.name: Multiverse
multiverse.seoTitle: What Is the Multiverse? Science or Speculation?
multiverse.tagline: Maybe our universe is one of many — maybe the question isn't science.
multiverse.body: Several ideas in physics hint that our universe might not be the only one. In eternal inflation, space keeps inflating forever, budding off 'bubble universes' with different properties. String theory appears to allow around 10⁵⁰⁰ possible vacuum states, each a universe with its own laws. And the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics suggests reality branches with every quantum measurement. None of these can currently be tested, and many physicists question whether an unobservable multiverse counts as science at all.
multiverse.narrative: A multiverse has no measurable size — by definition, the other universes lie beyond any horizon we can see. Even our own observable universe, 93 billion light-years across, would be one bubble among many.
multiverse.funFact: Some of the multiverse's sharpest critics helped build the theory behind it. Paul Steinhardt, one of the founders of cosmic inflation, now argues that eternal inflation predicts every possible outcome somewhere — and so, he says, predicts nothing.

image.alt: Webb's First Deep Field: thousands of distant galaxies, some smeared into arcs by gravitational lensing, around a few bright spiky stars.

facts.fact1: String theory's 'landscape' allows roughly 10⁵⁰⁰ possible vacua.
facts.fact2: Many-worlds interpretation proposed by Hugh Everett in 1957.
facts.fact3: Searches for 'bubble collision' marks in the CMB have found none so far.
facts.fact4: No observational evidence for any other universe exists.

multiverse.metaDescription: Could our universe be one of many? Inflation, string theory and quantum mechanics all hint at a multiverse, but none of it can be tested yet.

string_theory.name: String Theory
string_theory.seoTitle: What Is String Theory? Explained Simply
string_theory.tagline: Everything might be made of vibrating strings — if only we could test it.
string_theory.body: String theory proposes that nature's smallest building blocks are not points but tiny vibrating strings. Like notes on a violin, each vibration pattern would show up as a different particle — and one of those patterns has exactly the properties of the graviton, which makes the theory a leading candidate for quantum gravity. The catch is that its mathematics only works in 10 dimensions (11 in M-theory), so the extra ones must be curled up far too small to see — in the classic picture, six of them folded into a shape called a Calabi–Yau manifold. More than 50 years on, string theory has no experimental confirmation, and the LHC has found none of the supersymmetric particles many versions hoped for. Yet it has reshaped pure mathematics and given physics the AdS/CFT correspondence, a bridge between gravity and quantum theory that Juan Maldacena proposed in 1997.
string_theory.narrative: Strings have no measured size: they are usually pictured near the Planck length, about 10⁻³⁵ m — some 10²⁰ times smaller than a proton. Nothing remotely that small has ever been probed, so if strings exist, their true scale is still unknown.
string_theory.funFact: String theory began as a theory of the wrong thing. In 1968 Gabriele Veneziano found a formula that fit data on the strong force, and physicists soon realised it described vibrating strings. When quantum chromodynamics won out as the theory of the strong force, strings looked like a dead end — until in 1974 Joël Scherk and John Schwarz noticed that the theory unavoidably contained a graviton.

image.alt: A twisted, many-lobed surface in pastel orange, pink and blue — a slice of a six-dimensional Calabi–Yau shape.

facts.fact1: Needs 10 dimensions — 11 in M-theory, proposed by Edward Witten in 1995.
facts.fact2: Its 'landscape' allows roughly 10⁵⁰⁰ possible vacua.
facts.fact3: Witten won the 1990 Fields Medal — the only physicist ever to receive it.
facts.fact4: No experimental confirmation; the LHC has found no superpartners so far.

string_theory.metaDescription: String theory says the smallest building blocks may be tiny vibrating strings, uniting gravity with quantum physics. Elegant, but still untested.

m87_black_hole.name: M87*
m87_black_hole.seoTitle: M87*: The First Black Hole Ever Photographed
m87_black_hole.tagline: The first black hole humanity ever saw — a shadow wider than our whole planetary system.
m87_black_hole.body: M87* is the supermassive black hole at the heart of Messier 87, a giant elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 55 million light-years away. It weighs about 6.5 billion Suns, and its event horizon is roughly 38 billion km across — wide enough to hold the orbits of all eight planets several times over. On 10 April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, a network of radio dishes around the globe linked into one Earth-sized virtual telescope, released its picture: a glowing ring of hot gas around a dark shadow, just the shape general relativity predicted. Later images revealed the ring's magnetic fields (2021) and showed that the ring is still there, with its brightest patch shifted (2024).
m87_black_hole.narrative: Shrink M87*'s event horizon to the length of a football pitch and the Sun becomes a 4 mm bead, Earth a speck thinner than a human hair — and Neptune's entire orbit would barely spill out of the centre circle.
m87_black_hole.massNarrative: M87* weighs about 6.5 billion Suns — more than 1,500 times as much as Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the centre of our own galaxy.
m87_black_hole.funFact: Seeing M87* was like spotting an orange on the Moon from Earth: the ring is only 42 microarcseconds wide. No single dish can do that, so the Event Horizon Telescope synchronised eight observatories, from Hawaii and Arizona to Mexico, Chile and Spain, with atomic clocks — and the petabytes of data travelled by plane on hard drives, because it was far too much for the internet.

image.alt: The Event Horizon Telescope image of M87*: a lopsided orange ring of glowing gas around a dark central shadow.

facts.fact1: Mass: about 6.5 billion times the Sun (EHT, 2019).
facts.fact2: Event horizon: roughly 38 billion km across — more than 250 times the Earth–Sun distance.
facts.fact3: Distance: about 55 million light-years, in the galaxy Messier 87 in the Virgo Cluster.
facts.fact4: First image released on 10 April 2019, from data eight radio observatories gathered in April 2017.
facts.fact5: Its jet of particles moving at nearly the speed of light stretches about 5,000 light-years out of the galaxy.
facts.fact6: Hawaiian name: Pōwehi — "the embellished dark source of unending creation".
facts.fact7: In 2023 astronomers found that its jet wobbles on a roughly 11-year cycle — evidence that the black hole spins.

m87_black_hole.metaDescription: M87* was the first black hole ever photographed (2019): 6.5 billion Suns, an event horizon 38 billion km wide, 55 million light-years away.

gaia_bh1.name: Gaia BH1
gaia_bh1.seoTitle: Gaia BH1: The Closest Known Black Hole to Earth
gaia_bh1.tagline: The nearest known black hole — a silent one, given away only by the star circling it.
gaia_bh1.body: Gaia BH1 is a black hole of about 9.6 solar masses some 1,560 light-years away in the constellation Ophiuchus — the closest black hole known. Unlike the black holes that blaze in X-rays, it is dormant: it isn't swallowing anything, so it gives off no light at all. Astronomers found it in 2022 because ESA's Gaia spacecraft saw an ordinary Sun-like star tracing a small ellipse on the sky, circling an invisible partner every 186 days. Nothing that heavy and that dark can be anything but a black hole. Its event horizon is only about 57 km across — the width of a big city.
gaia_bh1.narrative: Gaia BH1 packs nearly ten Suns into a sphere you could drive across in half an hour on a motorway. Its companion star circles it at about 1.4 times the Earth–Sun distance — a little closer than Mars is to our Sun.
gaia_bh1.massNarrative: Gaia BH1 weighs about 9.6 Suns. A neutron star can't be much heavier than about 2 Suns, so anything this heavy and this dark has to be a black hole.
gaia_bh1.funFact: Gaia BH1 has two record-setting siblings: Gaia BH2 (2023), circled by a red giant about 3,800 light-years away, and Gaia BH3 (2024), which at 33 solar masses is the heaviest stellar black hole known in the Milky Way — spotted from a star's wobble in Gaia's data before that data was even released.

image.alt: Artist's impression of Gaia BH1: a glowing Sun-like star beside a black hole whose gravity bends the starlight behind it into a ring.

facts.fact1: Mass: about 9.6 times the Sun (El-Badry et al., 2023).
facts.fact2: Distance: about 1,560 light-years, in the constellation Ophiuchus.
facts.fact3: Event horizon: roughly 57 km across.
facts.fact4: Its Sun-like companion orbits every 186 days, at about 1.4 times the Earth–Sun distance.
facts.fact5: Discovered in 2022 from Gaia's precise star positions, then confirmed with telescopes on the ground.
facts.fact6: Dormant: no X-rays or radio waves — it isn't feeding on its companion.
facts.fact7: The previous closest known black hole, A0620-00, is about twice as far away (~3,300 light-years).

gaia_bh1.metaDescription: Gaia BH1 is the closest known black hole: 9.6 solar masses, 1,560 light-years away, found in 2022 from a Sun-like star circling something invisible.

neutrino.name: Neutrino
neutrino.seoTitle: What Is a Neutrino? The Ghost Particle Explained
neutrino.tagline: The ghost particle: trillions pass through you every second, and almost none ever touch you.
neutrino.body: Neutrinos are elementary particles with no electric charge and an almost unimaginably small mass — under a millionth of an electron's. They come in three flavours (electron, muon and tau) and are made wherever atomic nuclei change: in the Sun's core, in nuclear reactors, in supernovae, even in the potassium in your bones. Because they feel only the weak force and gravity, they slip through whole planets as if they were empty space: tens of billions from the Sun cross every square centimetre of your skin each second, by day and by night. Wolfgang Pauli proposed them in 1930 to balance the books in radioactive decay; it took until 1956 to catch one.
neutrino.narrative: Hold up your thumb: tens of billions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through its nail every second. In your whole lifetime, perhaps only a handful of them will ever actually hit an atom in your body.
neutrino.massNarrative: A neutrino weighs less than 0.45 electronvolts (KATRIN, 2025) — under a millionth of an electron. Yet with about 340 left over from the Big Bang in every cubic centimetre of space, neutrinos are the second most common particle in the universe, after photons.
neutrino.funFact: In February 1987 three underground detectors caught about two dozen neutrinos in 13 seconds — roughly three hours before anyone saw the light of Supernova 1987A in a neighbouring galaxy. The neutrinos had escaped the collapsing star's core at once, while the light had to wait for the blast to reach the star's surface.

image.alt: The IceCube Laboratory at the South Pole at night, lit red, under the Milky Way and a green aurora.

facts.fact1: Charge: none. Mass: under 0.45 eV — less than a millionth of an electron (KATRIN, 2025).
facts.fact2: Three flavours — electron, muon and tau — and they switch between them as they travel.
facts.fact3: About 65 billion solar neutrinos pass through every square centimetre of Earth each second.
facts.fact4: Proposed by Wolfgang Pauli in 1930; first detected in 1956 at a nuclear reactor by Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines.
facts.fact5: Neutrino oscillations proved they have mass — Nobel Prize in Physics 2015 (Takaaki Kajita, Arthur McDonald).
facts.fact6: IceCube uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, watched by 5,160 light sensors, as its detector.
facts.fact7: Your body gives off about 4,000 neutrinos a second, from radioactive potassium-40.
facts.fact8: In 2025 the KM3NeT sea-floor telescope reported the most energetic neutrino ever seen: about 220 PeV.

neutrino.metaDescription: Neutrinos are ghostly, almost massless particles: 65 billion from the Sun cross every square centimetre of you each second. What they are, simply explained.

mariana_trench.name: Mariana Trench
mariana_trench.seoTitle: How Deep Is the Mariana Trench? Deeper Than Everest
mariana_trench.tagline: The deepest place in the ocean — drop Everest in and its summit would still be two kilometres underwater.
mariana_trench.body: The Mariana Trench is a crescent-shaped gash in the floor of the western Pacific, about 2,550 km long, east of the Mariana Islands near Guam. It forms where the Pacific Plate dives beneath the smaller Mariana Plate. Its deepest point, Challenger Deep, lies roughly 10,935 m below sea level according to the latest sonar and pressure surveys. Down there the water presses with more than 1,000 times the pressure at the surface, it is pitch dark and only just above freezing — and still there is life: shrimp-like amphipods, giant single-celled xenophyophores and mats of microbes.
mariana_trench.narrative: Drop Mount Everest into Challenger Deep and its summit would still sit about 2 km underwater. Airliners cruise at around 11 km — almost exactly as far above the sea as the bottom of the trench lies below it.
mariana_trench.funFact: Only a few dozen people have ever reached the bottom. The first, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, got there in the bathyscaphe Trieste on 23 January 1960 and spent 20 minutes on the floor, their view clouded by stirred-up silt. Nobody went back until film-maker James Cameron dived alone in 2012; since 2019 Victor Vescovo's submersible Limiting Factor has taken a couple of dozen more.

image.alt: The bathyscaphe Trieste afloat in rough grey seas over the Mariana Trench in January 1960, a US Navy ship behind it.

facts.fact1: Deepest point (Challenger Deep): about 10,935 m below sea level.
facts.fact2: Length: about 2,550 km; average width about 69 km.
facts.fact3: Pressure at the bottom: about 1,086 bar — more than 1,000 times that at the surface.
facts.fact4: Water temperature at the bottom: about 1–4 °C.
facts.fact5: First reached on 23 January 1960 by Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in the Trieste.
facts.fact6: Made by subduction: the Pacific Plate sinks beneath the Mariana Plate.
facts.fact7: A plastic bag has been spotted at 10,898 m — the deepest known piece of plastic litter.
facts.fact8: Life thrives there: amphipods, sea cucumbers and xenophyophores — single cells up to 10 cm across.

mariana_trench.metaDescription: The Mariana Trench plunges about 10,935 m at Challenger Deep — Everest would vanish under 2 km of water. Pressure, life and the people who reached the bottom.

iss.name: International Space Station
iss.seoTitle: International Space Station: How Big, How Fast, How High
iss.tagline: A football-pitch-sized laboratory falling around Earth 16 times a day — home to people without a break since 2000.
iss.body: The International Space Station is the largest structure humans have ever put in space: about 109 m across its solar-array truss — roughly the length of a football pitch — and some 450 tonnes in mass. It circles Earth about 400 km up at around 7.7 km/s, once every 92 minutes, so its crew sees about 16 sunrises and sunsets a day. Built from 1998 by the space agencies of the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada, it has been continuously crewed since 2 November 2000. Its astronauts float not because there is no gravity up there — it is still about 90% as strong as on the ground — but because the station and everyone in it are in constant free fall around the planet.
iss.narrative: Shrink Earth to a 30 cm desk globe and the ISS would orbit just 1 cm above its surface — closer than a fingertip hovering over the globe. The Moon, at the same scale, would be about 9 metres away.
iss.massNarrative: The ISS weighs about 450 tonnes — more than 300 cars. Its pressurised volume, about 900 m³, is bigger than a six-bedroom house.
iss.funFact: The station's first piece, the Russian module Zarya, was launched on 20 November 1998. Since then more than 280 people from over 20 countries have visited. The plan is to retire it around 2030: a SpaceX-built deorbit vehicle will push it down over a remote stretch of the South Pacific, where most of it will burn up on re-entry.

image.alt: The International Space Station against black space, its long truss lined with eight pairs of golden-brown solar arrays.

facts.fact1: Size: about 109 m × 73 m — roughly a football pitch.
facts.fact2: Mass: about 450 tonnes.
facts.fact3: Altitude: about 400 km; speed about 7.7 km/s (27,600 km/h).
facts.fact4: One orbit every ~92 minutes — about 16 sunrises a day.
facts.fact5: Continuously crewed since 2 November 2000.
facts.fact6: Partners: NASA, Roscosmos, ESA, JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency.
facts.fact7: Visible to the naked eye — at its brightest it outshines Venus.
facts.fact8: Planned retirement: around 2030, followed by a controlled re-entry over the South Pacific.

iss.metaDescription: The ISS is about 109 m across, weighs 450 tonnes and circles Earth 400 km up every 92 minutes. Its size, speed and how people live aboard.

james_webb.name: James Webb Space Telescope
james_webb.seoTitle: James Webb Space Telescope: Size, Distance and Discoveries
james_webb.tagline: A gold-plated eye on a tennis-court-sized shield, parked 1.5 million km away to see the first galaxies.
james_webb.body: The James Webb Space Telescope is the largest telescope ever sent into space. Its primary mirror is 6.5 m across, built from 18 hexagonal segments of gold-coated beryllium, and it rides on a five-layer sunshield about the size of a tennis court. Launched on 25 December 2021, it works from an orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point, 1.5 million km from Earth on the side away from the Sun, where one shield can block the Sun, Earth and Moon at once. Webb sees mainly in infrared, so it has to stay extremely cold: its shaded side sits at about −233 °C. That lets it catch light from galaxies that formed less than 300 million years after the Big Bang, peer through dust into stellar nurseries and read the chemistry of exoplanet atmospheres.
james_webb.narrative: Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court, yet each of its five layers is thinner than a human hair. Together they cut the Sun's heat about a million times — like sunscreen with an SPF of a million.
james_webb.massNarrative: Webb weighs about 6.2 tonnes — roughly a large African elephant. Its mirrors carry only about 48 grams of gold, in a layer some 100 nanometres thick: about the mass of a golf ball.
james_webb.funFact: After launch Webb had to unfold itself: 344 steps that each had to work first time, with no way to send anyone up to fix a fault. It all went so smoothly — and the Ariane 5 launch was so precise — that the telescope saved enough fuel to keep working for well over 20 years instead of the planned ten.

image.alt: Webb's gold hexagonal primary mirror, fully unfolded and hanging from a crane in a NASA clean room, with technicians in white suits below.

facts.fact1: Primary mirror: 6.5 m across, 18 gold-coated beryllium segments.
facts.fact2: Sunshield: about 21 × 14 m — the size of a tennis court — in five layers.
facts.fact3: Distance: about 1.5 million km from Earth, near the Sun–Earth L2 point — roughly four times farther than the Moon.
facts.fact4: Launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 from Kourou, French Guiana.
facts.fact5: Cold side: about −233 °C; the MIRI instrument is cooled further, to about −266 °C.
facts.fact6: First full-colour images released on 11–12 July 2022.
facts.fact7: A joint mission of NASA, ESA and the Canadian Space Agency, costing about 10 billion dollars.
facts.fact8: It has seen galaxies as they were less than 300 million years after the Big Bang.

james_webb.metaDescription: The James Webb Space Telescope has a 6.5 m gold mirror and a tennis-court-sized sunshield, and works 1.5 million km from Earth. Size, distance and discoveries.
james_webb.temperatureNote: cold, shaded side of the sunshield

fermi_paradox.name: Fermi Paradox
fermi_paradox.seoTitle: What Is the Fermi Paradox? Where Is Everybody?
fermi_paradox.tagline: Billions of planets, billions of years — and not a single sign of anyone else. Where is everybody?
fermi_paradox.body: In 1950, over lunch at Los Alamos, the physicist Enrico Fermi asked a simple question: "Where is everybody?" The Milky Way holds hundreds of billions of stars, many of them billions of years older than the Sun, and we now know that planets are the rule rather than the exception — more than 6,000 have been confirmed around other stars. Even a civilisation travelling far slower than light could spread across the galaxy in a few million years, a blink compared with its age. Yet we see no visitors, no signals and no giant feats of engineering. That contradiction is the Fermi paradox. The question is real; every answer so far — from "life is rare" to "they're hiding" — is speculation.
fermi_paradox.narrative: Squeeze the Milky Way's 13 billion years into a single calendar year and a civilisation with slow starships could settle the entire galaxy in about half a day — while all of recorded human history fits into the final 12 seconds.
fermi_paradox.funFact: We've barely started looking. A 2018 estimate found that all the radio searches for alien signals so far add up to examining about one hot tub's worth of water from all of Earth's oceans. Finding no fish in a hot tub tells you very little about the sea.

image.alt: Radio dishes of the ALMA observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert under the arch of the Milky Way at night.

facts.fact1: Named after Enrico Fermi, who asked "Where is everybody?" at Los Alamos in 1950.
facts.fact2: The Milky Way has an estimated 100–400 billion stars; many are billions of years older than the Sun.
facts.fact3: More than 6,000 planets around other stars have been confirmed since 1995.
facts.fact4: The Drake equation (1961) splits the number of detectable civilisations into factors — most of them still unknown.
facts.fact5: The "Great Filter" idea: some step from dead chemistry to star-faring life is extremely hard — and it may lie behind us, or ahead.
facts.fact6: The 1977 "Wow!" signal is the most famous candidate alien radio blip; it has never been picked up again.
facts.fact7: Proposed answers include rare life, short-lived civilisations, vast gaps in time between them — or simply that we haven't looked enough.

fermi_paradox.metaDescription: Billions of stars and thousands of known planets, yet no sign of aliens. What the Fermi paradox is and the main proposed answers, simply explained.

speed_of_light.name: Speed of Light
speed_of_light.seoTitle: How Fast Is the Speed of Light? 299,792 km/s Explained
speed_of_light.tagline: The universe's speed limit: 299,792,458 metres every second — exactly.
speed_of_light.body: In a vacuum, light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second — about 300,000 km/s, or 1.08 billion km/h. The number is exact because since 1983 the metre itself has been defined by it. Einstein's special relativity (1905) made it more than a speed: it is the same for every observer, however fast they are moving, and nothing with mass can ever reach it — the closer you get, the more energy each extra sliver of speed costs. Gravity and every kind of electromagnetic wave, from radio to gamma rays, travel at the same speed. Light slows down in glass, water or diamond, but that is a collective effect of the material — the speed limit itself never changes.
speed_of_light.narrative: Light circles Earth about seven and a half times in a second. Yet it needs 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, 8 minutes 20 seconds to get here from the Sun, over 4 years from the nearest star and 2.5 million years from the Andromeda Galaxy.
speed_of_light.funFact: The first estimate came from a moon. In 1676 Ole Rømer noticed that Jupiter's moon Io slipped out of eclipse later when Earth was farther from Jupiter — the light simply had farther to go. Christiaan Huygens turned his numbers into a speed of about 220,000 km/s: off by a quarter, but proof that light takes time to travel.

image.alt: A thin orange laser beam shoots from a telescope dome towards the centre of the Milky Way in a star-filled sky.

facts.fact1: Exactly 299,792,458 m/s in a vacuum — fixed by definition since 1983.
facts.fact2: About 1.08 billion km/h, or 186,282 miles per second.
facts.fact3: In water light moves at about 225,000 km/s; in diamond at about 124,000 km/s.
facts.fact4: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
facts.fact5: First estimated in 1676 from the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io, by Ole Rømer.
facts.fact6: In 1999 Lene Hau slowed light to about 17 m/s — around 61 km/h — in an ultracold cloud of atoms.
facts.fact7: Particles that move faster than light does in water give off a blue glow — Cherenkov radiation.
facts.fact8: Distant galaxies can recede faster than light because space itself expands — locally, nothing outruns light.

speed_of_light.metaDescription: Light travels at exactly 299,792,458 m/s — the cosmic speed limit. Why the number is exact, why nothing can beat it, and how long light takes to reach us.

eiffel_tower.name: Eiffel Tower
eiffel_tower.seoTitle: How Tall Is the Eiffel Tower? 330 m of Iron
eiffel_tower.tagline: 330 metres of wrought iron, built in two years as a temporary fairground arch — and never taken down.
eiffel_tower.body: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1887–1889 as the entrance arch to the Exposition Universelle in Paris, the world's fair that marked the centenary of the French Revolution. It was designed by Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, engineers at Gustave Eiffel's company, and assembled from 18,038 wrought-iron parts held together by 2.5 million rivets. At 330 metres including its antennas, it was by far the tallest structure in the world for 41 years, until the Chrysler Building overtook it in 1930. It was supposed to be dismantled in 1909; it survived because its height made it the perfect mast for the new technology of radio.
eiffel_tower.narrative: Stand a person beside it and the tower is almost 200 times taller. Yet it is astonishingly light for its size: melt its 7,300 tonnes of iron down and the metal would cover its 125-metre-square base only about 6 cm deep.
eiffel_tower.funFact: The tower never stands perfectly still. On a hot day the iron on the sunny side expands more than the shaded side, so the top leans away from the sun by up to 18 cm — then straightens again as the evening cools.

image.alt: The Eiffel Tower seen from the Champ de Mars on a clear day, its iron lattice rising from four arched legs into a deep blue sky.

facts.fact1: Height: 330 m to the tip of its antennas — about as tall as an 81-storey building.
facts.fact2: Base: a square 125 m on each side.
facts.fact3: Iron structure: 7,300 tonnes; about 10,100 tonnes with lifts, shops and antennas.
facts.fact4: 18,038 iron parts joined by 2.5 million rivets.
facts.fact5: Built in just over two years for the 1889 World's Fair (Exposition Universelle).
facts.fact6: Tallest structure in the world from 1889 until the Chrysler Building in 1930.
facts.fact7: On hot days the top shifts away from the sun by up to 18 cm.
facts.fact8: 5.9 million visitors in 2022 — the most-visited paid monument in the world.

eiffel_tower.metaDescription: The Eiffel Tower is 330 m tall: 7,300 tonnes of wrought iron and 2.5 million rivets, built in two years for 1889. How it compares with people, pyramids and peaks.

burj_khalifa.name: Burj Khalifa
burj_khalifa.seoTitle: How Tall Is the Burj Khalifa? The 828 m Skyscraper
burj_khalifa.tagline: The tallest building ever made — 828 metres, so high that the sun sets later at the top.
burj_khalifa.body: Burj Khalifa in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, has been the tallest building in the world since it opened on 4 January 2010. Designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it rises 828 m to the top of its spire (829.8 m to the tip of the antenna) and has 163 floors above ground. Its Y-shaped plan — three wings braced around a central core — keeps it steady in desert winds, and the tower steps back 27 times in a spiral as it climbs, so the wind cannot organise itself into rhythmic, shaking vortices. Building it took about 330,000 m³ of concrete and 55,000 tonnes of steel reinforcement.
burj_khalifa.narrative: You would need 487 people standing on each other's heads to reach its top, or two and a half Eiffel Towers stacked end to end. About 244 m of that height is spire, though — without it the building would be 585 m tall.
burj_khalifa.funFact: The building is tall enough to stretch the sunset. On its upper floors the sun stays visible for a few minutes after it has set at street level — so during Ramadan, residents above the 80th floor wait two extra minutes to break their fast, and those above the 150th floor wait three.

image.alt: Burj Khalifa's silver, tapering spire rising far above the surrounding towers of downtown Dubai under a clear blue sky.

facts.fact1: Height: 828 m to the top of the spire; 829.8 m to the antenna tip.
facts.fact2: 163 floors above ground — more than any other building.
facts.fact3: Opened on 4 January 2010 after six years of construction.
facts.fact4: About 330,000 m³ of concrete and 55,000 tonnes of steel rebar.
facts.fact5: The spire alone is about 244 m — taller than the Great Pyramid.
facts.fact6: Foundation: 192 piles, each 1.5 m wide and 43 m long.
facts.fact7: 57 lifts; 2,909 stairs from the ground floor to the 160th.
facts.fact8: At its highest point the tower sways about 1.5 m.

burj_khalifa.metaDescription: The Burj Khalifa is 828 m tall with 163 floors — the tallest building on Earth since 2010. See how it compares with the Eiffel Tower, Everest and you.

general_sherman.name: General Sherman Tree
general_sherman.seoTitle: How Big Is the General Sherman Tree? Largest on Earth
general_sherman.tagline: The largest living tree on Earth — 1,487 cubic metres of wood, still growing after more than two thousand years.
general_sherman.body: General Sherman is a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) in the Giant Forest of Sequoia National Park, California. It is not the tallest tree — that is Hyperion, a coast redwood about 116 m high — nor the widest, but by volume it is the largest single-stem tree known: its trunk holds about 1,487 m³ of wood. It stands 83.8 m tall, its trunk is 7.7 m across at chest height (about 11 m at the very base), and it is estimated to be 2,300–2,700 years old. Giant sequoias owe their long lives partly to fire: spongy bark up to about 90 cm thick shields the living wood, and the heat of a blaze helps their cones open and drop seeds onto freshly cleared ground.
general_sherman.narrative: Its trunk alone would fill more than half an Olympic swimming pool. To match its height you would need 49 people standing on each other's heads — or three blue whales, the largest animals ever, balanced nose to tail.
general_sherman.funFact: In January 2006 the tree's largest branch — over 2 m thick and 30 m long, bigger than the trunks of most trees — snapped off on its own and smashed the fence and part of the path below. Nobody saw it fall. In 2021, as a wildfire approached, firefighters wrapped the base of the tree in protective foil; it came through unharmed.

image.alt: Looking up the enormous red-brown trunk of the General Sherman tree, from its buttressed base to its small green crown high above the surrounding forest.

facts.fact1: Height: 83.8 m.
facts.fact2: Trunk volume: about 1,487 m³ — the largest of any known single-stem tree.
facts.fact3: Trunk diameter: 7.7 m at chest height, about 11 m at the very base.
facts.fact4: Estimated age: 2,300–2,700 years.
facts.fact5: A giant sequoia — a species that grows wild only on the western slopes of California's Sierra Nevada.
facts.fact6: Not the tallest tree: Hyperion, a coast redwood, reaches about 116 m.
facts.fact7: Named in 1879 after the American Civil War general William Tecumseh Sherman.
facts.fact8: Its largest branch, over 2 m thick and 30 m long, broke off in 2006.

general_sherman.metaDescription: General Sherman, a giant sequoia in California, is the largest living tree: 83.8 m tall, 1,487 m³ of wood and over 2,000 years old. See how it compares.

betelgeuse.name: Betelgeuse
betelgeuse.seoTitle: How Big Is Betelgeuse? The Red Supergiant in Orion
betelgeuse.tagline: Orion's red shoulder — a star so swollen it would swallow the orbit of Mars, and one day it will explode.
betelgeuse.body: Betelgeuse is the reddish star marking Orion's shoulder, usually the tenth-brightest in the night sky. It is a red supergiant: born less than 10 million years ago with perhaps 15 to 20 times the Sun's mass, it has already used up the hydrogen in its core and swollen enormously. Its radius is roughly 640–764 times the Sun's — the spread comes mostly from how hard its distance is to pin down, somewhere around 400–600 light-years (548 in a 2020 study). Put it where the Sun is and its surface would reach into or beyond the asteroid belt, engulfing the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
betelgeuse.narrative: If the Sun were a 1 cm marble, Betelgeuse would be a ball about 7.6 m across — wider than a two-storey house is tall.
betelgeuse.funFact: Betelgeuse will end as a supernova, most likely within the next 100,000 years. When it does, it will shine about as brightly as a half Moon for months and be visible in daylight — yet at roughly 550 light-years it is far too distant to harm us. Its sudden fading in 2019–2020, the "Great Dimming", was not the countdown: Hubble showed the star had thrown off a cloud of gas that cooled into dust and blocked part of its light.

image.alt: Betelgeuse imaged by the ALMA radio telescopes: a fuzzy orange disc with a brighter patch, against a black sky.

facts.fact1: Radius: about 640–764 times the Sun's — roughly a billion km across.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 400–600 light-years; a 2020 study gives 548.
facts.fact3: Surface temperature: about 3,600 K — cool enough to glow orange-red.
facts.fact4: Mass: roughly 15–20 times the Sun's; age under 10 million years.
facts.fact5: Expected to explode as a supernova within about 100,000 years.
facts.fact6: In the Great Dimming of 2019–2020 it lost more than half its brightness — a change visible to the naked eye.
facts.fact7: It probably has a small companion star, Siwarha, first seen in 2025.
facts.fact8: The brightest star in the night sky at near-infrared wavelengths.

betelgeuse.metaDescription: Betelgeuse, the red supergiant in Orion, is about 700 times wider than the Sun and would swallow the orbit of Mars. Size, distance and its coming supernova.

oort_cloud.name: Oort Cloud
oort_cloud.seoTitle: How Big Is the Oort Cloud? The Solar System's Edge
oort_cloud.tagline: A vast, unseen shell of icy bodies around the Sun — so far out that it reaches a good part of the way to the next star.
oort_cloud.body: The Oort cloud is a theorised shell of icy planetesimals — leftover building blocks of the planets, flung outward by the giant planets — surrounding the Sun from roughly 2,000 to 100,000 astronomical units or more: about 1.6 light-years, and by some estimates twice that. No telescope has ever seen an object in it; the bodies are too small, dark and distant. Its existence is inferred from long-period comets, which fall towards the Sun from every direction of the sky, not just from the plane of the planets. Estonian astronomer Ernst Öpik suggested such a reservoir in 1932, and Dutch astronomer Jan Oort worked out the argument in detail in 1950.
oort_cloud.narrative: Shrink the Sun–Earth distance to one metre and every planet fits within 30 metres of the Sun, while the Oort cloud's outer edge would be about 100 km away. Voyager 1, the most distant spacecraft, will not even reach the inner edge for about 300 years — and would need about 30,000 more to cross it.
oort_cloud.funFact: The cloud may hold trillions of icy bodies larger than a kilometre, yet all of them together might weigh only about five Earths. Every so often a passing star or the tug of the Milky Way nudges one inward, and it may arrive — perhaps a million years later — as a great comet — like Comet McNaught, pictured here in 2007.

image.alt: Comet McNaught's broad, feathered tail arching over the telescope domes of Paranal Observatory in the Chilean night sky, January 2007.

facts.fact1: Thought to extend from about 2,000 to 100,000 AU or more from the Sun — up to 1.6 light-years, possibly 3.
facts.fact2: Never directly observed: its existence is inferred from long-period comets.
facts.fact3: May contain trillions of icy bodies larger than 1 km.
facts.fact4: Total mass perhaps about five Earths.
facts.fact5: Proposed by Ernst Öpik (1932) and Jan Oort (1950).
facts.fact6: Voyager 1 will reach it in about 300 years and need about 30,000 to pass through.
facts.fact7: Long-period comets arrive from all directions, so the outer cloud is a sphere, not a disc like the Kuiper Belt.
facts.fact8: Its outer edge marks the limit of the Sun's gravitational hold (its Hill sphere).

oort_cloud.metaDescription: The Oort cloud is a vast shell of icy bodies thought to surround the Sun out to 100,000 AU or more — over a light-year. Its size, its comets and why we have never seen it.

red_blood_cell.name: Red Blood Cell
red_blood_cell.seoTitle: How Big Is a Red Blood Cell? Size, Shape & Numbers
red_blood_cell.tagline: The body's oxygen courier — a squashed disc 7.5 micrometres wide, and the most numerous cell you own.
red_blood_cell.body: Red blood cells (erythrocytes) carry oxygen from the lungs to every tissue and bring carbon dioxide back. A human one is a flexible biconcave disc — thick at the rim, thin in the middle — about 6.2–8.2 µm across and 2–2.5 µm thick. To make room for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin it throws out its nucleus as it matures, so it can neither divide nor repair itself; after about 100–120 days in circulation it is broken down and recycled. An adult has roughly 20–30 trillion of them, more than 80% of all the cells in the body by number.
red_blood_cell.narrative: Line up 130 red blood cells and they would just span a millimetre. The ones in your body, laid edge to edge, would wrap around Earth four to five times.
red_blood_cell.funFact: A red blood cell is wider than the narrowest capillaries it has to pass through, so it bends into a bullet or cigar shape and squeezes along in single file. It makes a full lap of your circulation in about a minute — and your bone marrow replaces them at roughly 2.4 million new cells every second.

image.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of human blood: smooth, dimpled red blood cells crowded around a few round, bumpy white blood cells.

facts.fact1: Diameter: about 6.2–8.2 µm; about 2–2.5 µm thick at the rim and under 1 µm in the centre.
facts.fact2: Each one holds about 270 million haemoglobin molecules.
facts.fact3: An adult carries roughly 20–30 trillion — more than 80% of all body cells by number.
facts.fact4: Lifespan in the bloodstream: about 100–120 days.
facts.fact5: No nucleus: it is expelled during development to make room for haemoglobin.
facts.fact6: About 2.4 million new red blood cells are made every second, in the bone marrow.
facts.fact7: Red blood cells make up about 40–45% of the blood's volume.
facts.fact8: A full lap of the circulation takes about one minute.

red_blood_cell.metaDescription: A red blood cell is a dimpled disc about 7.5 µm wide — 270 million haemoglobin molecules, no nucleus, 20–30 trillion in your body. See how it compares.

statue_of_liberty.name: Statue of Liberty
statue_of_liberty.seoTitle: How Tall Is the Statue of Liberty? 93 m to the Torch
statue_of_liberty.tagline: 93 metres from the ground to the torch — a copper skin as thin as two pennies, hung on a skeleton designed by Gustave Eiffel.
statue_of_liberty.body: The Statue of Liberty — officially Liberty Enlightening the World — was a gift from the people of France to the United States, dedicated on Liberty Island in New York Harbor on 28 October 1886. The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi shaped the figure; Gustave Eiffel's company designed the iron framework inside it, a few years before his tower rose in Paris. The statue itself measures 46 m from its base to the torch; on its granite pedestal and concrete foundation it reaches 93 m above the ground. Its skin is hammered copper just 2.4 mm thick — shiny brown at first, it had turned completely green with a protective patina by about 1906.
statue_of_liberty.narrative: Her index finger alone is 2.44 m long — taller than a door — and her nose is 1.37 m. Stand her beside the Eiffel Tower and, pedestal and all, she would come up well past its first floor but short of the second.
statue_of_liberty.funFact: The copper skin weighs about 80 tonnes, yet the whole statue is built to flex: in strong winds it can sway up to about 7.5 cm, and the torch up to 15 cm. The torch you see today is a 1986 replacement covered in 24-carat gold leaf; the original is on display in the Statue of Liberty Museum.

image.alt: The green copper Statue of Liberty raising her torch above her stone pedestal on Liberty Island, against a cloudy sky.

facts.fact1: Height: 93 m from the ground to the tip of the torch; the statue alone is 46 m.
facts.fact2: Dedicated on 28 October 1886, a gift from the people of France.
facts.fact3: Copper skin 2.4 mm thick — about the thickness of two pennies.
facts.fact4: The copper weighs about 80 tonnes; the internal framework about 200 tonnes.
facts.fact5: Its iron framework was designed by Gustave Eiffel's company.
facts.fact6: Index finger: 2.44 m; nose: 1.37 m; right arm: 12.8 m.
facts.fact7: Turned from copper-brown to green as a patina formed, by about 1906.
facts.fact8: The crown has 25 windows and seven rays.

statue_of_liberty.metaDescription: The Statue of Liberty stands 93 m from the ground to the torch: a 46 m copper statue, its skin as thin as two pennies, on a framework by Gustave Eiffel's company.

african_elephant.name: African Elephant
african_elephant.tagline: The largest animal on land — a six-tonne giant that talks in rumbles too deep for us to hear.
african_elephant.body: The African bush elephant is the biggest living land animal: a grown bull stands about 3.2 metres at the shoulder and weighs around 6 tonnes, and the largest on record reached roughly 4 metres and 10 tonnes. Its trunk is a fused nose and upper lip with tens of thousands of muscle bundles — strong enough to tear down branches, delicate enough to pick up a single peanut. Elephants keep in touch with low-frequency rumbles, part of it infrasound, that travel kilometres through air and ground. Ivory poaching and shrinking habitat have cut their numbers sharply; the species is listed as Endangered.
african_elephant.narrative: A big bull is almost twice as tall as an adult human at the shoulder alone — and as heavy as about 80 people.
african_elephant.massNarrative: A 6-tonne bull weighs about as much as four family cars, and it eats roughly 150 kg of plants a day to keep going.
african_elephant.funFact: Those huge ears are radiators: blood flows through a dense web of vessels just under the thin skin, and flapping them on a hot day can cool that blood by several degrees before it returns to the body.
african_elephant.seoTitle: How Big Is an African Elephant? Height & Weight
african_elephant.metaDescription: An African bush elephant bull stands about 3.2 m at the shoulder and weighs around 6 tonnes — the largest land animal alive. Size compared to a human.

image.alt: An African elephant with long curved tusks grazing in tall green savanna grass.

facts.fact1: Bull shoulder height: about 3.2 m; cows: about 2.6 m.
facts.fact2: Bull weight: around 6 tonnes; the record is roughly 10 tonnes.
facts.fact3: Pregnancy lasts about 22 months — the longest of any land mammal.
facts.fact4: Eats around 150 kg of grass, leaves and bark a day.
facts.fact5: Tusks are enlarged incisor teeth that keep growing throughout life.
facts.fact6: Listed as Endangered by the IUCN since 2021.

giraffe.name: Giraffe
giraffe.tagline: The tallest animal alive — a neck nearly two metres long, built from just seven bones.
giraffe.body: Giraffes are the tallest living animals: males reach about 5.5 metres, tall enough to look into a second-floor window, and females about 4.3 m. The neck alone can be close to 2 metres long, yet it has the same seven vertebrae as yours, each one simply stretched. Pumping blood that high takes a heart of around 11 kg and a blood pressure roughly twice a human's; tight skin on the legs works like a pilot's pressure suit so blood doesn't pool in the feet. Giraffes live in the savannas and open woodlands of Africa, where their height lets them browse acacia leaves no other grazer can reach.
giraffe.narrative: A tall male is more than three times your height — stand three adults on each other's shoulders and the top one would still be looking up at its eyes.
giraffe.funFact: A giraffe's tongue is about 45–50 cm long and dark blue-black, probably to protect it from sunburn during hours of browsing — and tough enough to wrap around thorny acacia branches.
giraffe.seoTitle: How Tall Is a Giraffe? The Tallest Animal Alive
giraffe.metaDescription: Male giraffes stand about 5.5 m tall — the tallest living animals — with a 2 m neck made of just seven vertebrae. Height compared to a human.

image.alt: A giraffe walking through dry golden grass in Nairobi National Park under a pale blue sky.

facts.fact1: Males: about 5.5 m tall; females: about 4.3 m.
facts.fact2: Neck: up to about 2 m long, with only seven vertebrae — the same number as a human.
facts.fact3: Heart: around 11 kg, pumping at about twice human blood pressure.
facts.fact4: A newborn calf is already about 1.8 m tall and drops some 2 m at birth.
facts.fact5: The horn-like knobs on its head are ossicones — bone covered in skin and hair.
facts.fact6: Roughly 117,000 giraffes remain in the wild in Africa.

sahara.name: Sahara
sahara.tagline: The largest hot desert on Earth — almost as big as the United States, and green only 6,000 years ago.
sahara.body: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million km² of North Africa, stretching some 4,800 km from the Atlantic to the Red Sea and reaching into eleven countries. Only about a quarter of it is sand dunes; most is bare rock plateau and gravel plain. Summer afternoons regularly pass 40 °C, yet the dry air lets nights fall close to freezing. It hasn't always been desert: during the African Humid Period, roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago, lakes, grassland and hippos covered much of it, and rock art from that time shows cattle herders where there is now only sand.
sahara.narrative: Lay the Sahara over Europe and it would stretch from Lisbon to beyond Moscow — Mercury, the smallest planet, is barely wider.
sahara.funFact: The desert feeds the rainforest: winds carry about 28 million tonnes of Saharan dust across the Atlantic to the Amazon basin every year, and its phosphorus helps replace what the rain washes out of the rainforest soil.
sahara.seoTitle: How Big Is the Sahara Desert? Size Compared
sahara.metaDescription: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million km² and stretches some 4,800 km across North Africa — the largest hot desert on Earth. How big, how hot, and once green.

image.alt: Rippled orange sand dunes of Erg Chebbi in the Moroccan Sahara stretching to the horizon in evening light.

facts.fact1: Area: about 9.2 million km² — the largest hot desert on Earth.
facts.fact2: About 4,800 km from east to west and up to about 1,800 km from north to south.
facts.fact3: Only about 25% of it is sand dunes; the rest is rock, gravel and mountains.
facts.fact4: Highest point: Emi Koussi volcano in Chad, about 3,415 m.
facts.fact5: Summer days often top 40 °C, while desert nights can drop near freezing.
facts.fact6: Green with lakes and grassland roughly 11,000 to 5,000 years ago.

amazon_river.name: Amazon River
amazon_river.tagline: The river that carries a fifth of all the world's river water to the sea.
amazon_river.body: The Amazon runs about 6,400 km from the Peruvian Andes to the Atlantic — whether it or the Nile is longest depends on where you decide the source is. By volume there is no contest: about 209,000 cubic metres of water a second pour from its mouth, around a fifth of all the river water reaching the world's oceans and more than the next seven largest rivers combined. Its basin, roughly 7 million km², holds the largest rainforest on Earth. In the wet season the river can spread tens of kilometres wide, and not a single bridge crosses its main channel.
amazon_river.narrative: Stretched out straight, the Amazon would reach from New York to Berlin — about half the width of the whole Earth.
amazon_river.funFact: Twice a month, around the new and full Moon, the Atlantic tide pushes upriver as a wave called the pororoca — up to 4 m high and heard long before it arrives — and surfers have ridden it for more than 10 km.
amazon_river.seoTitle: How Long Is the Amazon River? Length & Size
amazon_river.metaDescription: The Amazon River runs about 6,400 km and carries about a fifth of all river water reaching the oceans. Its length compared to a human, Earth and more.

image.alt: Satellite view of the Amazon's muddy brown mouth branching into channels and islands among green rainforest, with clouds dotting the sky.

facts.fact1: Length: about 6,400 km (some measurements give over 6,900 km).
facts.fact2: Average flow: about 209,000 m³ of water a second.
facts.fact3: Carries about 20% of all the river water that reaches the oceans.
facts.fact4: Drainage basin: about 7 million km², shared by eight countries and French Guiana.
facts.fact5: No bridge crosses the main river anywhere along its length.
facts.fact6: Home to more than 2,500 known species of fish.

grand_canyon.name: Grand Canyon
grand_canyon.tagline: Carved by the Colorado River: 447 km long, nearly 1.9 km deep, and 1.8 billion years of rock on show.
grand_canyon.body: The Grand Canyon in Arizona winds 447 km along the Colorado River, up to 29 km wide from rim to rim and nearly 1.9 km deep at its deepest. Its walls are a stack of rock layers like the pages of a book: limestone and sandstone near the rim are around 270 million years old, while the dark schist at the bottom is about 1.8 billion years old. The river began cutting its present course roughly 5 to 6 million years ago, helped by the slow uplift of the Colorado Plateau. It became a US national park in 1919 and now draws around 5 million visitors a year.
grand_canyon.narrative: Stack two Burj Khalifas on top of each other and they would still not reach the rim from the river at the deepest point.
grand_canyon.funFact: The canyon makes its own climate: the river at the bottom can be about 11 °C warmer than the rim above, so you can leave snow at the top in the morning and hike into desert heat by afternoon.
grand_canyon.seoTitle: How Deep Is the Grand Canyon? Size Compared
grand_canyon.metaDescription: The Grand Canyon is nearly 1.9 km deep, 447 km long and up to 29 km wide, with rocks 1.8 billion years old at the bottom. Its size compared to Everest and more.

image.alt: Evening light on layered red and orange cliffs of the Grand Canyon under clouds, seen from Powell Point.

facts.fact1: Length: about 447 km along the Colorado River.
facts.fact2: Depth: about 1.6 km on average and up to about 1,860 m.
facts.fact3: Width: from about 180 m to 29 km rim to rim.
facts.fact4: Oldest rocks at the bottom: about 1.8 billion years old.
facts.fact5: The Colorado River set its present course about 5–6 million years ago.
facts.fact6: A US national park since 1919; about 5 million visitors a year.

titanic.name: Titanic
titanic.tagline: The largest ship afloat in 1912 — 269 metres of steel that sank on its first voyage.
titanic.body: RMS Titanic was 269 metres long, 28 metres wide and 53 metres tall from keel to funnel tops — when it sailed from Southampton on 10 April 1912 it was the largest moving object people had ever built. Late on 14 April, about 600 km south-east of Newfoundland, it struck an iceberg that opened a row of its watertight compartments to the sea. It sank in 2 hours 40 minutes. Of the roughly 2,224 people aboard, more than 1,500 died, partly because the 20 lifeboats had room for only 1,178. The wreck lies in two pieces about 3,800 m down and was found in 1985.
titanic.narrative: Stand the Titanic on its bow and it would have been about four-fifths as tall as the Eiffel Tower — and taller than the Great Pyramid.
titanic.massNarrative: Fully loaded it displaced about 52,000 tonnes — roughly the weight of 8,700 African elephants.
titanic.funFact: Only three of its four funnels were real. The fourth, at the back, was mostly for show — four funnels looked more powerful — and was used for ventilation and as a chimney for the kitchens.
titanic.seoTitle: How Big Was the Titanic? Size Compared
titanic.metaDescription: The Titanic was 269 m long and 53 m tall — the largest ship afloat in 1912. Its size compared to the Eiffel Tower, a football pitch and a human.

image.alt: Black-and-white photo of RMS Titanic with its four funnels, steaming out of Southampton in April 1912.

facts.fact1: Length: about 269 m; width: about 28 m.
facts.fact2: Height from keel to the top of the funnels: about 53 m.
facts.fact3: Struck an iceberg at 23:40 on 14 April 1912; sank at 2:20 the next morning.
facts.fact4: About 2,224 people aboard; more than 1,500 died.
facts.fact5: 20 lifeboats with room for 1,178 people — about half of those on board.
facts.fact6: The wreck lies about 3,800 m deep and was found on 1 September 1985.

colosseum.name: Colosseum
colosseum.tagline: Rome's great arena: 189 metres of stone that held some 50,000 spectators nearly 2,000 years ago.
colosseum.body: The Colosseum in Rome is the largest amphitheatre ever built: an ellipse 189 metres long and 156 metres wide, with walls rising about 48 metres. Begun under Emperor Vespasian around AD 70–72 and opened by his son Titus in AD 80 with 100 days of games, it seated an estimated 50,000 or more people on tiers ordered by social rank. Gladiator fights, animal hunts and executions were staged above the hypogeum, a maze of tunnels, cages and lifts beneath the arena floor. Earthquakes and centuries of stone-robbing took away about two-thirds of the outer wall, but the rest still stands.
colosseum.narrative: The Colosseum is almost twice as long as a football pitch, and its outer wall is as tall as a 15-storey building.
colosseum.funFact: On hot days sailors from the Roman fleet rigged the velarium, a huge awning of canvas stretched on ropes and masts around the top of the wall, to shade the crowd — you can still see the stone brackets that held the masts.
colosseum.seoTitle: How Big Is the Colosseum? Size Compared
colosseum.metaDescription: The Colosseum is 189 m long, 156 m wide and 48 m tall, and held about 50,000 spectators — the largest amphitheatre ever built. Size compared.

image.alt: The curved, arched travertine outer wall of the Colosseum in Rome under a clear blue sky.

facts.fact1: Outer ellipse: about 189 m by 156 m.
facts.fact2: Height of the outer wall: about 48 m.
facts.fact3: Opened in AD 80 by Emperor Titus with 100 days of games.
facts.fact4: Held an estimated 50,000 spectators or more.
facts.fact5: Built mostly of travertine, tuff and Roman concrete; 80 entrance arches.
facts.fact6: A UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the historic centre of Rome.

great_wall.name: Great Wall of China
great_wall.tagline: Not one wall but thousands of kilometres of them, built over 2,000 years — about 21,000 km in all.
great_wall.body: The Great Wall is a network of walls, trenches and natural barriers built across northern China from the 7th century BC to the 17th century AD. A 2012 survey counted 21,196 km of it, all dynasties and branches included; the best-known stone-and-brick sections, with their watchtowers, are the Ming wall of the 14th–17th centuries, about 8,850 km long. Rammed earth, stone, brick and even sticky rice mortar went into it, and it was manned by garrisons that signalled with smoke and fire. Despite the popular claim, astronauts can barely, if ever, pick it out with the naked eye from orbit: it is only a few metres wide and much the same colour as the land around it.
great_wall.narrative: Counting every branch, the wall would stretch more than halfway around the Earth — about 1.7 times the planet's width.
great_wall.funFact: Builders in the Ming dynasty mixed sticky rice soup into their lime mortar. The rice's amylopectin makes the mortar stronger and more water-resistant, which is part of why those sections have lasted 500 years.
great_wall.seoTitle: How Long Is the Great Wall of China? Length Compared
great_wall.metaDescription: The Great Wall of China measures about 21,196 km counting all branches, and the Ming wall about 8,850 km. How long it is, compared to Earth and more.

image.alt: The Great Wall winding over green, forested mountain ridges at Mutianyu under a blue sky with white clouds.

facts.fact1: Total length, all branches and dynasties: about 21,196 km (2012 survey).
facts.fact2: The Ming-dynasty wall alone: about 8,850 km.
facts.fact3: Built and rebuilt from the 7th century BC to the 17th century AD.
facts.fact4: Ming sections are typically 6–8 m tall and 4–5 m wide on top.
facts.fact5: Practically invisible to the naked eye from orbit, and not visible at all from the Moon.
facts.fact6: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987.

great_red_spot.name: Great Red Spot
great_red_spot.tagline: A storm on Jupiter wider than the whole Earth — raging for at least 150 years.
great_red_spot.body: The Great Red Spot is a giant high-pressure storm in Jupiter's southern hemisphere: an oval about 16,350 km wide when NASA's Juno flew over it in 2017, roughly 1.3 times the width of Earth. Winds around its edge reach about 430 km/h, and the whole vortex turns once every four to six days. It has been watched continuously since 1878, and in the late 1800s it was about 40,000 km long — it has been shrinking and becoming rounder ever since. Juno's microwave measurements suggest its roots reach some 200–500 km down into the atmosphere; its red colour probably comes from chemicals in the cloud tops altered by sunlight.
great_red_spot.narrative: Drop Earth into the Great Red Spot and it would fit with room to spare — and in the 1800s, three Earths would have fitted side by side.
great_red_spot.funFact: A dark spot seen on Jupiter by Giovanni Cassini from 1665 to 1713 was long thought to be the same storm, which would make it over 350 years old. A 2024 study of old drawings concluded it was probably a different storm that faded away — today's spot was first recorded in 1831.
great_red_spot.seoTitle: How Big Is the Great Red Spot? Jupiter's Giant Storm
great_red_spot.metaDescription: Jupiter's Great Red Spot was about 16,350 km wide in 2017 — wider than Earth — with winds near 430 km/h. Its size, its shrinking, and how it compares.

image.alt: Close-up from NASA's Juno spacecraft of the swirling orange-red clouds of Jupiter's Great Red Spot.

facts.fact1: Width: about 16,350 km (Juno, 2017) — about 1.3 times Earth.
facts.fact2: In the late 1800s it was about 40,000 km long; it has been shrinking since.
facts.fact3: Winds at its edge: about 430 km/h.
facts.fact4: Turns once every 4–6 Earth days.
facts.fact5: Reaches roughly 200–500 km down into Jupiter's atmosphere.
facts.fact6: Watched continuously since 1878; first recorded in 1831.

sirius.name: Sirius
sirius.tagline: The brightest star in the night sky — a hot white star with a dead, Earth-sized companion.
sirius.body: Sirius, the Dog Star in Canis Major, outshines every other star in the night sky because it is both powerful and close: only 8.6 light-years away. The bright star, Sirius A, is about twice the Sun's mass and 1.7 times its width, with a surface near 9,700 °C that gives it its blue-white colour, and it gives off about 25 times as much light as the Sun. Every 50 years it is circled by Sirius B, a white dwarf — the burnt-out core of a star that once outshone it — packing about the Sun's mass into a ball roughly the size of Earth. In ancient Egypt, the first dawn appearance of Sirius each year announced the coming flood of the Nile.
sirius.narrative: Swap the Sun for Sirius A and it would look 1.7 times as wide in our sky, shine about 25 times brighter — and Earth would be scorched.
sirius.funFact: Sirius B was found by its pull before it was seen. In 1844 Friedrich Bessel noticed Sirius wobbling as if tugged by an unseen partner; in 1862 Alvan Graham Clark, testing a new telescope lens, spotted the faint companion right where it was predicted.
sirius.seoTitle: How Big Is Sirius? The Brightest Star Compared
sirius.metaDescription: Sirius A, the brightest star in the night sky, is about 2.4 million km wide — 1.7 times the Sun — and 8.6 light-years away. Its size compared to the Sun.

image.alt: Artist's impression of the brilliant white star Sirius A with its small blue-white companion, the white dwarf Sirius B, against a field of stars.

facts.fact1: Sirius A: about 2.4 million km wide — 1.7 times the Sun.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 8.6 light-years — one of our nearest neighbours.
facts.fact3: Mass: about 2 Suns; brightness: about 25 Suns.
facts.fact4: Surface temperature: about 9,940 K.
facts.fact5: Companion Sirius B: a white dwarf about Earth's size with roughly the Sun's mass.
facts.fact6: The two orbit each other every 50 years.

asteroid_belt.name: Asteroid Belt
asteroid_belt.tagline: A ring of leftover rubble between Mars and Jupiter — far emptier than the movies suggest.
asteroid_belt.body: The main asteroid belt circles the Sun between Mars and Jupiter, roughly 330 to 480 million km out, so measured across its outer edge it is close to a billion kilometres wide. It holds more than a million asteroids larger than 1 km and countless smaller ones, yet all of them together add up to only about 3% of the Moon's mass — and more than half of that is in Ceres, Vesta, Pallas and Hygiea. They are leftovers from the birth of the Solar System that never formed a planet, because Jupiter's gravity kept stirring them up. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited Vesta and then Ceres, the belt's one dwarf planet.
asteroid_belt.narrative: The asteroids are on average about a million kilometres apart — more than twice the distance to the Moon. Fly straight through and you would almost certainly never see one.
asteroid_belt.funFact: Since the 1970s more than a dozen spacecraft have crossed the belt — Pioneer 10 first — and none has ever been hit. Mission planners have to work hard to get close to an asteroid on purpose.
asteroid_belt.seoTitle: How Big Is the Asteroid Belt? Size Compared
asteroid_belt.metaDescription: The asteroid belt orbits 330–480 million km from the Sun, nearly a billion km across, yet all its asteroids weigh only 3% of the Moon. Its size compared.

image.alt: Grey, heavily cratered asteroid Vesta, the second-largest body in the asteroid belt, photographed by NASA's Dawn spacecraft.

facts.fact1: Lies about 2.2–3.2 AU from the Sun (roughly 330–480 million km).
facts.fact2: Across its outer edge: close to 1 billion km.
facts.fact3: More than a million asteroids bigger than 1 km.
facts.fact4: Total mass: only about 3% of the Moon's.
facts.fact5: Largest member: the dwarf planet Ceres, about 940 km across.
facts.fact6: Average distance between asteroids: about 1 million km.

water_molecule.name: Water Molecule
water_molecule.tagline: Two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen, bent at 104.5° — the small, lopsided molecule that makes life possible.
water_molecule.body: A water molecule is one oxygen atom holding two hydrogen atoms at an angle of about 104.5°, and the whole thing is roughly 0.28 nanometres across. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, so the molecule has a slightly negative end and two slightly positive ones. That lopsidedness lets neighbouring molecules cling together with hydrogen bonds, which is why water is liquid at room temperature when much heavier molecules are gases, why it soaks up so much heat, and why so many substances dissolve in it. It also makes ice open and airy: water expands by about 9% as it freezes, so ice floats. Its atoms are ancient: the hydrogen dates from the Big Bang, the oxygen was forged inside stars, and as much as half of Earth's water may be older than the Sun itself. How the water reached Earth is still debated — the leading idea is that water-rich asteroids from the outer Solar System delivered much of it to the young planet, though some was probably locked in Earth's own rocks from the start.
water_molecule.narrative: It would take about 3.6 million water molecules lined up side by side to span a single millimetre.
water_molecule.funFact: There are more water molecules in one glass of water — about 8 million billion billion — than there are glasses of water in all the world's oceans, by a factor of more than a thousand.
water_molecule.seoTitle: How Big Is a Water Molecule? Size Compared
water_molecule.metaDescription: A water molecule is about 0.28 nm across — one oxygen and two hydrogens at 104.5°. How small that is, and how many are in a single glass of water.

image.alt: A drop of water bouncing up from a blue water surface, with rings spreading out around it.

facts.fact1: Size: about 0.28 nm (280 pm) across.
facts.fact2: Angle between the two hydrogen atoms: about 104.5°.
facts.fact3: O–H bond length: about 0.096 nm.
facts.fact4: A 250 ml glass holds about 8 × 10²⁴ water molecules.
facts.fact5: Water expands by about 9% when it freezes — that's why ice floats.
facts.fact6: Each molecule weighs about 3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg.
facts.fact7: Hydrogen: made in the Big Bang. Oxygen: forged inside stars.
facts.fact8: How it reached Earth: probably partly on water-rich asteroids (still debated).

pollen_grain.name: Pollen Grain
pollen_grain.tagline: A plant's sperm carrier in an armoured shell — tough enough to last for millions of years.
pollen_grain.body: A pollen grain carries a flowering plant's or conifer's male cells to another flower or cone. Most grains are 10 to 100 micrometres across — a typical one about 25 µm, a quarter the width of a human hair — though forget-me-not pollen is only about 5 µm and pumpkin pollen reaches about 200 µm.
