Each species has its own shape: spiky balls, smooth beads, grains with air sacs that let pine pollen drift for hundreds of kilometres. The outer wall is made of sporopollenin, one of the toughest natural materials known, so pollen survives in lake mud and rock for millions of years and lets scientists read past climates and even solve crimes.
pollen_grain.narrative: Three or four typical pollen grains side by side are about as wide as a single human hair.
pollen_grain.funFact: A single ragweed plant can release up to a billion pollen grains in one season — and hay fever, the immune system's overreaction to them, affects roughly 10 to 30% of adults around the world.
pollen_grain.seoTitle: How Big Is a Pollen Grain? Size Compared
pollen_grain.metaDescription: Most pollen grains are 10–100 µm across, typically about 25 µm — a quarter the width of a human hair. Size, shapes and why pollen lasts for millions of years.

image.alt: Colourised scanning electron microscope image of pollen grains from several plants: spiky yellow balls, green beans and small pink spheres.

facts.fact1: Most grains: 10–100 µm across; a typical one about 25 µm.
facts.fact2: Among the smallest: forget-me-not, about 5 µm.
facts.fact3: Among the largest: pumpkin, about 200 µm — just visible to the eye.
facts.fact4: A single ragweed plant can release up to a billion grains a season.
facts.fact5: Its outer wall, sporopollenin, can survive for hundreds of millions of years.
facts.fact6: Wind-blown pollen can travel hundreds of kilometres.

ant.name: Ant
ant.tagline: A few millimetres of animal — and about 20 quadrillion of them, together outweighing all wild birds and mammals.
ant.body: Ants are social insects that live in colonies built around one or more egg-laying queens and thousands of wingless female workers. A worker of a common garden species, such as Europe's black garden ant, is about 3–5 mm long; across more than 13,800 known species, workers range from under a millimetre to the 3 cm bullet ant of Central and South American rainforests. Ants find their way and share out work mostly by smell: a forager that finds food lays a pheromone trail home, and nestmates that follow it reinforce the best route. Black garden ants even farm aphids, guarding them from ladybirds in exchange for their sugary honeydew. Ants live on every continent except Antarctica and evolved from wasp-like ancestors more than 100 million years ago.
ant.narrative: A 5 mm worker is about as long as a grain of rice, and ten times longer than a tardigrade. It would take about 340 of them, lined up nose to tail, to match the height of an adult.
ant.funFact: A 2022 estimate put the number of ants on Earth at about 20 quadrillion (20,000,000,000,000,000), roughly 2.5 million for every person alive. Together they contain more carbon than all wild birds and wild mammals combined.
ant.seoTitle: How Big Is an Ant? Ant Sizes From 1 mm to 3 cm
ant.metaDescription: A common garden ant worker is about 3–5 mm long, and ant species range from under 1 mm to the 3 cm bullet ant. See an ant's size compared to familiar things.

image.alt: A shiny black garden ant tending a group of brown aphids on a bright green thuja sprig, seen in close-up.

facts.fact1: Black garden ant worker: about 3–5 mm long; its queen: up to about 9 mm.
facts.fact2: Smallest ant workers: about 0.75 mm; bullet ant workers: 18–30 mm.
facts.fact3: About 20 quadrillion ants live on Earth (2022 estimate).
facts.fact4: More than 13,800 species are known, most of them in the tropics.
facts.fact5: Black garden ant workers live a few months, but a queen can live at least 19 years.
facts.fact6: The bullet ant's sting tops the Schmidt sting pain index; the pain can last up to 24 hours.

honeybee.name: Honey Bee
honeybee.tagline: A 13 mm insect that dances directions to flowers — one of tens of thousands in a single hive.
honeybee.body: The western honey bee is the bee kept in hives around the world for honey and crop pollination. A worker (every honey bee you see on a flower is female) has a body length of about 12–15 mm, while the queen, the colony's only egg-layer, reaches 18–22 mm. In midsummer a healthy hive can hold 40,000 to 80,000 bees, nearly all of them workers. Foragers that find good flowers come home and perform the waggle dance on the comb: the angle of the dance shows the direction relative to the Sun, and the length of each waggle run tells how far to fly.
honeybee.narrative: At about 13 mm, a worker bee would just about cover your thumbnail. She is as long as two and a half garden ants, and about 130 bees lined up nose to tail would reach the height of an adult.
honeybee.massNarrative: A worker weighs about 100 mg, so ten bees together weigh about as much as a paper clip.
honeybee.funFact: A summer forager lives only a few weeks, yet in that time she flies about 800 km, roughly the distance from Paris to Berlin, before her wings wear out.
honeybee.seoTitle: How Big Is a Honey Bee? Worker and Queen Size
honeybee.metaDescription: A western honey bee worker is about 12–15 mm long and weighs about 100 mg; the queen reaches 18–22 mm. See a honey bee's size compared to familiar things.

image.alt: A honey bee worker with pollen-dusted legs drinking nectar from the yellow centre of a purple aster flower.

facts.fact1: Worker body length: about 12–15 mm; queen: about 18–22 mm.
facts.fact2: A worker weighs about 100 mg; a queen about twice as much.
facts.fact3: A healthy hive in midsummer: about 40,000–80,000 bees and a single queen.
facts.fact4: Its wings beat about 230 times a second while hovering — that is the buzz you hear.
facts.fact5: Summer workers live only about 15–38 days; a queen can live up to 3 years.
facts.fact6: Karl von Frisch shared the 1973 Nobel Prize, partly for decoding the waggle dance.

ceres.name: Ceres
ceres.tagline: The biggest thing in the asteroid belt — a dwarf planet with salty water hidden under its crust.
ceres.body: Ceres is a dwarf planet about 940 km across, circling the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter. Giuseppe Piazzi spotted it on 1 January 1801 and it was hailed as a new planet, later reclassed as an asteroid, and since 2006 it has been the only dwarf planet in the inner Solar System. On its own it holds about 40% of the mass of the entire asteroid belt. NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018 and found a crust of rock, ice and salts, bright salt deposits in Occator Crater and a lone ice volcano about 4 km high, Ahuna Mons — signs that briny water still lies deep below.
ceres.narrative: Peel off Ceres's whole surface and lay it flat, and it would cover about 2.8 million km² — almost exactly the area of Argentina. Its width, about 940 km, is roughly the straight-line distance from London to Berlin.
ceres.massNarrative: Ceres alone holds about 40% of the asteroid belt's mass, yet it weighs only about 1/78 as much as our Moon. Its gravity is so weak that a person who weighs 70 kg on Earth would feel as light as 2 kg there.
ceres.funFact: The chemical element cerium, discovered in 1803, was named after Ceres — and Ceres itself is named after the Roman goddess of farming and grain, the same name that gave us the word "cereal".
ceres.seoTitle: How Big Is Ceres? The Asteroid Belt's Dwarf Planet
ceres.metaDescription: Ceres is about 940 km across — a quarter of the Moon's width, with a surface as big as Argentina — yet it holds 40% of the asteroid belt's mass.

image.alt: Ceres in natural colour, photographed by NASA's Dawn spacecraft: a grey, cratered globe with a few small bright spots.

facts.fact1: Mean diameter about 940 km (939.4 km, measured by Dawn) — roughly a quarter of the Moon's.
facts.fact2: Orbits the Sun about 413 million km out on average (2.8 AU); one year there lasts 4.6 Earth years.
facts.fact3: Holds about 40% of the total mass of the asteroid belt.
facts.fact4: Surface gravity is about 1/35 of Earth's.
facts.fact5: Discovered on 1 January 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi; classed as a dwarf planet since 2006.
facts.fact6: Average surface temperature around 170 K (about −100 °C).

olympus_mons.name: Olympus Mons
olympus_mons.tagline: A volcano on Mars two and a half times taller than Everest — and covering nearly as much ground as Italy.
olympus_mons.body: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano on Mars and the tallest volcano known in the Solar System. Its summit stands about 22 km above the surrounding plains — roughly two and a half times the height of Mount Everest above sea level — and its base is about 600 km wide, covering an area close to that of Italy. Cliffs up to 8 km high ring its edge, and the top holds six collapsed craters nested together, about 60 by 80 km across and up to 3 km deep. It grew so big because Mars has no moving tectonic plates: the crust stayed put over the same hot spot, so lava kept piling up in one place, and Mars's weaker gravity let the pile stand taller.
olympus_mons.narrative: Airliners cruise about 11 km up; the summit of Olympus Mons would stand twice as high. Yet its slopes are so gentle — about 5% on average — that someone standing on them would hardly notice being on a mountain at all: the volcano is so wide that its summit and most of its slope lie beyond the horizon.
olympus_mons.funFact: Astronomers had seen a bright patch at this spot since the 19th century and called it Nix Olympica, "the Snow of Olympus". When Mariner 9 reached Mars in 1971, in the middle of a planet-wide dust storm, the volcano's summit was one of the few things poking up above the dust.
olympus_mons.seoTitle: How Tall Is Olympus Mons? Mars Volcano vs Everest
olympus_mons.metaDescription: Olympus Mons on Mars rises about 22 km — 2.5 times Mount Everest — and is 600 km wide, close to the area of Italy. The Solar System's tallest volcano.

image.alt: Olympus Mons seen from directly above in a Viking orbiter mosaic: a broad, round volcano with a collapsed summit crater, ringed by steep cliffs.

facts.fact1: Height: about 22 km above the surrounding plains — about 2.5 times Everest's height above sea level.
facts.fact2: Base about 600 km wide; it covers about 300,000 km², close to the area of Italy.
facts.fact3: Summit caldera: six nested craters, about 60 × 80 km and up to 3.2 km deep.
facts.fact4: Ringed by cliffs up to 8 km high.
facts.fact5: Average slope only about 5% — a gentle shield volcano, like those of Hawaii.
facts.fact6: Some lava flows on its flanks are thought to be only about 25 million years old — young for Mars.

titan.name: Titan
titan.tagline: Saturn's giant moon — the only other world with rain, rivers and seas on its surface.
titan.body: Titan is Saturn's largest moon, 5,150 km across — bigger than the planet Mercury and about one and a half times as wide as our Moon; only Jupiter's Ganymede is larger. It is the only moon with a thick atmosphere: mostly nitrogen, with a surface pressure about one and a half times Earth's, wrapped in an orange haze. At −179 °C, methane and ethane take the place of water — they fall as rain, carve river channels and fill lakes and seas near the poles. In January 2005 the European Huygens probe parachuted onto its surface, still the most distant landing ever made, and NASA's Dragonfly rotorcraft is set to launch in July 2028 and, after arriving in 2034, fly from site to site.
titan.narrative: Titan's biggest sea, Kraken Mare, is slightly larger than the Caspian Sea, the biggest lake on Earth. And the air is so thick and the gravity so weak — weaker even than the Moon's — that a person with wings strapped to their arms could, in principle, fly by flapping.
titan.massNarrative: Titan is wider than Mercury but has only about 40% of its mass: Mercury is mostly iron and rock, Titan mostly ice.
titan.funFact: Saturn hangs in Titan's sky looking more than ten times as wide as the Moon does from Earth — but from the ground the thick orange haze would almost certainly hide it.
titan.seoTitle: How Big Is Titan? Saturn's Moon Bigger Than Mercury
titan.metaDescription: Titan, Saturn's largest moon, is 5,150 km wide — bigger than Mercury — with a thick nitrogen atmosphere and seas of liquid methane. Its size compared.

image.alt: Titan in true colour from NASA's Cassini spacecraft: a smooth orange globe wrapped in thick haze, with no surface visible.

facts.fact1: Diameter 5,150 km — larger than Mercury and about 1.5 times our Moon.
facts.fact2: Second-largest moon in the Solar System, after Jupiter's Ganymede.
facts.fact3: Surface pressure about 1.5 times Earth's; the atmosphere is mostly nitrogen.
facts.fact4: Surface temperature about 94 K (−179 °C).
facts.fact5: The Huygens probe landed on 14 January 2005 — the most distant landing so far.
facts.fact6: NASA's Dragonfly: launch planned for July 2028, arrival in 2034.

europa.name: Europa
europa.tagline: Jupiter's icy moon — probably hiding more liquid water under its shell than all of Earth's oceans.
europa.body: Europa is one of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons, 3,122 km across — a little smaller than our Moon. Its surface is water ice, criss-crossed by reddish-brown cracks and almost free of craters, which makes it the smoothest solid object known in the Solar System. Beneath an ice shell probably 15 to 25 km thick, magnetic measurements by the Galileo spacecraft point to a global ocean of salty water 60 to 150 km deep, kept liquid by tidal heating as Jupiter's gravity squeezes the moon. That makes Europa one of the best places to look for life beyond Earth: NASA's Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024 and is due to reach Jupiter in April 2030.
europa.narrative: Europa is only about a quarter as wide as Earth, yet its hidden ocean may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans put together — because it may be up to 150 km deep, while Earth's oceans average less than 4 km.
europa.funFact: Every time Ganymede goes once around Jupiter, Europa goes around exactly twice and Io four times. This steady gravitational tug-of-war keeps Europa's orbit slightly stretched, so Jupiter keeps flexing it — and that flexing is what heats its ocean.
europa.seoTitle: How Big Is Europa? Jupiter's Ocean Moon Compared
europa.metaDescription: Europa, Jupiter's icy moon, is 3,122 km wide — a little smaller than our Moon — yet its hidden ocean may hold twice the water of Earth's oceans.

image.alt: Europa in realistic colour from NASA's Galileo spacecraft: a pale icy globe criss-crossed by reddish-brown cracks.

facts.fact1: Diameter 3,122 km — about 90% of our Moon's.
facts.fact2: Ice shell probably 15–25 km thick, over an ocean 60–150 km deep.
facts.fact3: Orbits Jupiter about 671,000 km out, once every 3.55 days.
facts.fact4: Average surface temperature at the equator about 102 K (−171 °C).
facts.fact5: Discovered by Galileo Galilei in January 1610.
facts.fact6: Europa Clipper launched on 14 October 2024; arrival at Jupiter planned for April 2030.

orion_nebula.name: Orion Nebula
orion_nebula.tagline: A star nursery you can see with your own eyes — the fuzzy middle "star" of Orion's sword.
orion_nebula.body: The Orion Nebula (M42) is a glowing cloud of gas and dust about 24 light-years across, lying roughly 1,300 light-years away. It is the nearest place to Earth where big, heavy stars are being born. Its brightest young stars, a tight group called the Trapezium, flood the surrounding gas with ultraviolet light and make it shine — which is why it is the classic example of an emission nebula. Below Orion's belt it shows up to the naked eye as the fuzzy middle "star" of the sword, and through binoculars it becomes an obvious misty patch.
orion_nebula.narrative: Centre the Orion Nebula on the Sun and it would reach about 12 light-years out in every direction — swallowing Alpha Centauri, Sirius and every other one of our nearest stars. Light needs 24 years just to cross it.
orion_nebula.funFact: On 30 September 1880 Henry Draper exposed a photographic plate for 51 minutes and caught the Orion Nebula — the first photograph ever taken of a nebula. Since then it has become one of the most photographed objects in the sky.
orion_nebula.seoTitle: How Big Is the Orion Nebula? Size and Distance of M42
orion_nebula.metaDescription: The Orion Nebula is about 24 light-years across and 1,300 light-years away — the nearest nursery of massive stars, visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword.

image.alt: Hubble mosaic of the heart of the Orion Nebula: glowing pink, red and orange clouds of gas and dark dust lanes, sprinkled with thousands of young stars.

facts.fact1: Size: about 24 light-years across — in long-exposure photos it spans about twice the width of the full Moon.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 1,300 light-years (389 parsecs, measured by radio parallax of its young stars); older books say 1,344 or 1,500.
facts.fact3: The nearest region to Earth where massive stars are forming.
facts.fact4: About 2,800 young stars crowd into a cluster about 20 light-years wide; its four brightest, the Trapezium, sit within 1.5 light-years.
facts.fact5: Hubble has photographed dusty discs around newborn stars there — planetary systems still in the making.
facts.fact6: At magnitude 4 it is visible to the naked eye, even from light-polluted towns.

crab_nebula.name: Crab Nebula
crab_nebula.tagline: The wreckage of a star that exploded in plain sight in 1054 — still flying apart, with a spinning neutron star at its heart.
crab_nebula.body: The Crab Nebula (M1) is the expanding debris of a supernova that astronomers in China, Japan and the Arab world recorded in July 1054. It is an oval cloud about 11 light-years long, lying some 6,500 light-years away in the constellation Taurus, and it is still flying outward at about 1,500 km/s. At its centre spins the Crab Pulsar, the crushed core of the star that exploded — a neutron star only 28–30 km across that turns about 30 times a second. Its energy keeps the whole cloud glowing, nearly a thousand years after the blast.
crab_nebula.narrative: Centre the Crab Nebula on the Sun and it would reach about 5.5 light-years in every direction — past Alpha Centauri, our nearest neighbouring star. It is growing so fast that its edge would cross from London to New York in under four seconds.
crab_nebula.funFact: When the star blew up, it stayed visible in broad daylight for 23 days and in the night sky for almost two years. Yet the explosion was old news even then: its light had been travelling for about 6,500 years, so the star actually died thousands of years before anyone on Earth had invented writing.
crab_nebula.seoTitle: How Big Is the Crab Nebula? The Supernova of 1054
crab_nebula.metaDescription: The Crab Nebula is about 11 light-years across and 6,500 light-years away — the debris of a supernova seen in 1054, with a pulsar spinning 30 times a second.

image.alt: Hubble mosaic of the Crab Nebula: an oval web of orange and red filaments around a hazy blue core, against black space.

facts.fact1: Size: about 11 light-years along its longest axis — an oval shell of glowing filaments.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 6,500 light-years, in the constellation Taurus (give or take some 1,600).
facts.fact3: The supernova that made it, SN 1054, was recorded in July 1054 by Chinese, Japanese and Arab astronomers.
facts.fact4: Still expanding at about 1,500 km/s — half a percent of the speed of light.
facts.fact5: The Crab Pulsar at its centre is 28–30 km across and spins about 30 times a second — like a car engine at 1,800 rpm.
facts.fact6: Too faint for the naked eye today (magnitude 8.4), but binoculars show it from a dark site; it is the first entry, M1, in Messier's catalogue.

large_magellanic_cloud.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
large_magellanic_cloud.tagline: The Milky Way's biggest companion galaxy — a cloud of 20 billion stars hanging in the southern sky.
large_magellanic_cloud.body: The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way, about 160,000 light-years away. It is roughly 32,000 light-years across — about a third of the Milky Way's width — and holds some 20 billion stars. From the southern hemisphere it looks like a detached piece of the Milky Way, a faint cloud about 20 full Moons long; it is named after Ferdinand Magellan, whose 1519–1522 voyage made the Clouds widely known in Europe, though people in the south had always known it. It contains the Tarantula Nebula, the busiest star factory in our neighbourhood of galaxies, and in 1987 it produced the closest supernova seen in almost 400 years.
large_magellanic_cloud.narrative: If the Milky Way were a dinner plate 27 cm wide, the Large Magellanic Cloud would be a biscuit about 9 cm across lying some 40 cm away — while Andromeda, the next big galaxy, would be about 6 metres away.
large_magellanic_cloud.funFact: The light you see from the Large Magellanic Cloud set out about 160,000 years ago, when our own species, Homo sapiens, still lived almost entirely in Africa.
large_magellanic_cloud.seoTitle: How Big Is the Large Magellanic Cloud? Our Satellite Galaxy
large_magellanic_cloud.metaDescription: The Large Magellanic Cloud is about 32,000 light-years across and 160,000 light-years away — the Milky Way's largest satellite galaxy, home of SN 1987A.

image.alt: The Large Magellanic Cloud photographed from Chile: a pale, lopsided band of stars with pink star-forming clouds, against a dense field of Milky Way stars.

facts.fact1: Size: about 32,000 light-years across (to a standard brightness limit) — roughly a third of the Milky Way.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 160,000 light-years (49.6 kiloparsecs), measured to 1% with eclipsing double stars in 2019.
facts.fact3: Holds about 20 billion stars — and the Tarantula Nebula, the most active star-forming region in the Local Group.
facts.fact4: Supernova 1987A, seen there in February 1987, was the closest naked-eye supernova in nearly 400 years.
facts.fact5: Visible to the naked eye from the southern hemisphere and as far north as about 20° N.
facts.fact6: Expected to fall into the Milky Way and merge with it in roughly 2.4 billion years.

house_cat.name: House Cat
house_cat.tagline: About 46 cm of tamed wildcat — hundreds of millions of them now share our homes.
house_cat.body: The domestic cat (Felis catus) is a small carnivore descended from the African wildcat, and the only member of the cat family that humans have truly domesticated. An adult averages about 46 cm from nose to the base of the tail, with a tail of about 30 cm more; it stands 23–25 cm at the shoulder and typically weighs 4–5 kg, males being larger than females. Wildcats were probably drawn to the first farming villages of the Near East by mice raiding stored grain, and farmers tolerated, then tamed them. A cat still hunts like its wild ancestors: it sees in one-sixth of the light a person needs, hears the ultrasonic squeaks of rodents and judges gaps with its whiskers. Estimates of the world's cat population range widely, from about 200 to 600 million.
house_cat.narrative: Measured from nose to the base of the tail, a 46 cm cat is as long as about 35 honey bees lined up nose to tail. An adult person is about 3.7 times taller than that, and the cat's shoulder, at 23–25 cm, sits lower than the top of a 30 cm school ruler stood on end.
house_cat.massNarrative: An adult cat weighs about 4–5 kg — roughly as much as 45,000 worker honey bees, the population of a whole hive in midsummer.
house_cat.funFact: On Cyprus, archaeologists found a cat buried beside a person in a grave about 9,500 years old. Cyprus has no native wild cats, so people must have brought it across the sea by boat — the earliest known sign of cats living with humans, thousands of years before the cat-loving Egyptians.
house_cat.seoTitle: How Big Is a House Cat? Length, Height and Weight
house_cat.metaDescription: An adult house cat is about 46 cm long without its 30 cm tail, stands 23–25 cm at the shoulder and weighs 4–5 kg. See a cat's size compared to familiar things.

image.alt: A grey-brown striped tabby cat walking across bright snow, looking back over its shoulder with yellow-green eyes, its ringed tail raised.

facts.fact1: Head-and-body length: about 46 cm on average; the tail adds about 30 cm (about 76 cm in total).
facts.fact2: Shoulder height: about 23–25 cm; adult weight: typically 4–5 kg, males larger than females.
facts.fact3: It hears from about 55 Hz to 79 kHz; humans hear only 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
facts.fact4: It can see in one-sixth of the light humans need, thanks to the reflective tapetum lucidum behind the retina.
facts.fact5: Sleeps 12–16 hours a day, 13–14 hours on average.
facts.fact6: Pet cats now live about 13 years on average; the oldest on record, Creme Puff of Texas, lived 38 years and 3 days.

omega_centauri.name: Omega Centauri
omega_centauri.tagline: The Milky Way's biggest ball of stars — some 10 million suns, so far away that for centuries it was taken for a single star.
omega_centauri.body: Omega Centauri (NGC 5139) is the largest and most massive globular cluster of the Milky Way: a ball of roughly 10 million old stars about 150 light-years across, lying some 17,000 light-years away in the southern constellation Centaurus. Its stars are about 12 billion years old, yet they were not all born at once — and the cluster spins faster and is more flattened than an ordinary globular cluster. That is why many astronomers think it is really the stripped core of a small galaxy that the Milky Way swallowed long ago. From a dark southern site it is visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy "star" almost as wide as the full Moon.
omega_centauri.narrative: Centre Omega Centauri on the Sun and it would reach about 75 light-years out in every direction. In its crowded core the stars are on average only about 0.1 light-years apart — some 40 times closer than Proxima Centauri is to us. Light needs about 150 years to cross the whole cluster.
omega_centauri.funFact: Kapteyn's Star, a faint red dwarf only 13 light-years from Earth, is thought to have come from Omega Centauri — a refugee from the cluster's lost galaxy, now passing through our neighbourhood.
omega_centauri.seoTitle: How Big Is Omega Centauri? The Milky Way's Largest Cluster
omega_centauri.metaDescription: Omega Centauri is about 150 light-years across and 17,000 light-years away — the Milky Way's largest globular cluster, with some 10 million stars.

image.alt: Omega Centauri photographed from ESO's La Silla Observatory: a huge, dense ball of countless white, yellow and orange stars that glows brightest at its centre, against a black sky.

facts.fact1: Size: about 150 light-years across — the commonly quoted diameter of its bright part; its faint outer stars reach much further, and NASA quotes about 450 light-years.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 17,000 light-years; published estimates range from about 15,800 to 17,700.
facts.fact3: Roughly 10 million stars with about 4 million times the Sun's mass — some 10 times as massive as other big globular clusters.
facts.fact4: In 2024 Hubble found seven central stars moving too fast to stay unless a black hole of at least 8,200 Suns holds them — the best case yet for an "intermediate-mass" black hole, but not confirmed and questioned by later work.
facts.fact5: Its stars are about 12 billion years old but formed in several generations — a hint that it was once the heart of a small galaxy.
facts.fact6: Ptolemy listed it as a star nearly 2,000 years ago and Johann Bayer named it Omega Centauri in 1603; in 1677 Edmond Halley saw that it was not a star at all.

local_group.name: Local Group
local_group.tagline: Our home group of galaxies — the Milky Way, Andromeda and a swarm of dwarf galaxies held together by gravity.
local_group.body: The Local Group is the small family of galaxies the Milky Way belongs to. It spans roughly 10 million light-years and is dominated by two big spirals, the Milky Way and Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years apart; the smaller Triangulum Galaxy is the third spiral. Almost everything else — more than 100 known members, including the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds — is a dwarf galaxy, and faint new ones keep turning up. Edwin Hubble gave it its name in 1936. It is a galaxy group, not a cluster: the Virgo Cluster, about 54 million light-years away, holds over a thousand galaxies, and the Local Group sits on the outskirts of the supercluster that Virgo anchors.
local_group.narrative: If the Milky Way were a dinner plate 27 cm wide, the whole Local Group would fill a space about 25 metres across — a little longer than a tennis court — holding one other big plate (Andromeda), one side plate (Triangulum) and more than a hundred crumbs, most of them gathered around the two big plates.
local_group.massNarrative: The whole group weighs roughly 2 trillion Suns — and nearly all of that is the Milky Way and Andromeda, mostly in their unseen dark-matter halos.
local_group.funFact: When Edwin Hubble coined the name in 1936, he could list just eleven members, plus one maybe. Today 134 galaxies are known within about 3 million light-years of the group's centre — most of them dim dwarfs you can't see without a big telescope.
local_group.seoTitle: How Big Is the Local Group? Our Galaxy Neighbourhood
local_group.metaDescription: The Local Group is about 10 million light-years across: the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum and more than 100 smaller galaxies bound together by gravity.

image.alt: A top-down map of the Local Group: the Milky Way and its labelled satellite galaxies at upper right, Andromeda and Triangulum with theirs at lower left, on a black background.

facts.fact1: Size: about 10 million light-years across — but the edge is fuzzy, and published estimates go up to about 17 million (5.1 megaparsecs).
facts.fact2: Members: 134 known galaxies within about 3 million light-years of its centre (2025 count) — almost all of them dwarfs.
facts.fact3: Three spiral galaxies: Andromeda, the Milky Way and Triangulum (M33); the rest are dwarfs.
facts.fact4: Total mass: roughly 2 trillion Suns, nearly all of it in the Milky Way and Andromeda.
facts.fact5: Its centre of mass lies between the two big spirals, about 1.5 million light-years from us — a little closer to Andromeda.
facts.fact6: Future: a 2025 Hubble + Gaia study gives the Milky Way and Andromeda about a 50:50 chance of merging within the next 10 billion years.

local_group.insideNote: We're inside it — its centre is about 1.5 million light-years away, toward Andromeda

sloan_great_wall.name: Sloan Great Wall
sloan_great_wall.tagline: A chain of galaxies and superclusters some 1.4 billion light-years long — one of the largest patterns ever mapped.
sloan_great_wall.body: The Sloan Great Wall is one of the largest patterns ever mapped in the universe: a wall-like band of galaxies, galaxy groups and several superclusters about 1.37 billion light-years long, roughly a billion light-years from us in the direction of the constellations Hydra, Corvus and Centaurus. J. Richard Gott III, Mario Jurić and colleagues at Princeton announced it in 2003 after spotting it in data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey; by their measure it is about 80% longer than the Great Wall found in 1989, the previous record holder. Despite the name, it is not one object held together by gravity but a loose chain of superclusters that cosmic expansion is slowly pulling apart — some astronomers even argue it is a chance alignment of separate structures. Above about 1.2 billion light-years the universe is expected to look smooth (the "end of greatness"), and even larger claimed structures, such as the 3.3-billion-light-year Giant Arc, remain debated.
sloan_great_wall.narrative: If the Milky Way were a dinner plate 27 cm wide, the Sloan Great Wall would be a loose, patchy ribbon of plates about 3.5 km long — more than twice the length of our own supercluster, Laniakea, at that scale (about 1.4 km), yet still small next to the observable universe, a sphere some 240 km across.
sloan_great_wall.funFact: The light we see from the Sloan Great Wall set out about a billion years ago — some 400 million years before the first large animals appeared in Earth's seas.
sloan_great_wall.seoTitle: How Big Is the Sloan Great Wall? A Wall of Galaxies
sloan_great_wall.metaDescription: The Sloan Great Wall is a chain of galaxies about 1.37 billion light-years long and a billion light-years away — found in 2003, not bound by gravity.

image.alt: A 3D map of galaxies from the 2dF Galaxy Redshift Survey: two pale wedges of clumpy filaments on a dark background, with the Sloan Great Wall labelled as a long band down the left wedge.

facts.fact1: Length: about 1.37 billion light-years as measured by its discoverers.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 1 billion light-years (redshift 0.073), in the direction of Hydra, Corvus and Centaurus.
facts.fact3: Found in 2003 by J. Richard Gott III and Mario Jurić in Sloan Digital Sky Survey data — the most prominent feature of their logarithmic "Map of the Universe".
facts.fact4: About 80% longer than the CfA2 Great Wall of 1989 (Geller and Huchra), the previous record holder; other comparisons put it at 1.8 to 2.7 times as long.
facts.fact5: Not gravitationally bound: it is a chain of several superclusters, and only regions about 35 million light-years in radius at the hearts of the richest ones may be collapsing.
facts.fact6: Mass: at least about 3.5 × 10¹⁶ Suns, according to a 2016 lower limit.

saturn_v.name: Saturn V
saturn_v.seoTitle: How Tall Was the Saturn V? The 111 m Moon Rocket
saturn_v.tagline: 111 metres of rocket, nearly 3,000 tonnes at liftoff — the machine that carried astronauts to the Moon.
saturn_v.body: The Saturn V was the rocket NASA built to send astronauts to the Moon. Stacked with the Apollo spacecraft on top, it stood about 111 m (363 ft) tall and 10 m wide, and weighed roughly 2,800–2,970 tonnes fully fuelled — almost all of it propellant. It had three stages: the first, with five F-1 engines, burned for about two and a half minutes and pushed with some 34–35 meganewtons of thrust, then dropped away so the lighter upper stages could carry on. Thirteen Saturn Vs flew between 1967 and 1973; nine of them launched 24 astronauts toward the Moon, from Apollo 8 to Apollo 17, including Apollo 11 on 16 July 1969. Only a handful of rockets have ever lifted off with more thrust, among them NASA's SLS and SpaceX's Starship, which pushes more than twice as hard.
saturn_v.narrative: Stand a Saturn V next to the Statue of Liberty and the rocket is about 18 m taller — pedestal and torch included. Stood on end it matched a 36-storey building; laid on its side, it would be about as long as a football pitch.
saturn_v.massNarrative: Fully fuelled, a Saturn V weighed about 2,800 tonnes — as much as roughly 450 elephants. Its first stage alone held more than 2 million litres of kerosene and liquid oxygen, and burned through nearly all of it in about two and a half minutes.
saturn_v.funFact: The last Saturn V had only two stages: on 14 May 1973 it launched Skylab, America's first space station, which had been converted from a Saturn V third stage. And from Apollo 13 onwards, the spent third stages were deliberately crashed into the Moon so that seismometers left by earlier crews could feel the impacts and help map the Moon's interior.

image.alt: A white Saturn V rocket lifting off beside its red launch tower, flames and billowing clouds of exhaust at its base, under a deep blue sky.

facts.fact1: Height: about 111 m (363 ft) with the Apollo spacecraft on top; diameter 10 m.
facts.fact2: Mass at liftoff: about 2,800–2,970 tonnes, depending on the mission.
facts.fact3: Liftoff thrust: about 34–35 meganewtons (7.5–7.9 million pounds-force, depending on the flight), from five F-1 engines.
facts.fact4: 13 launches from 1967 to 1973; 24 astronauts sent toward the Moon on nine missions.
facts.fact5: Could send about 43.5 tonnes to the Moon.
facts.fact6: Three complete Saturn Vs are on display: in Huntsville, Houston and at the Kennedy Space Center.

saturn_v.metaDescription: The Saturn V stood about 111 m tall — 18 m taller than the Statue of Liberty — and weighed nearly 3,000 tonnes. The Apollo Moon rocket in numbers.

large_hadron_collider.name: Large Hadron Collider
large_hadron_collider.seoTitle: How Big Is the Large Hadron Collider? Size of CERN's LHC
large_hadron_collider.tagline: A 27-kilometre ring of magnets under Geneva, built to smash protons together and look inside matter.
large_hadron_collider.body: The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN is the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator: a ring about 26.7 km around, buried on average 100 m underground beneath the French–Swiss border near Geneva. Two beams of protons race around it in opposite directions, steered by 1,232 superconducting magnets chilled to 1.9 K (−271.3 °C) — colder than outer space. Where the beams cross, giant detectors record the debris of collisions at 13.6 TeV and use it to test the Standard Model. In 2012 two of them, ATLAS and CMS, discovered the Higgs boson this way. A machine 27 km around, built to study things far smaller than a proton.
large_hadron_collider.narrative: Walking once around the LHC ring would take you about five and a half hours. A proton does it 11,245 times every second — in one second it covers almost 300,000 km, about three-quarters of the way to the Moon.
large_hadron_collider.funFact: The ring is about 8.5 km across, yet what it studies is almost unimaginably small: by smashing protons together, the CMS experiment has shown that quarks, if they have any parts at all, must be smaller than about 10⁻²⁰ m — less than a hundred-thousandth of a proton's width. The biggest particle accelerator ever built is a microscope for the smallest things.
large_hadron_collider.metaDescription: CERN's Large Hadron Collider is a ring 26.7 km around, 100 m underground, where protons collide at 13.6 TeV — the machine that found the Higgs boson.

image.alt: The LHC tunnel at CERN: a long line of blue cylindrical superconducting magnets curving away into the distance beneath cable trays and lights.

facts.fact1: Circumference: about 26.7 km (26,659 m) — a ring about 8.5 km across.
facts.fact2: Depth: 50–175 m underground, about 100 m on average; the ring crosses the border between France and Switzerland.
facts.fact3: 1,232 superconducting dipole magnets, each 15 m long and weighing 35 tonnes, bend the beams around the ring.
facts.fact4: The magnets run at 1.9 K (−271.3 °C), colder than outer space, cooled by about 96 tonnes of superfluid helium.
facts.fact5: Collision energy: 13.6 TeV (two beams of 6.8 TeV each), during Run 3 (2022–2026).
facts.fact6: Protons reach about 99.999999% of the speed of light — only about 3 m/s slower than light — and lap the ring 11,245 times a second.
facts.fact7: First beam: 10 September 2008. In 2012 its ATLAS and CMS experiments discovered the Higgs boson.
facts.fact8: Switched off since the end of June 2026 for its biggest upgrade, the High-Luminosity LHC (about 10 times more collisions), planned to start running around mid-2030.

stonehenge.name: Stonehenge
stonehenge.tagline: A ring of giant stones about 30 metres across, raised on Salisbury Plain some 4,500 years ago and lined up with the midsummer sunrise.
stonehenge.body: Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain in southern England, was built and rebuilt over some 1,500 years. Around 3000 BC people dug a circular ditch and bank roughly 100–110 metres across and buried the cremated remains of their dead inside it; around 2500 BC they raised the stones at its centre: a circle of 30 sarsen uprights about 30 metres across, capped by a ring of lintels, around a horseshoe of five giant trilithons. The sarsens, about 25 tonnes each on average, came from West Woods some 25 km to the north, while the smaller bluestones were brought about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales. The monument's main axis points to the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset, so those days clearly mattered to its builders, but what it was for — a temple, a monument to the dead, a gathering place — is still debated, and claims that it worked as a precise astronomical calculator are speculation.
stonehenge.narrative: The sarsen circle is about 30 metres across, so a 25-metre blue whale would fit across it with a little room to spare. The earthwork ring around it is more than three times wider, and the tallest trilithon once stood about 7.3 metres high, taller than a two-storey house.
stonehenge.funFact: The builders shaped the stones the way a carpenter shapes timber: each lintel sits on knobs carved on top of the uprights (mortise and tenon joints), and neighbouring lintels slot together with tongue-and-groove joints. Even the lintels' faces were gently curved so the ring would look like one continuous band of stone.
stonehenge.seoTitle: How Big Is Stonehenge? Size of the Stone Circle
stonehenge.metaDescription: Stonehenge's sarsen circle is about 30 m across, inside an earthwork ring 100–110 m wide, and its sarsens weigh about 25 tonnes each. Size compared.

image.alt: The ruined sarsen circle of Stonehenge on green grass under a blue sky with white clouds, a row of lintels still resting on the upright stones.

facts.fact1: Sarsen circle: about 30 m across — 30 uprights capped by a ring of lintels.
facts.fact2: Surrounding ditch and bank: about 100–110 m across, dug around 3000 BC.
facts.fact3: Sarsens: about 25 tonnes each on average; the tallest trilithon stood about 7.3 m high.
facts.fact4: Bluestones: 2–5 tonnes each, brought about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales.
facts.fact5: Altar Stone: a 6-tonne sandstone slab; a 2024 study traced it to north-east Scotland, but a 2026 study concluded its exact source is still unknown.
facts.fact6: Part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, together with Avebury, since 1986.

absolute_zero.name: Absolute Zero
absolute_zero.seoTitle: What Is Absolute Zero? −273.15 °C and Why It's Out of Reach
absolute_zero.tagline: The coldest anything could ever be: −273.15 °C — a floor we can creep towards but never touch.
absolute_zero.body: Temperature is a measure of how hard the atoms and molecules in something are jiggling: cool them and they slow down. Absolute zero, 0 kelvin, is the point where they would have no energy left to give — exactly −273.15 °C, or −459.67 °F. The number is exact because the Celsius scale is defined as the kelvin scale shifted by exactly 273.15; since 20 May 2019 the kelvin itself has been defined by fixing the Boltzmann constant. Even there, quantum physics leaves atoms a tiny motion that can never be removed, called zero-point motion. And the third law of thermodynamics says the floor can never actually be reached: each cooling step takes away a smaller share of what is left, so getting to exactly zero would take infinitely many steps.
absolute_zero.narrative: Space is not the coldest it gets. The afterglow of the Big Bang keeps the whole universe at about 2.7 K, and the magnets of the Large Hadron Collider run colder still, at 1.9 K. The coldest natural place known, the Boomerang Nebula about 5,000 light-years away, sits at roughly 1 K. Laboratories beat all of them about a hundred billion times over: in 2026 atoms on China's Tiangong space station reached an effective temperature of about 10 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero.
absolute_zero.funFact: Helium refuses to freeze. Its atoms are so light and so weakly attracted to each other that their zero-point jiggling alone keeps them from locking into a crystal — at normal pressure helium stays liquid all the way down to absolute zero. Willem Keesom first made solid helium in 1926, and only by squeezing it.

image.alt: A 3D false-colour graph of three clouds of atoms: a broad red-and-yellow mound on the left, then sharp blue-and-white peaks rising as the gas turns into a Bose–Einstein condensate.

facts.fact1: 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F — exact by definition (the Celsius scale is the kelvin minus 273.15).
facts.fact2: Third law of thermodynamics (Walther Nernst, 1912): no process can reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps.
facts.fact3: The cosmic microwave background keeps empty space at about 2.7 K (−270.5 °C).
facts.fact4: The Boomerang Nebula, about 5,000 light-years away in Centaurus, is about 1 K — the coldest natural place known.
facts.fact5: The Large Hadron Collider's magnets run at 1.9 K (−271.3 °C), cooled by superfluid helium.
facts.fact6: First Bose–Einstein condensate: 5 June 1995 — about 2,000 rubidium atoms below 170 billionths of a kelvin (Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman, JILA).
facts.fact7: Lab record: an equivalent temperature of about 10 trillionths of a kelvin (about 10 pK) on the Tiangong space station, published in 2026; the previous record, 38 pK, came from a drop tower in Bremen in 2021.
facts.fact8: Guillaume Amontons guessed at a lowest temperature in 1703; in 1848 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a scale that starts from it.

absolute_zero.metaDescription: Absolute zero is exactly −273.15 °C, where atoms would stop jiggling. Why no lab can reach it, how close we get, and the coldest places in the universe.

uncertainty_principle.name: Uncertainty Principle
uncertainty_principle.seoTitle: What Is the Uncertainty Principle? Heisenberg Explained
uncertainty_principle.tagline: Pin down where a particle is and its motion blurs — not because we are clumsy, but because it is a wave.
uncertainty_principle.body: In 1927 Werner Heisenberg found that a particle's position and its momentum (mass times velocity) can never both be sharp at once: the spread in one multiplied by the spread in the other is never smaller than a tiny fixed amount, written Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2. It is often explained as clumsy measuring — the light you use to see an electron knocks it aside — and Heisenberg himself first argued that way, but that picture is misleading: even perfect instruments could not beat the limit. It comes from the fact that particles behave as waves. A wave squeezed into a short blip has to be built from many different wavelengths, and a wave with one clean wavelength has to stretch out far, so a particle simply does not have an exact position and an exact momentum at the same time. The same rule keeps atoms from collapsing: an electron squeezed closer to the nucleus would have to move ever more wildly, and the energy that costs holds it at a distance.
uncertainty_principle.narrative: The uncertainty principle has no size of its own — it is a rule about how sharply nature lets things be defined. Its limit is fixed and tiny, so it only bites in the micro world: confine an electron to the width of an atom and its speed becomes uncertain by hundreds of kilometres per second, while for a football the same limit is far too small ever to notice.
uncertainty_principle.funFact: Pin a 430-gram football's position down to a thousandth of a millimetre and the uncertainty principle forces its speed to be uncertain by about 10⁻²⁸ m/s. At that rate the ball would drift less than the width of a single atom in the entire 13.8-billion-year age of the universe.
uncertainty_principle.metaDescription: Why a particle can't have an exact position and speed at once — not clumsy measurement but waves — and why Heisenberg's principle keeps atoms from collapsing.

image.alt: The famous black-and-white photo of 29 physicists at the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels — Einstein and Marie Curie sit in the front row, and a young Heisenberg stands third from the right at the back.

facts.fact1: Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2, where ħ, the reduced Planck constant, is about 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds.
facts.fact2: Heisenberg published the idea in 1927; Earle Kennard proved its exact mathematical form later the same year.
facts.fact3: It holds for every kind of wave, not only quantum ones: a very short sound or radio pulse can't have one exact pitch either.
facts.fact4: Confined to an atom about 0.1 nm across, an electron's speed is uncertain by several hundred kilometres per second.
facts.fact5: Nothing can be perfectly still: even at absolute zero particles keep a 'zero-point' jiggle — which is why helium stays liquid at absolute zero unless squeezed under high pressure.
facts.fact6: A matching energy–time relation means short-lived states have blurred energies: excited atoms emit slightly spread-out colours, and fast-decaying particles have fuzzy masses.
facts.fact7: 'Virtual particles' that briefly borrow energy are a picture used in quantum field theory calculations, not something seen popping in and out.
facts.fact8: Heisenberg received the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics (awarded in 1933) for creating quantum mechanics.

house_mouse.name: House Mouse
house_mouse.tagline: About 8 cm of whiskers and fur that followed people from the first grain stores to every corner of the world.
house_mouse.body: The house mouse (Mus musculus) is a small rodent that has lived alongside people for so long that it is now found almost everywhere humans live. An adult measures about 7.5–10 cm from nose to the base of the tail, with a nearly hairless tail about as long again, and weighs only 11–30 g. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent; it reached the eastern Mediterranean about 15,000 years ago, feeding on the food stores of the first settled villages, and has since travelled with people around the globe. A female can raise 5 to 10 litters a year of about six pups each, which is why a few mice can become many so quickly. Bred in laboratories, the same species has become a mainstay of medical research, because its genes are remarkably close to ours.
house_mouse.narrative: Measured from nose to the base of the tail, an 8 cm mouse is a little shorter than a bank card (8.6 cm) and as long as about six honey bees lined up nose to tail. A house cat's body is nearly six mice long, and about 21 mice stacked nose to tail would reach the height of an adult person.
house_mouse.massNarrative: A mid-sized adult of about 20 g weighs as much as about 200 worker honey bees, or four sheets of ordinary printer paper. It would take roughly 200–250 mice to balance one house cat.
house_mouse.funFact: Male mice sing. When they smell a female, they produce songs of repeated phrases built from several kinds of syllables, at 30–110 kHz — far above the 20 kHz limit of human hearing. A cat, which hears up to about 79 kHz, can pick up much of the serenade that we never hear.
house_mouse.seoTitle: How Big Is a House Mouse? Length, Tail and Weight
house_mouse.metaDescription: An adult house mouse is about 7.5–10 cm long plus a tail about as long again, and weighs 11–30 g. See a mouse's size compared to familiar things.

image.alt: A grey-brown house mouse with large rounded ears, black eyes and a pink nose crouching on bright snow, its long pink tail curled beside it.

facts.fact1: Head-and-body length (nose to the base of the tail): about 7.5–10 cm; the tail adds another 5–10 cm.
facts.fact2: Adult weight: typically 11–30 g — a few large coins' worth.
facts.fact3: It can squeeze under a door gap only 6 mm (¼ inch) tall — about the width of a pencil — and through openings about 1 cm wide.
facts.fact4: At rest its heart beats about 550–725 times a minute, roughly eight times faster than a resting human heart.
facts.fact5: Mice and humans share virtually the same set of genes; on average, the protein-coding parts of the two genomes are 85% identical.
facts.fact6: Wild house mice usually live less than a year; in protected settings they often reach 2–3 years.

tarantula_nebula.name: Tarantula Nebula
tarantula_nebula.tagline: The biggest, brightest star factory near the Milky Way — a glowing web of gas in a neighbouring galaxy, home of the heaviest star known.
tarantula_nebula.body: The Tarantula Nebula, also called 30 Doradus, is a vast glowing cloud of gas and dust in the Large Magellanic Cloud, about 160,000 light-years away. It is nearly 1,000 light-years across, and its bright filaments stretch out like the legs of a spider — hence the name. It is the largest and brightest star-forming region in the Local Group, the family of galaxies that includes our own. At its heart sits a cluster of young stars only 1 to 2 million years old, including R136a1, the most massive star known. Even from a neighbouring galaxy it is visible to the naked eye from the southern hemisphere as a fuzzy patch.
tarantula_nebula.narrative: Centre the Tarantula Nebula on the Sun and it would reach about 500 light-years out in every direction — swallowing the Pleiades and millions of other stars. Some 40 Orion Nebulae would fit side by side across it, and light needs about 1,000 years to cross it from edge to edge.
tarantula_nebula.funFact: The Tarantula shines so fiercely that if it were as close to us as the Orion Nebula, it would stretch about 30° across the sky — as wide as 60 full Moons side by side — and its glow would cast shadows on the ground at night.
tarantula_nebula.seoTitle: How Big Is the Tarantula Nebula? Size of 30 Doradus
tarantula_nebula.metaDescription: The Tarantula Nebula is nearly 1,000 light-years across and 160,000 light-years away — the brightest star factory near the Milky Way, home of R136a1.

image.alt: Webb infrared mosaic of the heart of the Tarantula Nebula: a cavity of bright blue young stars surrounded by pale, wispy gas filaments and rust-red clouds of dust, against a dark star field.

facts.fact1: Size: nearly 1,000 light-years across — the width of its glowing gas in wide photographs, worked out from its size in the sky and its distance. Because its faint edges fade gradually, published figures range from about 650 to 1,860 light-years.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 160,000 light-years, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way; sources quote 160,000 to 170,000.
facts.fact3: The largest and brightest star-forming region in the Local Group of galaxies.
facts.fact4: R136a1, in the central cluster R136, is the most massive star known: recent estimates put it at about 200 times the Sun's mass (earlier ones reached over 300), and it shines millions of times brighter than the Sun.
facts.fact5: In 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a 340-light-year-wide patch of it and found tens of thousands of young stars that dust had hidden from earlier telescopes.
facts.fact6: Supernova 1987A, the closest supernova seen since the invention of the telescope, was seen exploding on its outskirts in February 1987.

small_magellanic_cloud.name: Small Magellanic Cloud
small_magellanic_cloud.tagline: The Milky Way's smaller companion galaxy — the faint cloud where astronomers found their ruler for the universe.
small_magellanic_cloud.body: The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way, about 200,000 light-years away and roughly 18,900 light-years across — a little more than half the width of its bigger neighbour, the Large Magellanic Cloud. From the southern hemisphere it looks like a faint, detached wisp of the Milky Way, about eight full Moons wide; it is named after Magellan, whose 1519–1522 voyage made the Clouds widely known in Europe, but Aboriginal Australians and Pacific islanders had known it long before. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt used pulsating stars in this cloud to discover the rule that lets astronomers measure the distances to other galaxies. The two Clouds tug at each other: a bridge of gas and young stars, the Magellanic Bridge, joins them, and a long trail of gas, the Magellanic Stream, follows them across more than 100° of the sky. Recent studies suggest the larger Cloud is slowly pulling the smaller one apart — and that what we see may really be two separate structures, one behind the other.
small_magellanic_cloud.narrative: If the Milky Way were a dinner plate 27 cm wide, the Small Magellanic Cloud would be a hazy biscuit about 5 cm across lying some 55 cm away — a little beyond the 9 cm Large Magellanic Cloud, while Andromeda would be almost 7 metres away.
small_magellanic_cloud.funFact: The ruler for measuring the universe was found here. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt noticed that, among 25 pulsating stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud, the brighter ones took longer to pulse. Since they all lie at about the same distance, once the rule was calibrated, any such star became a distance marker — the method Edwin Hubble later used to show that other galaxies lie far beyond our own.
small_magellanic_cloud.seoTitle: How Big Is the Small Magellanic Cloud? Size & Distance
small_magellanic_cloud.metaDescription: The Small Magellanic Cloud is about 18,900 light-years across and 200,000 light-years away — the dwarf galaxy where Leavitt found the key to cosmic distances.

image.alt: The Small Magellanic Cloud photographed through a telephoto lens from Cerro Pachón in Chile: a pale bluish-white cloud of stars dotted with pink star-forming regions, with the bright globular star cluster 47 Tucanae to its left, against a dense field of stars.

facts.fact1: Size: about 18,900 light-years across (5.78 kiloparsecs), measured to a standard brightness limit — a little more than half the width of the Large Magellanic Cloud.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 200,000 light-years (62.4 kiloparsecs), measured to about 2% with eclipsing double stars in 2020.
facts.fact3: Total mass about 7 billion times the Sun's, counting stars, gas and dark matter.
facts.fact4: Henrietta Leavitt catalogued 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds (1908) and in 1912 found the period–luminosity rule from 25 of them in this cloud.
facts.fact5: Visible to the naked eye (magnitude 2.7) in the constellation Tucana — about 4° across, eight times the Moon's width — from anywhere south of about 15° N.
facts.fact6: A 2024 study found two star-forming structures about 5 kiloparsecs (16,000 light-years) apart along our line of sight; a 2025 study of 7,426 stars suggests the Large Magellanic Cloud is pulling it apart.

electron.name: Electron
electron.seoTitle: What Is an Electron? The Particle Behind Electricity
electron.tagline: The first elementary particle ever found — and the one that runs your chemistry, your lights and your phone.
electron.body: The electron was the first elementary particle ever discovered: in 1897 J. J. Thomson showed that the glowing 'cathode rays' in a glass tube pumped almost empty of air were a stream of negatively charged particles more than a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom. Every atom holds its electrons around a tiny nucleus, and almost everything an atom does depends on them: chemical bonds are electrons shared or handed over between atoms, an electric current is electrons pushed along a wire, and the colours of a neon sign or a sodium streetlamp come from electrons jumping between energy levels. Every electron carries exactly the same charge and the same tiny mass — about 1/1836 of a proton's — plus a built-in spin that turns it into a minute magnet. Like every particle it also behaves as a wave, which is why the electrons in an atom spread into clouds instead of circling in orbits. As far as any experiment can tell, an electron has no size and no parts at all.
electron.narrative: No experiment has ever measured an electron's size. Collider data show it must be smaller than about 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ m — under a thousandth of a proton's width. Blow a proton up to the size of the Earth and an electron would still have to fit inside a town a few kilometres across; for all we know, it is a true point with no size at all.
electron.funFact: The electron is astonishingly round. If its charge were even slightly lopsided, it would shift its energy in a strong electric field — so in 2023 a team at JILA in Colorado watched electrons inside trapped hafnium fluoride molecular ions for exactly that shift, and saw none. In NIST's own comparison: if an electron were blown up to the size of the Earth, any bulge on it would have to be smaller than a single atom.
electron.metaDescription: The electron: the first particle ever discovered, the carrier of electricity and chemistry — and so small that no experiment has found any size of it.

image.alt: J. J. Thomson's 1897 cathode-ray tube: a long, clear glass tube with a round bulb at one end, a coil of copper-coloured wire around its middle and a metal electrode sealed into the other end, on a pale grey background.

facts.fact1: Charge: −1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb, exact by definition. Mass: 9.1093837139 × 10⁻³¹ kg (CODATA 2022).
facts.fact2: About 1,836 times lighter than a proton — and it seems never to decay: experiments show it lasts at least 6.6 × 10²⁸ years.
facts.fact3: J. J. Thomson announced the discovery on 30 April 1897 and won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physics. The name 'electron' was coined by George Johnstone Stoney in 1891, before the particle itself was found.
facts.fact4: No size has ever been detected: LEP collider data put its radius below 2.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ m (95% confidence). The 'classical electron radius' of 2.8 femtometres — bigger than a proton — is a length calculated from its charge and mass in pre-quantum physics, not a measured size.
facts.fact5: A current of one ampere means about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons passing a point every second.
facts.fact6: Spin ½, proposed by Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck in 1925, makes every electron a tiny magnet — the source of the pull of an ordinary fridge magnet.
facts.fact7: Its magnetic strength (g/2 = 1.00115965218059) has been measured to 0.13 parts per trillion, testing the Standard Model's most precise prediction to about one part in a trillion (2023).
facts.fact8: Fast electrons have far shorter waves than visible light, so electron microscopes can make out details smaller than an atom — under 0.05 nm, against about 200 nm for an ordinary light microscope.

wave_particle_duality.name: Wave–Particle Duality
wave_particle_duality.seoTitle: Wave–Particle Duality: Is Light a Wave or a Particle?
wave_particle_duality.tagline: Light and matter travel like waves and arrive like particles — every single time.
wave_particle_duality.body: For more than a century physicists argued over whether light is a wave or a stream of particles. Between 1801 and 1803 Thomas Young split a beam of light in two and saw bands of light and dark — waves adding up and cancelling out — but in 1905 Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by treating light as packets of energy, later called photons: light below a certain frequency frees no electrons from a metal however bright it is, while light above it does even when dim. In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that matter has waves too, and three years later electrons scattered off crystals in exactly the patterns waves would make. The clearest demonstration sends particles towards two slits one at a time: each arrives as a single dot, yet thousands of dots slowly build up a wave's striped pattern — as if the wave describing each particle went through both slits. That does not mean a particle flips between being a wave and being a tiny ball, and no conscious observer is involved: any device that records which slit was used wipes out the stripes. The experiments are settled; what they 'mean' is still argued over by rival interpretations of quantum mechanics.
wave_particle_duality.narrative: Wave–particle duality has no size of its own, but it decides where quantum behaviour can show. An object's matter wave is shorter the heavier and faster it is: for a 70-kilogram person walking at 1 m/s it is about 10⁻³⁵ m — shorter even than the Planck length — so a person will never spread out like a wave passing through a doorway. Experiments have still pushed the limit from electrons up to molecules of 2,000 atoms (2019) and sodium clusters of more than 7,000 atoms, about 8 nm across (2026).
wave_particle_duality.funFact: J. J. Thomson, the physicist most responsible for discovering the electron as a particle, had a son, George Paget Thomson, who shared the 1937 Nobel Prize for showing that electrons diffract like waves. Father and son were both right.
wave_particle_duality.metaDescription: Light and matter travel like waves but land like particles. How Young, Einstein, de Broglie and the double-slit experiment showed it, and what it doesn't mean.

image.alt: Four black-and-white panels from Akira Tonomura's 1989 Hitachi experiment: single electrons land as scattered white dots, and as tens of thousands pile up they form vertical light and dark stripes.

facts.fact1: Thomas Young described the interference of light to the Royal Society in 1801 and demonstrated it with sunlight in 1803.
facts.fact2: Einstein's 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics (awarded in 1922) was 'especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect' — not for relativity.
facts.fact3: Louis de Broglie proposed electron waves in his 1924 doctoral thesis and won the 1929 Nobel Prize for 'the wave nature of electrons'.
facts.fact4: In 1927 Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer, and independently George Paget Thomson, saw electrons diffract like waves; Davisson and Thomson shared the 1937 Nobel Prize.
facts.fact5: In 1909 G. I. Taylor still got interference stripes with light as faint as a candle a little over 1.6 km (a mile) away.
facts.fact6: In Tonomura's 1989 experiment there was never more than one electron in the apparatus at a time; the stripes took over 20 minutes to build up from about 140,000 dots.
facts.fact7: The same wave behaviour has been seen in C₆₀ 'buckyball' molecules (1999), molecules of up to 2,000 atoms (2019) and sodium clusters of over 7,000 atoms weighing more than 170,000 daltons (2026).
facts.fact8: The word 'photon' only came into use in 1926 — in 1905 Einstein had spoken of 'light quanta'.

mass_energy_equivalence.name: E = mc²
mass_energy_equivalence.seoTitle: What Does E = mc² Really Mean? Mass–Energy Equivalence
mass_energy_equivalence.tagline: Mass is energy — and the exchange rate is the speed of light, squared.
mass_energy_equivalence.body: In September 1905 Albert Einstein sent a three-page follow-up to his relativity paper, asking whether the inertia of a body depends on the energy it contains. His answer, now written E = mc², says that a body's mass is a measure of the energy it contains, and the conversion factor c² — the speed of light squared — is enormous: one kilogram corresponds to about 9 × 10¹⁶ joules. It is not only about bombs, and it is not really 'matter turning into energy': any energy a body holds adds to its mass. A 250 ml cup of tea heated from 20 °C to boiling gets heavier by about a billionth of a gram — far too little for any scale, but real. In nuclear reactions the effect becomes large: the products weigh slightly less than what went in, and the missing mass leaves as light, heat and fast-moving particles.
mass_energy_equivalence.narrative: E = mc² has no size; its scale is the exchange rate. One kilogram of mass is worth about 21 megatons of TNT — more than 1,400 Hiroshima bombs, while that bomb itself turned only about 0.7 grams of mass into energy. The Sun sheds about 4.26 million tonnes of mass every second as sunlight, yet even at that rate 4.6 billion years of shining add up to only around 0.03% of its mass.
mass_energy_equivalence.funFact: Einstein never wrote E = mc² in 1905. He called the energy L and the speed of light V, and concluded that a body giving off energy L as radiation loses mass L/V². He even suggested how to test it: with radium salts, whose energy content changes strongly as they decay.
mass_energy_equivalence.metaDescription: E = mc² says mass is energy: 1 kg equals about 21 megatons of TNT. What it really means, why a hot cup weighs more and how the Sun loses mass.

image.alt: A paragraph of old German print from Einstein's 1905 paper: if a body gives off energy L as radiation, its mass shrinks by L/V²; the mass of a body is a measure of its energy content; radium salts might put the theory to the test.

facts.fact1: The quarks inside a proton account for only about 1% of its mass; the rest is the energy of quarks and gluons in motion: in 2008 supercomputer calculations of quarks and gluons (lattice QCD) reproduced the proton's mass to within a few percent.
facts.fact2: c² ≈ 9 × 10¹⁶ joules per kilogram: 1 kg of mass equals about 21.5 megatons of TNT.
facts.fact3: The Hiroshima bomb (about 15 kilotons) converted only about 0.7 g of mass into energy.
facts.fact4: Fission of uranium-235 turns about 0.1% of the mass into energy, fusing hydrogen into helium in the Sun about 0.7%, and matter–antimatter annihilation 100%.
facts.fact5: The Sun loses about 4.26 million tonnes of mass every second as light.
facts.fact6: A charged phone battery (about 15 Wh) is heavier than a flat one by roughly 0.6 nanograms — 0.6 billionths of a gram.
facts.fact7: In 2005 teams at NIST and MIT tested E = mc² directly, comparing a nucleus's loss of mass with the energy of the gamma rays it gave off: the two agreed to better than 0.00004%.
facts.fact8: The full formula is E² = (pc)² + (mc²)², where p is momentum. E = mc² is the case of a body at rest; light has no mass, so all its energy comes from momentum: E = pc.

entropy.name: Entropy
entropy.seoTitle: What Is Entropy? The Arrow of Time Explained
entropy.tagline: Why ice melts, eggs never unscramble and time runs only one way: there are simply far more ways to be mixed up.
entropy.body: Entropy counts the ways. The atoms in anything — a cup of tea, a balloon of air — can be arranged in an enormous number of ways that look exactly the same from outside, and entropy measures how many: Ludwig Boltzmann's formula S = k log W says it is the logarithm of that number, W, scaled by a tiny constant, k. The second law of thermodynamics says the total entropy of an isolated system never goes down, and the reason is plain statistics: states that can happen in more ways are overwhelmingly more likely, so things drift towards them and stay there. That is why heat flows from hot tea into a cooler room, why a drop of ink spreads through water and why ice in a warm drink melts — nothing forbids the reverse, it is just absurdly improbable. Entropy is often called disorder, but that is a loose shorthand: when water freezes into neat snowflakes on a cold day, the heat it gives off raises the entropy of the surrounding air by more than the crystal lowers its own. Living things work the same way — they build order inside themselves by pushing even more entropy out, mostly as heat.
entropy.narrative: Almost every law of physics works just as well backwards: a film of two billiard balls colliding looks perfectly natural in reverse. A film of an egg smashing does not — and the second law is the reason, which is why it is often called the arrow of time. Why that arrow points the same way everywhere comes down to the beginning: the universe started, some 13.8 billion years ago, in a state of extraordinarily low entropy, and everything since has been the slow spending of that head start. Why it started that way — the assumption the philosopher David Albert called the 'past hypothesis' — is unexplained and genuinely open. The far end is less certain than it sounds, too: if dark energy keeps the universe expanding, entropy may creep towards a maximum, a cold, even 'heat death' in which nothing interesting happens any more — but not before the last black holes, as heavy as galaxies, have spent something like 10¹⁰⁰ years evaporating — and the whole picture rests on physics nobody has tested that far.
entropy.funFact: Boltzmann himself never wrote his equation quite the way it is carved on his grave. He developed the idea in the 1870s; Max Planck gave it today's form, S = k log W, around 1900, introducing the constant k that now bears Boltzmann's name. Boltzmann died in 1906, and the formula now stands in gilded letters above his bust in Vienna's Central Cemetery.
entropy.metaDescription: Entropy counts the ways atoms can be arranged. Why ice melts, eggs don't unscramble, life sheds heat — and why time seems to run only forwards.

image.alt: A white marble gravestone between two hedges: a bust of a bearded Ludwig Boltzmann on a pillar inscribed 'Ludwig Boltzmann 1844–1906', with the formula S = k log W carved in gilded letters above his head.

facts.fact1: Boltzmann's formula: S = k log W — entropy is the Boltzmann constant k (1.380649 × 10⁻²³ joules per kelvin) times the logarithm of W, the number of microscopic arrangements.
facts.fact2: Rudolf Clausius coined the word 'entropy' in 1865, from the Greek tropē, 'transformation', and summed it up: 'The entropy of the universe tends to a maximum.'
facts.fact3: Probability, not prohibition: the chance that 100 gas molecules in a box all happen to sit in its left half at once is 1 in 2¹⁰⁰ — about 1 in 10³⁰. For the trillions of trillions of molecules in a real room, it would not happen once in the age of the universe.
facts.fact4: The Sun's surface is over 20 times hotter than the 255 K at which Earth glows, so for every photon of sunlight Earth absorbs it sends about 20 infrared photons back to space — carrying away about 20 times the entropy.
facts.fact5: Erwin Schrödinger's 1944 book What Is Life? argued that living things survive by feeding on 'negative entropy' — keeping their order by exporting disorder.
facts.fact6: Information has entropy too: Rolf Landauer showed in 1961 that erasing one bit must release at least about 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ joules of heat at room temperature — a limit measured in the lab in 2012.
facts.fact7: The entropy of the observable universe is estimated at about 3 × 10¹⁰⁴ k — most of it locked in supermassive black holes (Chas Egan and Charles Lineweaver, 2010).
facts.fact8: Open question: why the universe began with such low entropy. Philosopher David Albert named this starting assumption the 'past hypothesis' in 2000; explanations such as cosmic inflation have been proposed, but none is settled.

ribosome.name: Ribosome
ribosome.tagline: A 25-nanometre machine that reads your genes and builds every protein in your body.
ribosome.body: A ribosome is the machine that builds proteins inside every living cell. It clamps onto a strand of messenger RNA, reads its genetic code three letters at a time and links the matching amino acids into a chain that folds into a protein — about 20 amino acids a second in a fast-growing bacterium, roughly 6 a second in mammalian cells. Ribosomes are about 20–30 nanometres across: the bacterial kind is around 20 nm and the larger kind in human cells 25–30 nm, so we use 25 nm, the figure given in the Nobel Prize materials. Each one has a small and a large subunit built from ribosomal RNA and dozens of proteins — and the key step, joining one amino acid to the next, is carried out by the RNA, not by the proteins. A growing human cell holds millions of ribosomes; a fast-growing E. coli bacterium has about 72,000, more than a third of its dry mass.
ribosome.narrative: A 25 nm ribosome is about 12 times wider than the DNA double helix (2 nm), and four of them side by side would span a 100 nm virus. About 300 would line up across a red blood cell (7.5 µm), and about 3,000 across the width of a human hair. If a ribosome were the size of a tennis ball, DNA would be about as thick as a drinking straw, a virus would be a bit bigger than a football, and a red blood cell would be 20 metres across.
ribosome.funFact: Biologists call the bacterial ribosome '70S' and its two halves '50S' and '30S' — yet 50 + 30 is not 70. The S stands for svedberg, a unit for how fast a particle sinks when spun in a centrifuge. That speed depends on shape as well as mass, so the numbers of the parts don't add up to the whole.
ribosome.seoTitle: How Big Is a Ribosome? Size of the Cell's Protein Factory
ribosome.metaDescription: A ribosome is about 20–30 nm across — 12 times wider than DNA, a quarter of a virus. See how the cell's protein factory compares with familiar things.

image.alt: A space-filling model of a bacterial (E. coli) ribosome on a white background: a lumpy, roughly oval cluster of thousands of tiny pink, grey and lavender spheres, each one an atom.

facts.fact1: Size: a bacterial ribosome is about 20 nm across; the larger ribosomes of human and other eukaryotic cells are 25–30 nm.
facts.fact2: Speed: about 20 amino acids per second in E. coli, 3–10 in yeast and about 6 in mouse cells — so a 300-amino-acid protein takes roughly 15 seconds in a bacterium and under a minute in a mammalian cell.
facts.fact3: Numbers: measurements in human HeLa cells give about 3–10 million ribosomes per cell; a fast-growing E. coli has about 72,000, which make up more than a third of its dry mass.
facts.fact4: A ribosome is a ribozyme — an RNA enzyme. No protein sits close to the spot where amino acids are joined; the ribosomal RNA does the chemistry, which hints that ribosomes may date back to an early 'RNA world'.
facts.fact5: First spotted in 1955 as tiny grains in electron micrographs by George Palade (Nobel Prize 1974), the ribosome was mapped atom by atom with X-ray crystallography by Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, Thomas Steitz and Ada Yonath — Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2009.
facts.fact6: Many antibiotics — tetracyclines, macrolides, aminoglycosides such as gentamicin — work by jamming bacterial ribosomes. Ours are built differently enough that these drugs leave them largely alone.

el_castillo.name: El Castillo at Chichén Itzá
el_castillo.tagline: A 30-metre Maya pyramid in Mexico whose staircases add up to 365 steps — and down which a serpent of sunlight crawls around the equinoxes.
el_castillo.body: El Castillo (“the Castle”), also called the Temple of Kukulcán after the Maya feathered-serpent god, rises over the centre of Chichén Itzá on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Nine sloping terraces make a stepped pyramid about 24 metres high with a base about 55.5 metres square, and a temple on top brings it to about 30 metres. A stairway climbs each of the four sides; the balustrades of the north stair end in carved serpent heads at the bottom. The building we see probably dates from around AD 900–1000, when Chichén Itzá was a leading city of the northern Maya and shared feathered-serpent imagery with central Mexico — how strong that “Toltec” link was is still debated. It was built over an older pyramid, found inside it in the 1930s, and 2016 scans detected a third, smaller one inside that.
el_castillo.narrative: At about 30 metres, El Castillo is roughly as tall as a 10-storey building — under a quarter of the height of the Great Pyramid. Giza's pyramid, at 139 metres, is about 4.6 times taller and its base is about four times wider (230 m against 55.5 m) — about 17 El Castillos would fit side by side on its footprint. Stonehenge's sarsen circle, 30 metres across, would fit on El Castillo's base almost twice over.
el_castillo.funFact: Clap your hands at the foot of the north stair and the echo comes back as a short falling chirp, which some people compare with the call of the quetzal, a sacred bird to the Maya. Acoustic studies explain it: each step reflects the sound a fraction of a second after the one below it, so the regular staircase works like a diffraction grating for sound. Whether the Maya designed it on purpose is unknown — that idea is speculation.
el_castillo.seoTitle: How Tall Is El Castillo at Chichén Itzá?
el_castillo.metaDescription: El Castillo at Chichén Itzá is about 30 m tall with its temple, on a 55.5 m base: a 365-step Maya pyramid under a quarter the height of Giza's.

image.alt: El Castillo at Chichén Itzá in bright daylight: a grey stone stepped pyramid with two steep stairways climbing to a square temple on top, under a blue sky with white clouds, a few tourists on the lawn at its base.

facts.fact1: Height: about 30 m to the top of the summit temple — about 24 m of stepped pyramid plus a temple about 6 m tall.
facts.fact2: Base: about 55.5 m on each side, built as nine sloping terraces with a stairway on each of the four sides.
