facts.fact3: Each stairway is usually counted at 91 steps: 4 × 91 = 364, and with the top platform as the last step, 365 — the days of the Maya solar year (Haabʼ). The south stair is eroded, so the total relies partly on the restored sides.
facts.fact4: On afternoons around the equinoxes, the stepped corner casts seven triangles of light on the north stair's balustrade, joining the stone serpent head at its foot; INAH researchers record seven triangles from about 15 to 25 March. The effect is real, but it lasts for weeks and changes all year, so whether the builders planned it is debated.
facts.fact5: Inside: 1930s excavations found an older pyramid with a temple holding a Chac Mool statue (1935) and a red-painted jaguar throne (1936). In 2016 electrical-resistivity scans by INAH and UNAM detected a third, about 10 m tall, probably built around AD 500–800.
facts.fact6: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of Chichén Itzá since 1988. Visitors have not been allowed to climb it since 2006.

antikythera_mechanism.name: Antikythera Mechanism
antikythera_mechanism.tagline: A shoebox-sized bronze calculator of the sky, more than 2,000 years old, pulled from an ancient shipwreck.
antikythera_mechanism.body: In 1900 sponge divers from the island of Symi found an ancient shipwreck 45 metres down off the Greek island of Antikythera, and in 1900–1901 they and the Greek navy brought up statues, pottery, coins — and a corroded lump of bronze and wood that turned out to hold gear wheels. The ship sank around 70–60 BC; the mechanism itself is usually dated to the 2nd century BC (the National Archaeological Museum in Athens says probably 150–100 BC), though the exact date is still debated. Today it survives as 82 fragments with 30 bronze gears, 27 of them in the largest piece, Fragment A — only about a third of the original machine. Turned by a hand crank, it showed the positions of the Sun and Moon, the Moon's phase and even the Moon's changing speed across the sky, using a clever pin-and-slot pair of gears; dials on the back followed the 19-year Metonic calendar, predicted eclipses with the 18-year saros cycle and counted the four-year cycle of the Olympic and other Panhellenic games. Inscriptions show that it also displayed the five planets known in antiquity, but almost nothing of that gearing survives (one gear in Fragment D may belong to it, which is debated): the planetary gearing in every model, including the 2021 University College London reconstruction, is a modern reconstruction.
antikythera_mechanism.narrative: The wooden case that held the gears is thought to have been about 33–34 cm long, 18 cm wide and 9–10 cm deep — roughly the size of a shoebox and a little longer than a 30 cm school ruler. A house cat's body, at 46 cm, is about 1.4 times longer, and an adult person is about five cases tall. The largest surviving piece, Fragment A, is about 18 cm across, a little more than half the length of the case, and its biggest gear, about 13 cm wide, is one and a half times the length of a bank card.
antikythera_mechanism.funFact: For about a year after it reached the museum in Athens, nobody noticed it: staff were busy with the shipwreck's bronze and marble statues, and only in 1902 was a gear wheel spotted in the lump of corroded bronze. Nothing of similar mechanical complexity is known again for more than a thousand years, until the astronomical clocks of medieval Europe.
antikythera_mechanism.seoTitle: How Big Was the Antikythera Mechanism?
antikythera_mechanism.metaDescription: The Antikythera mechanism, a 2,000-year-old Greek bronze calculator, sat in a case about 33 cm long; 82 fragments and 30 gears survive. Size compared.

image.alt: Fragment A of the Antikythera mechanism: a flat, roughly square slab of corroded green and dark bronze in a clear display mount, with the outline of a large four-spoked gear wheel visible in its centre.

facts.fact1: Original case: about 33–34 cm long, 18 cm wide and 9–10 cm deep — an estimate, since only fragments survive.
facts.fact2: Surviving today: 82 fragments with 30 bronze gears, 27 of them in Fragment A.
facts.fact3: Fragment A, the largest piece: about 18 cm across (180 × 150 mm) and 369.1 g.
facts.fact4: Largest gear: about 13 cm across, originally with about 223 teeth.
facts.fact5: Made probably around 150–100 BC (proposals range from about 205 BC to 87 BC); the ship sank around 70–60 BC.
facts.fact6: Found in 1900–1901 by sponge divers 45 m down; X-ray CT scans in 2005 revealed hidden gears and thousands of text characters.

nebra_sky_disc.name: Nebra Sky Disc
nebra_sky_disc.tagline: A bronze disc about 31 cm across, inlaid with a gold Sun or full Moon, a crescent Moon and a cluster of stars: the oldest known concrete picture of the sky.
nebra_sky_disc.body: The Nebra Sky Disc is a hammered bronze plate about 31 centimetres across, now green with patina, with gold shapes set into it: a large circle (the Sun or a full Moon), a crescent Moon and 32 small stars, seven of them packed into a tight cluster that most researchers read as the Pleiades. Later someone added two gold arcs on opposite edges; each spans about 82°, which matches how far the setting (or rising) Sun travels along the horizon between midwinter and midsummer at the latitude where it was found. A third arc at the bottom, usually read as a ship carrying the Sun across the sky, was added after that. It was buried around 1600 BC on the Mittelberg hill near Nebra in Germany, together with two swords, axes, a chisel and spiral armbands. It is widely regarded as the oldest known concrete picture of the sky. Some readings go further — for example, that the crescent beside the Pleiades encodes a rule for when to add a 13th month to keep a lunar calendar in step with the seasons — but these are interpretations, not proven.
nebra_sky_disc.narrative: At about 31 cm across, the disc is almost exactly the size of a 12-inch vinyl record, and it weighs about 2 kg. Four house mice lined up nose to tail would just about span it. The stone circle of Stonehenge, raised some 700–900 years earlier and also aligned with the solstices, is about 30 metres across — roughly a hundred times wider.
nebra_sky_disc.funFact: The disc was looted before archaeologists ever saw it. Two metal-detectorists dug it up in July 1999, and it passed through dealers until February 2002, when state archaeologist Harald Meller posed as a buyer in a hotel in Basel, Switzerland, and the Swiss police seized it. The sellers had been asking 700,000 Deutsche marks.
nebra_sky_disc.seoTitle: How Big Is the Nebra Sky Disc? Size, Age and Meaning
nebra_sky_disc.metaDescription: The Nebra Sky Disc is a bronze and gold plate about 31 cm across, buried around 1600 BC: the oldest known concrete picture of the sky. Size compared.

image.alt: The Nebra Sky Disc on a black background: a round green-patinated bronze plate with a large gold disc, a gold crescent, scattered gold dots including a tight cluster of seven, a gold arc along the right edge, an empty groove where the left arc was, and a curved gold boat shape at the bottom.

facts.fact1: Diameter: about 31 cm (published figures range from 30 to 32 cm); weight about 2 kg; 4.5 mm thick at the centre, thinning to 1.7 mm at the rim.
facts.fact2: Gold inlays at first: a large disc, a crescent and 32 small stars, seven of them in a cluster usually identified as the Pleiades.
facts.fact3: The two horizon arcs each span about 82° — the angle between the midsummer and midwinter sunsets (or sunrises) on the horizon at about 51° north, where it was found. The left arc was already missing when the disc was buried.
facts.fact4: Buried around 1600 BC: birch bark from a sword hilt in the same hoard is radiocarbon-dated to about 1600–1560 BC. The disc itself may have been made a century or two earlier.
facts.fact5: Looted from the Mittelberg hill near Nebra in July 1999; recovered in a police sting in Basel on 23 February 2002.
facts.fact6: The copper matches ore from the Mitterberg in Austria, and the gold matches gold from the River Carnon in Cornwall.
facts.fact7: A 2020 paper argued it belongs to the Iron Age, centuries later; a team of 13 researchers rejected this the same year, citing the radiocarbon date, metal isotopes, soil from the find spot and the Bronze Age ship motif.
facts.fact8: Added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in June 2013; on show at the State Museum of Prehistory in Halle.

newgrange.name: Newgrange
newgrange.tagline: An 85-metre mound in Ireland's Boyne Valley, built around 3200 BC so that the midwinter sunrise would shine into its heart.
newgrange.body: Newgrange is a great round mound in Ireland's Boyne Valley, 8 km west of the town of Drogheda, built by Neolithic farmers around 3200 BC — some 600–700 years before the Great Pyramid and the stone circle at Stonehenge. It is about 85 metres across and 11–13 metres high, ringed at its foot by 97 large kerbstones, many carved with spirals and other patterns. From the entrance a 19-metre stone passage leads to a cross-shaped chamber under a corbelled stone roof about 6 metres high, where the bones of the dead were laid. Above the doorway sits a small opening, the roof-box: on the mornings around the winter solstice the rising Sun shines through it, along the passage and onto the chamber floor for about 17 minutes. So few people fit inside that places are drawn by lottery, with tens of thousands applying each year for a few dozen spots. The gleaming white quartz wall at the front is a modern reconstruction from the 1960s–70s based on Michael O'Kelly's excavation, and archaeologists still argue over whether the quartz originally stood as a wall or lay as a platform on the ground.
newgrange.narrative: At 85 metres across, Newgrange is almost three times the width of Stonehenge's sarsen circle (30 m), though it would still fit inside the ditch-and-bank ring around Stonehenge (100–110 m). General Sherman, the biggest tree on Earth (83.8 m tall), laid on its side would almost span the mound, and three and a half blue whales nose to tail would reach across it. At about 12 metres high it is as tall as a four-storey building — yet the Great Pyramid is more than ten times taller. The passage and chamber together reach only 24 metres in, about a quarter of the way across: most of the mound is solid stone and earth.
newgrange.funFact: Was the sunbeam planned or a lucky accident? In 1989 the astronomer Tom Ray measured the roof-box and passage and calculated the sky of 5,000 years ago, when Earth's axis was tilted slightly more. Today the light enters a few minutes after sunrise; back then it would have arrived with the very first rays of the rising Sun — strong evidence that the builders aimed it on purpose.
newgrange.seoTitle: How Big Is Newgrange? Size of Ireland's Solstice Tomb
newgrange.metaDescription: Newgrange is 85 m across and 11–13 m high, built around 3200 BC — older than Stonehenge's stones and the Great Pyramid. Size and solstice sunbeam explained.

image.alt: The great round mound of Newgrange seen across a wide green lawn under a blue sky with white clouds: a grassy dome above a long, curving wall of white quartz stones, with the dark entrance in the middle, large standing stones in front and a few visitors walking past.

facts.fact1: Mound: about 85 m across at its widest (the kerb ring varies from 79 to 85 m) and 11–13 m high, covering roughly half a hectare (about 5,000 m²).
facts.fact2: Age: built around 3200 BC (some estimates say about 3100 BC) — about 600–700 years before Stonehenge's sarsen circle (around 2500 BC) and the Great Pyramid (around 2560 BC).
facts.fact3: Inside: a 19-metre passage leads to a cross-shaped chamber with three side recesses under a corbelled roof about 6 m high; passage and chamber together are 24 m long.
facts.fact4: Midwinter Sun: on about 19–23 December, sunlight enters through the roof-box above the entrance and lights the chamber floor for about 17 minutes, starting around 9 am. It was first observed in modern times by Michael O'Kelly on 21 December 1967.
facts.fact5: Stone: 97 kerbstones, from about 1.7 to 4.5 m long, ring the base; the white quartz came from the Wicklow Mountains about 50 km to the south, and the dark rounded cobbles from the Mourne Mountains about 50 km to the north.
facts.fact6: Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Brú na Bóinne since 1993, together with the passage tombs of Knowth and Dowth; the Boyne Valley holds the largest collection of megalithic art in Western Europe.

pillars_of_creation.name: Pillars of Creation
pillars_of_creation.tagline: Three towers of cold gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, slowly worn away by starlight while new stars form inside them.
pillars_of_creation.body: The Pillars of Creation are three columns of cold gas and dust inside the Eagle Nebula (M16), about 6,500 light-years away in the constellation Serpens. The tallest, on the left, is about 4 light-years from base to tip. Hubble photographed them on 1 April 1995 in what became one of the most famous space images ever, revisited them in 2014 with a sharper camera, and in 2022 the James Webb Space Telescope looked through the dust in near-infrared light and showed young stars inside and around them. The pillars are being eroded: ultraviolet light from hot, massive stars nearby heats their surface and boils the gas off into space, a process called photoevaporation. Denser knots resist longer, and some of them are collapsing into new stars.
pillars_of_creation.narrative: Stand the left pillar on the Sun and its tip would reach about 4 light-years out — almost to Proxima Centauri, our nearest star, 4.24 light-years away. Light needs about four years to climb it from base to tip. Even so it is a small cloud by nebula standards: the Crab Nebula is nearly three times as long, and six such pillars laid end to end would just span the Orion Nebula.
pillars_of_creation.funFact: In 2007 a team using the Spitzer Space Telescope suggested that a supernova blast may have already destroyed the pillars about 6,000 years ago — so — taking their distance as 7,000 light-years, as that study did — we would not see them fall for roughly another 1,000 years. It is a popular story, but it was never confirmed: another astronomer argued that a supernova would leave stronger radio and X-ray signals than are seen, and that winds from massive stars could have heated the dust instead.
pillars_of_creation.seoTitle: How Big Are the Pillars of Creation? Size and Distance
pillars_of_creation.metaDescription: The tallest Pillar of Creation is about 4 light-years high, 6,500 light-years away in the Eagle Nebula — a star nursery shot by Hubble in 1995 and Webb in 2022.

image.alt: Hubble's 2014 view of the Pillars of Creation: three tall, dark brown columns of gas and dust with glowing golden edges rise against a blue-green haze dotted with bright stars.

facts.fact1: Height: the tallest (left) pillar is about 4 light-years from base to tip; NASA's 2015 release describes the pillars as about 5 light-years tall.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 6,500 light-years (2,000 parsecs) in the constellation Serpens; other estimates range from about 5,700 to 7,000.
facts.fact3: Hubble's first image, taken on 1 April 1995 by Jeff Hester and Paul Scowen, was assembled from 32 exposures on the four detectors of its WFPC2 camera.
facts.fact4: Hubble revisited them in 2014 with its newer Wide Field Camera 3; the sharper image was released in January 2015 for Hubble's 25th anniversary.
facts.fact5: Webb's NIRCam image (October 2022) shows red, newly formed stars at the pillars' edges, estimated to be only a few hundred thousand years old.
facts.fact6: The finger-like knots at the pillar tips are each larger than our Solar System; the name comes from a phrase in an 1857 sermon by Charles Spurgeon.

kuiper_belt.name: Kuiper Belt
kuiper_belt.tagline: A broad ring of icy worlds beyond Neptune — home of Pluto and of leftovers from the birth of the planets.
kuiper_belt.body: The Kuiper Belt is a wide, doughnut-shaped ring of icy bodies circling the Sun beyond Neptune, from about 30 to 50 astronomical units out (4.5 to 7.5 billion km), so measured across its outer edge it is roughly 15 billion km wide. It holds Pluto and the dwarf planets Haumea and Makemake, more than 100,000 objects larger than 100 km and probably millions of smaller ones — leftovers from the birth of the Solar System, made of rock and frozen water, methane and ammonia at about 50 K (−223 °C). Overlapping its outer edge is the scattered disc: bodies that Neptune flung onto long, tilted orbits reaching hundreds of AU, among them Eris, almost exactly Pluto's size but 27% heavier. After Pluto (1930) and its moon Charon (1978), the next member was found only in 1992, when David Jewitt and Jane Luu spotted 1992 QB1 — now named Albion — from Mauna Kea after five years of searching. In 2019 NASA's New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, a reddish, 35-km 'snowman' 6.4 billion km from Earth and the most distant object ever explored up close.
kuiper_belt.narrative: Measured across its outer edge, the Kuiper Belt is about 100 AU wide — some 16 times the width of the asteroid belt and two-thirds wider than Neptune's orbit. Shrink the Sun–Earth distance to one metre and the belt becomes a ring 30 to 50 metres from the Sun, about 100 metres across — the length of a football pitch — with Pluto a speck a fifth the width of a human hair. On the same scale the Oort cloud would reach 100 km out. Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach the belt's inner edge and 7 hours to reach its outer edge; New Horizons needed nine and a half years to get to Pluto and 13 to reach Arrokoth.
kuiper_belt.massNarrative: For all its size, the belt is light. The best current estimate (2018, from its pull on the planets) is about 2% of Earth's mass — roughly one and a half Moons — and NASA puts the upper limit at about 10%. That is still around 50 times the mass of the asteroid belt. Models suggest the region once held 7 to 10 Earth masses, and that the shifting orbits of the giant planets scattered nearly all of it away.
kuiper_belt.funFact: The belt is named after Gerard Kuiper, who in 1950–51 described icy bodies forming 38–50 AU from the Sun — but he assumed that Pluto, then thought to be far more massive, had long since scattered them away, so if he had been right there would be no Kuiper Belt today. Kenneth Edgeworth had suggested a similar reservoir in 1943, which is why some astronomers say 'Edgeworth–Kuiper belt', and David Jewitt, one of its discoverers, gives most credit to Julio Fernández, who in 1980 predicted a belt of comets beyond Neptune.
kuiper_belt.seoTitle: How Big Is the Kuiper Belt? Its Size Beyond Neptune
kuiper_belt.metaDescription: The Kuiper Belt circles the Sun 30–50 AU out, about 15 billion km across — home of Pluto, Haumea and Arrokoth. Its size, mass and discovery explained.

image.alt: Arrokoth, a reddish Kuiper Belt object made of two joined lobes like a flattened snowman, in a colour composite from NASA's New Horizons flyby on 1 January 2019.

facts.fact1: Extends from Neptune's orbit at about 30 AU to about 50 AU from the Sun (4.5–7.5 billion km).
facts.fact2: Across its outer edge: about 100 AU, or 15 billion km. The scattered disc beyond reaches about 1,000 AU.
facts.fact3: More than 100,000 objects larger than 100 km are thought to exist; over 2,000 had been found by 2018.
facts.fact4: Total mass: about 2% of Earth's (2018 estimate); NASA gives an upper limit of about 10%.
facts.fact5: Dwarf planets: Pluto (2,377 km), Haumea (about 2,100 km long, spinning in under 4 hours) and Makemake (about 1,430 km); Eris (2,326 km) orbits in the scattered disc.
facts.fact6: First found after Pluto and Charon: 1992 QB1 (Albion, roughly 110–170 km across), discovered by David Jewitt and Jane Luu on 30 August 1992.
facts.fact7: Arrokoth, passed by New Horizons on 1 January 2019, is about 35 km long — the most distant object ever explored up close.
facts.fact8: Most short-period (Jupiter-family) comets are thought to come from the scattered disc, the belt's restless outer part.

cosmic_microwave_background.name: Cosmic Microwave Background
cosmic_microwave_background.tagline: The oldest light we can see: a faint microwave glow from every direction, 2.7 degrees above absolute zero.
cosmic_microwave_background.body: The cosmic microwave background is a faint glow of microwaves that reaches us from every direction in the sky, day and night. In the Big Bang model it is light set free about 380,000 years after the beginning, when the universe had cooled to roughly 3,000 K and electrons and nuclei joined into the first atoms — before that, light could not get far without bouncing off a free electron, much as it cannot pass through thick fog. Since then the expansion of space has stretched that light about 1,100 times, from near-infrared into microwaves, and cooled it to 2.7255 K. Its spectrum is the most perfect black-body curve ever measured, and its temperature is the same all over the sky to about 1 part in 100,000. Those tiny ripples, mapped in ever finer detail by the COBE, WMAP and Planck satellites, are the imprint of slightly denser and thinner regions that gravity later grew into galaxies and galaxy clusters. Reading them lets cosmologists measure the age of the universe and what it is made of — though a few puzzles in the data are still open.
cosmic_microwave_background.narrative: The cosmic microwave background has no size of its own: it fills all of space, about 411 of its photons in every cubic centimetre around you. What we see comes from a shell around us. The matter that gave off this light is now about 45.7 billion light-years away, almost at the edge of the observable universe — but when the light set out, it was only about 42 million light-years from the matter that would become our galaxy, around 17 times the distance to Andromeda today. At 2.7 K the glow is far colder than Pluto (about 44 K), yet the magnets of the Large Hadron Collider run colder still, at 1.9 K. When the light was released, it was about 3,000 K — roughly as hot as the surface of the red dwarf Proxima Centauri.
cosmic_microwave_background.massNarrative: There are about 1.6 billion of these photons for every proton or neutron in the universe. Each one carries so little energy, though, that all of them together now make up only about 0.005% of the universe's total energy.
cosmic_microwave_background.funFact: Penzias and Wilson found the glow by accident, but others were searching for it on purpose. Not far away, at Princeton University, Robert Dicke's group was building a receiver to hunt for exactly this glow when a phone call came from Bell Labs about an unexplained hiss. After hanging up, Dicke reportedly told his team: "Boys, we've been scooped." Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman had predicted such a background back in 1948, putting it at about 5 K, but for years almost nobody went looking.
cosmic_microwave_background.seoTitle: What Is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB)?
cosmic_microwave_background.metaDescription: The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light we can see, released 380,000 years after the Big Bang and now a 2.7 K microwave glow. What it tells us.

image.alt: WMAP's nine-year all-sky map of the cosmic microwave background: a wide oval on black, mottled with dark and light blue, green, yellow and a few red specks marking tiny temperature differences.

facts.fact1: Temperature: 2.72548 ± 0.00057 K — about −270.4 °C (Fixsen 2009).
facts.fact2: Released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang at roughly 3,000 K; since then its wavelengths have been stretched about 1,100 times (redshift z ≈ 1,090).
facts.fact3: Brightest at around 160 GHz — wavelengths of about 1–2 mm. Space holds about 411 of its photons in every cubic centimetre.
facts.fact4: Discovered in 1964–65 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs, who measured an unexplained 3.5 K of extra noise; Nobel Prize in Physics 1978.
facts.fact5: Its temperature differs across the sky by only about 1 part in 100,000. COBE first detected these ripples in 1992 — Nobel Prize 2006 for John Mather and George Smoot — and WMAP (launched 2001) and Planck (2009) mapped them in finer detail.
facts.fact6: From the ripples, Planck (2018) finds an age of about 13.8 billion years and a universe of about 4.9% ordinary matter, 26% dark matter and 69% dark energy (often rounded to 5 / 27 / 68).
facts.fact7: The Sun moves at about 370 km/s relative to this glow, so the sky ahead of us looks about 0.1% warmer than average and the sky behind about 0.1% cooler.
facts.fact8: Still open: the Hubble tension — the expansion rate inferred from the CMB (67.4 km/s per megaparsec) is about 8% lower than nearby measurements (about 73) — and large-scale oddities such as an unusually big "cold spot", which Planck confirmed and which still has no agreed explanation.

trappist_1.name: TRAPPIST-1
trappist_1.tagline: A red dwarf barely wider than Jupiter, circled by seven Earth-sized rocky planets — a whole planetary system that would fit well inside Mercury's orbit.
trappist_1.body: TRAPPIST-1 is a small, cool red dwarf star about 40.7 light-years away in the constellation Aquarius — only about a fifth wider than Jupiter, but some 94 times heavier. It is famous for its planets: in February 2017 astronomers announced seven Earth-sized worlds passing in front of it, the most Earth-sized planets known around a single star. All seven appear to be rocky, and all orbit closer to their star than Mercury orbits the Sun, taking just 1.5 to 19 days per lap; they are probably tidally locked, with one side always facing the star. Three of them — e, f and g — are usually placed in the habitable zone, where liquid water could exist on the surface if the planet has a suitable atmosphere (some studies count d as well). Whether any of them has an atmosphere at all is still an open question: the James Webb Space Telescope has found no sign of a thick, Earth-like atmosphere on b, c or d (a hazy carbon-dioxide atmosphere on b is not ruled out), and its first results for e, in the habitable zone, are inconclusive. The star itself is thought to be about 7.6 billion years old — older than the Sun — and will keep shining for trillions of years.
trappist_1.narrative: At about 166,000 km across, TRAPPIST-1 is about 13 Earths wide and only about 20% wider than Jupiter; the Sun is more than eight times wider, and even Proxima Centauri (214,000 km) is a bit bigger. Its planets are packed in just as tightly. The outermost, h, orbits about 9.3 million km from the star, while Mercury orbits the Sun at about 58 million km — so Mercury's orbit is more than six times wider than the entire TRAPPIST-1 system. The innermost planet, b, circles only about 4.5 times as far from its star as the Moon is from Earth, and its year lasts about 36 hours.
trappist_1.massNarrative: TRAPPIST-1 holds about 9% of the Sun's mass — some 94 Jupiters — in a ball only about 20% wider than Jupiter. On average that is about 75 grams per cubic centimetre: roughly 50 times the Sun's average density and more than six times that of lead. Stars this small use their hydrogen so slowly that TRAPPIST-1 is expected to keep shining for about ten trillion years, some 700 times the present age of the universe.
trappist_1.funFact: Standing on TRAPPIST-1e, you would see the star about four times as wide as the Sun looks from Earth, but much dimmer and a deep orange-red. And because the planets are packed so close together, a neighbouring planet would often look bigger in the sky than the full Moon does from Earth.
trappist_1.seoTitle: How Big Is TRAPPIST-1? The Star With Seven Planets
trappist_1.metaDescription: TRAPPIST-1: a red dwarf about 20% wider than Jupiter, 40.7 light-years away, with seven Earth-sized rocky planets all closer to it than Mercury is to the Sun.

image.alt: Artist's illustration of the TRAPPIST-1 system, not to scale: a glowing orange star on the left with seven small planets of different colours spread across a dark surface marked with thin orbit lines, water puddles near the middle and frost patterns towards the outer edge.

facts.fact1: Diameter: about 166,000 km (0.119 of the Sun's radius) — about 13 Earths, or 1.2 Jupiters, across.
facts.fact2: Distance: about 40.7 light-years (roughly 385 trillion km), in Aquarius — about 9.6 times farther than Proxima Centauri and far too faint to see without a telescope.
facts.fact3: Mass: about 9% of the Sun's; surface temperature about 2,566 K (≈ 2,290 °C), less than half the Sun's 5,772 K.
facts.fact4: Seven known planets, b to h: 0.76 to 1.13 times Earth's width and 0.33 to 1.37 times its mass, orbiting 1.7 to 9.3 million km from the star in 1.5 to 18.8 days.
facts.fact5: The planets form a resonance chain: for every 8 orbits of b, c makes 5, and each pair further out keeps a simple ratio too (5:3, 3:2, 3:2, 4:3, 3:2). Their tugs on one another shift the timing of their transits slightly, which is how their masses were measured.
facts.fact6: Atmospheres: in 2023 JWST measured daysides of about 500 K (≈ 230 °C) on b and 380 K (≈ 110 °C) on c — consistent with bare rock or a thin atmosphere, and ruling out a thick CO₂-rich one on c. A 2025 study of b still allows a hazy CO₂ atmosphere, so the question is not settled. In 2025 JWST also ruled out an Earth-like atmosphere on d; first results for e are inconclusive.
facts.fact7: Age: about 7.6 ± 2.2 billion years — probably older than the Solar System (4.6 billion).

saturn_rings.name: Saturn's Rings
saturn_rings.tagline: A disc of ice more than 270,000 km across and, in most places, only about 10 metres thick.
saturn_rings.body: Saturn's main rings — the bright C, B and A rings — form a flat disc that reaches 136,775 km from the planet's centre, so it measures about 273,500 km from edge to edge. Yet the disc is astonishingly thin: typically around 10 metres top to bottom, with estimates for different rings and places ranging from a few metres to about a kilometre. It is made of countless separate pieces, about 99.9% water ice, from dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house, and each ring circles Saturn at its own speed. The darkest gap visible from Earth, the 4,700-km-wide Cassini Division, was spotted by Giovanni Cassini in 1675; its inner edge is kept clear by the gravity of the small moon Mimas. Farther out lie faint, dusty rings, among them the vast E ring, fed by icy jets from the moon Enceladus. How old the rings are is still debated: Cassini's 2017 measurements suggested they formed only 10–100 million years ago, while a 2024 study argued they could be as old as Saturn itself, about 4.5 billion years.
saturn_rings.narrative: At about 273,500 km across, the main rings are almost twice as wide as Jupiter (139,820 km) and about 2.3 times as wide as Saturn's own equator; about 21 Earths side by side would span them. Laid between Earth and the Moon, they would cover about seven-tenths of the 384,400 km gap, and light crosses them in under a second (0.91 s). What makes them extraordinary is the ratio of width to thickness: about 27 million to one, if they are 10 metres thick. Shrink the rings until they are as thin as a sheet of paper (0.1 mm) and they would still be almost 3 km wide. The main rings begin about 14,400 km above Saturn's cloud tops — a gap wider than Earth — although the faint D ring fills part of it.
saturn_rings.massNarrative: For all their size, the rings weigh surprisingly little. Cassini's final dives in 2017 put their mass at about 15 billion billion kilograms (1.54 × 10¹⁹ kg, give or take about a third) — roughly 0.4 times the mass of Mimas, a moon only 396 km across, and about two-thirds the mass of Antarctica's ice sheet. Squeezed into a single ball of ice, it would be only about 320 km wide (280–350 km within the uncertainty); instead it is spread over an area about 80 times Earth's surface.
saturn_rings.funFact: Every 13 to 15 years Earth passes through the plane of the rings, and for a while they shrink to a thin line that all but vanishes from view. It last happened on 23 March 2025, when Saturn was too close to the Sun in our sky to watch; the next crossings come in 2038–2039. Galileo was caught out by the same thing in 1612: the "ears" he had seen beside Saturn two years earlier simply disappeared, and he asked whether Saturn had swallowed his children.
saturn_rings.seoTitle: How Big Are Saturn's Rings? Width vs. Thickness
saturn_rings.metaDescription: Saturn's main rings are about 273,500 km across but typically only about 10 m thick, made almost entirely of ice. Their size, mass, age debate and comparisons.

image.alt: Natural-colour Cassini view of Saturn's main rings curving across black space: the bright, finely banded B ring on the left, the dark Cassini Division arcing through the middle, and the wide grey A ring beyond it, crossed near its outer edge by a thin dark gap.

facts.fact1: Size: the main rings (C, B and A) stretch from 74,658 km to 136,775 km from Saturn's centre — about 273,500 km from edge to edge and about 62,000 km from inner to outer edge.
facts.fact2: Thickness: typically about 10 m in the main rings. Estimates are about 5 m for the C ring, 5–10 m for the B ring and 10–30 m for the A ring, and some sources allow up to 1 km locally; vertical structures up to 2.5 km high at the B ring's outer edge are thought to be raised by small, unseen moonlets.
facts.fact3: Material: about 99.9% water ice with traces of rocky dust. Pieces range from dust-sized grains to chunks as big as a house, with a few as large as mountains. The rings lie inside Saturn's Roche limit, where tides stop the ice from clumping into a moon.
facts.fact4: Mass: 1.54 ± 0.49 × 10¹⁹ kg, measured from Cassini's 22 dives between Saturn and the rings in 2017 — about 0.41 times the mass of the moon Mimas.
facts.fact5: Gaps and faint rings: the Cassini Division between the A and B rings is about 4,700 km wide (some sources say 4,800 km). Beyond the main rings, the faint E ring, fed by the icy jets of Enceladus, reaches from about 180,000 to 480,000 km from Saturn and is more than 2,000 km thick.
facts.fact6: Age: an open question. Cassini's mass measurement and the rings' clean ice suggested an age of only 10–100 million years; a 2024 study in Nature Geoscience argued that incoming dust mostly vaporises instead of darkening the ice, so the rings could be billions of years old. Ice slowly raining onto Saturn could make them disappear within roughly 100–300 million years.

quantum_superposition.name: Quantum Superposition
quantum_superposition.seoTitle: Quantum Superposition and Schrödinger's Cat, Explained
quantum_superposition.tagline: Until it is measured, a quantum system can be in a blend of states at once — and Schrödinger invented his cat to show how strange that sounds.
quantum_superposition.body: In quantum mechanics a particle need not be in just one state: an electron can be in a combination, or superposition, of spin 'up' and spin 'down', and an atom in a blend of two places, each possibility with its own chance of showing up when you look. This is not just ignorance about a hidden answer — the possibilities interfere with each other like overlapping waves, which is what makes the stripes in the double-slit experiment and the calculations of quantum computers possible. Yet every measurement gives just one result. In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger imagined the fate of a single atom tied to a cat in a sealed box: if the atom decays, a hammer smashes a flask of poison. Taken literally, the equations leave the cat both alive and dead until someone looks — a case Schrödinger himself called 'quite ridiculous', meant as a criticism of how quantum theory was being interpreted, not as a claim that real cats can be half-dead. Today the usual explanation for why we never see a blurred cat is decoherence: a large object constantly bumps into air molecules and light, which carry its superposition off into the surroundings almost instantly — though what, if anything, then picks the single outcome is still argued over by rival interpretations.
quantum_superposition.narrative: Quantum superposition has no size of its own, but how big a superposition can get is one of the open questions of physics. Experiments have climbed from single electrons and atoms to molecules of 2,000 atoms (2019) and, in 2023, a sapphire crystal of 16 micrograms — about the mass of a fine grain of sand — whose two vibration states were superposed. A 4-kilogram cat is still some 250 million times heavier, and nobody yet knows whether superpositions simply get ever harder to protect as things grow, or whether some still-unknown effect stops them outright.
quantum_superposition.funFact: Before the cat came a keg of gunpowder. In their letters after the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paper of 1935, Einstein pointed out that, taken literally, the equations would leave an unstable keg of gunpowder both exploded and not exploded. Schrödinger turned the keg into a cat — and Einstein was still praising the cat in a letter in 1950.
quantum_superposition.metaDescription: What quantum superposition really is, why Schrödinger's cat was meant as a criticism, how decoherence hides it, and the heaviest objects superposed so far.

image.alt: A diagram of Schrödinger's thought experiment: in a box, a radioactive source is linked through a detector and a lever to a hammer that has smashed a flask of green poison, while two overlapping grey outlines show the cat both walking and lying down.

facts.fact1: Schrödinger described the cat in 'Die gegenwärtige Situation in der Quantenmechanik' ('The present situation in quantum mechanics'), published in Naturwissenschaften in November 1935 in response to the Einstein–Podolsky–Rosen paper of May 1935.
facts.fact2: In his set-up a tiny bit of radioactive material gives one atom a 50:50 chance of decaying within an hour; a Geiger counter, a relay and a hammer link that one atom to a flask of hydrocyanic acid.
facts.fact3: A qubit, the building block of a quantum computer, is a superposition of 0 and 1: two numbers called amplitudes set the odds of reading each result.
facts.fact4: 1996 was a landmark year: at NIST in the United States a single beryllium ion was put into a superposition of two separate positions, and in Paris Serge Haroche's team watched a superposition fade step by step through decoherence for the first time.
facts.fact5: Haroche and David Wineland shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physics for experimental methods that make it possible to measure and manipulate individual quantum systems.
facts.fact6: Decoherence became a field of its own with H. Dieter Zeh's 1970 paper. It explains why superpositions vanish from view, but physicists still disagree on whether it fully solves the 'measurement problem'.
facts.fact7: The heaviest 'cat' so far (2023): a 16-microgram sapphire crystal at ETH Zurich, held in a superposition of two vibrations whose positions differed by only about 10⁻¹⁸ m — far less than the width of a proton.
facts.fact8: Interpretations, not experiments, differ on what a measurement does: in the Copenhagen view the wave function 'collapses' to one result; in Hugh Everett's many-worlds view (1957) every outcome happens in its own branch; objective-collapse theories predict that big enough superpositions break down by themselves — something no experiment has seen yet.

quantum_tunnelling.name: Quantum Tunnelling
quantum_tunnelling.seoTitle: What Is Quantum Tunnelling? Passing Through Walls, Explained
quantum_tunnelling.tagline: A particle can turn up on the far side of a barrier it hasn't the energy to climb — and the Sun shines because of it.
quantum_tunnelling.body: Roll a ball too gently at a hill and it rolls back. A quantum particle is described by a wave, though, and its wave does not stop dead at a barrier: it fades away inside it, and if the barrier is thin enough a little of the wave reaches the far side — so the particle has a small chance of simply turning up there. That chance falls off steeply, exponentially, as the barrier gets higher or thicker, which is why tunnelling matters for electrons and atomic nuclei but will never let a person walk through a wall. In 1928 George Gamow, and independently Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon, used it to explain alpha decay: heavy nuclei throw out alpha particles that lack the energy to climb over the electric barrier holding them in. The same effect keeps the Sun burning: protons in its core, at about 15 million degrees, have on average only about a thousandth of the energy needed to overcome their mutual repulsion, and they fuse only because some of them tunnel through it. Technology relies on it too — scanning tunnelling microscopes that map single atoms, and the flash memory in phones and USB sticks.
quantum_tunnelling.narrative: Quantum tunnelling has no size of its own, but distance rules it: it works across gaps of a few nanometres or less. In a scanning tunnelling microscope the current drops about tenfold for every extra 0.1 nanometres between tip and surface — about the width of a single atom — which is what lets it feel out individual atoms. Bigger objects are made of countless particles that would all have to tunnel together, so the odds vanish — yet in 1984–85 a superconducting circuit on a chip about a centimetre across, with billions of electron pairs acting as one, did tunnel, earning the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics.
quantum_tunnelling.funFact: Tunnelling is exquisitely sensitive to energy. Alpha particles leave heavy nuclei with energies that differ only about twofold, from about 4 to 9 MeV, yet the half-lives range over 20 orders of magnitude — from about a tenth of a microsecond to about 10 billion years. Polonium-212's alpha particle carries 8.78 MeV against a barrier of about 26 MeV that it could never climb, yet half the nuclei in a sample decay within 0.3 microseconds.
quantum_tunnelling.metaDescription: How particles slip through barriers they can't climb: why the Sun can shine, how alpha decay, tunnelling microscopes and flash memory work, and the 2025 Nobel.

image.alt: The first scanning tunnelling microscope, built at IBM Zurich in 1981, seen from above in a glass dish at the Deutsches Museum: a gold-coloured round base with tiny metal holders and white ceramic parts, ringed by red wires and crinkled aluminium foil.

facts.fact1: Friedrich Hund first applied the new wave mechanics to tunnelling in 1927; the English name 'tunnel effect' first appeared in Yakov Frenkel's 1932 textbook.
facts.fact2: Alpha decay was the first thing tunnelling explained — by George Gamow and, separately, by Ronald Gurney and Edward Condon in 1928.
facts.fact3: Without tunnelling, protons would need a temperature of roughly 10 billion kelvin to fuse — hundreds of times hotter than the Sun's core, at about 15 million K.
facts.fact4: Leo Esaki built the tunnel diode in 1957 and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics with Ivar Giaever and Brian Josephson for tunnelling in semiconductors and superconductors.
facts.fact5: Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer built the scanning tunnelling microscope at IBM Zurich in 1981 and won half of the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics (the other half went to Ernst Ruska for the electron microscope). It resolves details smaller than 0.1 nm across and 0.01 nm in height.
facts.fact6: Flash memory in phones, SSDs and USB sticks writes and erases bits by pushing electrons through a thin insulating layer onto a 'floating gate' — by tunnelling.
facts.fact7: 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis, 'for the discovery of macroscopic quantum mechanical tunnelling and energy quantisation in an electric circuit' — experiments at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1984–85.
facts.fact8: Tunnelling is also a nuisance: in the tiniest transistors it lets current leak through insulating layers, wasting power as heat, and parts thinner than about 1 nm leak so much that it limits how far chips can shrink.

pauli_exclusion_principle.name: Pauli Exclusion Principle
pauli_exclusion_principle.seoTitle: Pauli Exclusion Principle: Why Matter Takes Up Space
pauli_exclusion_principle.tagline: No two electrons may share the same quantum state — one rule that builds the periodic table and keeps dead stars from collapsing.
pauli_exclusion_principle.body: In 1925 Wolfgang Pauli found the rule hidden in the patterns of the periodic table: no two electrons in an atom can have exactly the same four quantum numbers — the same orbital and the same spin. Because spin has only two settings, each orbital holds at most two electrons, so the shells fill up in steps of 2, 8, 18 and 32, and how full an atom's outer shell is decides how it bonds — which is why elements in the same column of the periodic table behave alike. The rule binds all fermions, particles with half-integer spin such as electrons, quarks, protons and neutrons, while bosons such as photons can pile into the same state without limit, which is how a laser works. It is also why ordinary matter takes up room: electrons cannot all sink into the lowest orbital, and in 1967 Freeman Dyson and Andrew Lenard proved that without the principle matter would collapse into a far smaller volume. In burnt-out stars the same resistance, called degeneracy pressure, holds up white dwarfs of up to about 1.44 times the Sun's mass, and at far greater densities helps hold up neutron stars.
pauli_exclusion_principle.narrative: The exclusion principle has no size of its own, but it sets the size of things. It is why atoms with dozens of electrons are not crushed smaller than hydrogen: each extra electron must take a place in a higher, wider shell. In a white dwarf it holds about the Sun's mass in a ball roughly the size of Earth, squeezing matter to about a tonne per cubic centimetre. Pile on more than about 1.44 solar masses and the electrons can no longer resist: they merge with protons into neutrons, whose own degeneracy pressure stops the collapse only at the far smaller size of a neutron star.
pauli_exclusion_principle.funFact: Helium shows the rule at work. Helium-4 atoms are bosons and turn into a superfluid that flows without friction at about 2.17 K. Helium-3, a fermion with one neutron fewer, can't crowd together that way: it only becomes superfluid at 0.0025 K — almost 900 times colder — once its atoms pair up so that each pair behaves like a boson.
pauli_exclusion_principle.metaDescription: Why no two electrons can share a state: how Pauli's 1925 rule builds the periodic table, makes matter take up space and holds up white dwarfs and neutron stars.

image.alt: An artist's impression comparing the white dwarf Sirius B with Earth against a starry sky: on the left a glowing blue-white ball, on the right Earth, about the same size, with Africa visible under white clouds.

facts.fact1: Pauli published the principle in 1925 in Zeitschrift für Physik and won the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physics 'for the discovery of the Exclusion Principle, also called the Pauli Principle'.
facts.fact2: His key clue was a 1924 paper by Edmund Stoner, who matched the number of electron energy levels to the numbers of electrons in the closed shells of the noble gases.
facts.fact3: Pauli needed a fourth quantum number with only two values; Samuel Goudsmit and George Uhlenbeck identified it as the electron's spin.
facts.fact4: Each shell holds at most 2n² electrons — 2, 8, 18, 32 — and each orbital at most 2, with opposite spins.
facts.fact5: Pauli's spin–statistics theorem of 1940 extended the rule to all fermions (half-integer spin); bosons (whole-number spin) do not obey it.
facts.fact6: Paul Ehrenfest suggested in 1931 that the principle is why matter takes up space; Dyson and Lenard proved it in 1967, and Elliott Lieb and Walter Thirring found a much simpler proof in 1975.
facts.fact7: R. H. Fowler explained white dwarfs with electron degeneracy pressure in 1926; Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar's limit of about 1.44 solar masses, worked out from 1930, helped win him the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
facts.fact8: White-dwarf matter typically weighs between 10 kg and 10 tonnes per cubic centimetre; in neutron stars electrons have merged with protons into neutrons, whose degeneracy pressure resists even stronger gravity.

atomic_nucleus.name: Atomic nucleus
atomic_nucleus.seoTitle: How Big Is an Atomic Nucleus? Size of the Atom's Core
atomic_nucleus.tagline: A knot of protons and neutrons about 14 femtometres across that holds almost all of an atom's mass.
atomic_nucleus.body: The nucleus is the tiny core at the centre of every atom: a tight cluster of protons and neutrons held together by the strong nuclear force. Ernest Rutherford discovered it in 1911, after Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil and saw a few bounce straight back — something only a small, heavy, positively charged centre could do. A nucleus grows with the number of particles in it: its radius is roughly 1.2 femtometres times the cube root of that number, so the 197 protons and neutrons of a gold nucleus make a ball about 14 fm (0.000000000014 mm) across — the size we use here. The whole atom is tens of thousands of times wider: about 20,000 times for gold, and about 60,000 times for hydrogen, whose nucleus is a single proton. Yet the nucleus holds more than 99.9% of the atom's mass, because each proton or neutron weighs about 1,836 times as much as an electron. Packed that tightly, nuclear matter has a density of about 2 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³ — a teaspoonful would weigh around a billion tonnes.
atomic_nucleus.narrative: If a gold nucleus were blown up to the size of a 1.4-centimetre marble, the gold atom around it would be a ball about 290 metres across — nearly as tall as the Eiffel Tower (330 m). Each of its 197 protons and neutrons would be a bead about 2 millimetres wide. A proton, about 1.7 fm across, fits roughly eight times across the nucleus, and the nucleus fills only about one ten-trillionth of the atom's volume: everything else belongs to the cloud of electrons.
atomic_nucleus.funFact: Rutherford later described his astonishment: "It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you." Under J. J. Thomson's "plum pudding" model, accepted at the time, the chance of an alpha particle bouncing back from the foil was so small that none should ever have been seen.
atomic_nucleus.metaDescription: A gold nucleus is about 14 femtometres across — 20,000 times narrower than its atom, yet it holds over 99.9% of the mass. Size, density and discovery.

image.alt: Diagram of a helium atom: a soft grey cloud of electrons, darkest at the centre, with a 1 ångström (100 pm) scale bar below. A tiny dot in the middle is magnified in an inset with a 1 femtometre scale bar, showing the nucleus as two red and two violet blobs — its protons and neutrons.

facts.fact1: Size: the radius is roughly 1.2 fm × A^(1/3), where A is the number of protons plus neutrons. That gives about 1.7 fm across for hydrogen (a single proton), about 14 fm for gold and roughly 12–15 fm for uranium, depending on how the fuzzy edge is measured.
facts.fact2: Mass: more than 99.9% of an atom's mass sits in the nucleus. A proton or neutron is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron, so even gold's 79 electrons add only about 0.02%.
facts.fact3: Density: about 2 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³, roughly the same in every nucleus — about 10 trillion times denser than solid gold (19.3 g/cm³). Because the density is constant, a nucleus with 8 times as many particles is only twice as wide.
facts.fact4: Discovery: in 1909 Geiger and Marsden found that gold foil scatters some alpha particles by more than 90°. Rutherford's 1911 explanation put all the positive charge in a tiny centre; his alpha particles could only show that the gold nucleus is smaller than about 27 fm in radius — the true value is about 7 fm.
facts.fact5: Glue: the residual strong force reaches only a few femtometres, about one or two nucleon widths, but up close it overpowers the electric repulsion between protons. Lead-208 (82 protons, 126 neutrons) is the largest nucleus known to be completely stable.
facts.fact6: Not all nuclei are round: some are stretched like a rugby ball, flattened like a discus or even pear-shaped. The word nucleus is Latin for "kernel", a little nut; Rutherford gave it its atomic meaning in 1912.

visible_light.name: Visible light
visible_light.seoTitle: How Long Is a Wave of Light? Wavelength of Visible Light
visible_light.tagline: Waves about half a micrometre long — the narrow slice of light our eyes can see, and the reason an ordinary microscope can't show you a virus.
visible_light.body: Visible light is the narrow band of electromagnetic waves the human eye can detect, with wavelengths from about 380 nanometres (violet) to about 750 nm (red). Each colour is a different wavelength: blue is about 450–485 nm, green 500–565 nm and red from about 625 nm up. We use 550 nm, close to 555 nm — the yellowish green the eye is most sensitive to in daylight, the wavelength written into the official definition of the lumen. Because light is a wave, no lens can focus it into a spot much smaller than half its wavelength: Ernst Abbe worked this out in 1873, and even the best ordinary light microscopes stop at about 200 nm. Cells, 1–100 µm across, are easy to see, but most viruses are smaller than that blur and need an electron microscope. The size of the waves also explains the blue sky: air molecules are far smaller than a wavelength and scatter short waves much more strongly (in proportion to 1/λ⁴), so blue sunlight at about 450 nm is scattered nearly six times more than red light at 700 nm.
visible_light.narrative: A 550-nanometre wave of green light is about five times longer than a 100 nm virus. A 2 µm bacterium is almost four waves long, a red blood cell (7.5 µm) about 14, and roughly 145 waves fit across a human hair (about 80 µm). Stretch one wave to a metre and, at the same scale, a virus would be 18 centimetres wide — but the hair would be 145 metres thick, a little more than the height of the Great Pyramid (139 m).
visible_light.funFact: For more than a century Abbe's limit looked like a law of nature. Then Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell and William Moerner found a way around it: instead of fighting the blur, they made fluorescent molecules in a sample glow only a few at a time, or switched off all the glow except a nanometre-sized spot. Their "nanoscopy" won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — the light waves are still just as long, but light microscopes can now follow single molecules inside living cells.
visible_light.metaDescription: Visible light has wavelengths of about 380–750 nm; green is 550 nm, five times a virus. Why light microscopes stop near 200 nm and why the sky is blue.

image.alt: A clear triangular glass prism on a dark surface. A thin beam of white light passes through it and fans out into a band of colour across the surface, from red and orange through yellow and green to blue and violet.

facts.fact1: Range: a typical eye sees wavelengths from about 380 to 750 nm, frequencies of roughly 400–790 trillion waves per second (THz). The edges are not sharp and vary from person to person.
facts.fact2: Colours by wavelength: violet 380–450 nm, blue 450–485, cyan 485–500, green 500–565, yellow 565–590, orange 590–625 and red 625–750. The spectrum is continuous — the boundaries are only approximate.
facts.fact3: In daylight the eye is most sensitive at 555 nm, a yellowish green. The lumen, the SI unit of how bright light looks, is defined at 540 THz, which is that same 555 nm.
facts.fact4: Abbe limit: the smallest detail a light microscope can separate is about λ / (2 × NA), where NA, the numerical aperture of the lens, reaches about 1.4–1.6 in the best optics — so about λ/2.8, roughly 200 nm for green light. Hermann von Helmholtz proved the same formula in 1874.
facts.fact5: Photon energy: each photon of visible light carries between about 1.65 electronvolts (deep red) and 3.26 eV (violet), so a violet photon has about twice the energy of a red one.
facts.fact6: Isaac Newton split white light with a prism and was the first to use the word spectrum this way in print, in 1671. He later added indigo to his list of colours because he believed seven was a perfect number.
facts.fact7: Sunsets: when the Sun is low, much of the blue has already been scattered out of its direct light, so the Sun itself looks yellow to red.

mitochondrion.name: Mitochondrion
mitochondrion.seoTitle: Mitochondrion Size: A Cell's Former Bacterium
mitochondrion.tagline: A capsule about 2 micrometres long inside your cells — the descendant of a bacterium that moved into another cell some 2 billion years ago.
mitochondrion.body: Mitochondria are organelles — small compartments wrapped in two membranes — found in the cells of animals, plants, fungi and most other complex life. Their folded inner membrane is packed with protein machines that use oxygen to turn the energy in food into ATP, the molecule cells spend to power their work; this releases about 30 ATP per glucose molecule, against just 2 without them, which is why they are nicknamed the "powerhouse of the cell". In textbook pictures a mitochondrion is a capsule about 1 µm wide and 2 µm long — the length we use here — but in many living cells they keep splitting and merging into branching networks that stretch over tens of micrometres. They were once free-living bacteria: Lynn Margulis made the case in 1967, and today it is the accepted explanation, because mitochondria still carry their own small DNA, use bacteria-like ribosomes and divide by splitting in two. Their closest relatives are among the alphaproteobacteria, and the partnership probably began 1.7–2 billion years ago. A human liver cell holds about 1,000–2,000 of them, filling a fifth of its volume, while a red blood cell has none at all.
mitochondrion.narrative: A mitochondrion about 2 µm long is the same size as a typical bacterium — a reminder of where it came from. About 80 ribosomes (25 nm) would line up along it, a red blood cell (7.5 µm) is less than four mitochondria wide, and 40 laid end to end would span a human hair (80 µm). Blow a mitochondrion up to 2 metres, about the length of a bed, and at the same scale a ribosome would be the size of a coin (2.5 cm), a red blood cell would be 7.5 metres across, and a single hair would be a column 80 metres thick.
mitochondrion.funFact: A mature human egg cell carries about 100,000 mitochondria, with up to one and a half million copies of their DNA — as much as 90% of all the DNA in the egg. The sperm's mitochondria also get in at fertilisation, but they are tagged and destroyed, so with rare exceptions every mitochondrion in your body descends from your mother's.
mitochondrion.metaDescription: A mitochondrion is about 1 µm wide and 2 µm long — bacterium-sized, because it once was one. Its own DNA, mother-only inheritance and ATP, explained.

image.alt: Grey transmission electron micrograph of mammalian lung tissue showing two mitochondria, each cut across into a rounded outline with a dark double membrane and thin wavy ridges (cristae) running through a grainy interior.

facts.fact1: Size: the textbook mitochondrion is a capsule about 1 µm wide and 2 µm long, usually 0.75–3 µm² in cross-section. In many cells they fuse into networks that spread over tens of micrometres.
facts.fact2: Numbers: mammalian cells typically hold 1,000–10,000 mitochondria. A liver cell has about 1,000–2,000 (a fifth of its volume), a lymphocyte about 3, a mature egg cell about 100,000 — and a red blood cell none.
facts.fact3: Their own DNA: human mitochondrial DNA is a ring of 16,569 base pairs carrying 37 genes — 13 for proteins of the energy-making machinery, 22 for transfer RNAs and 2 for ribosomal RNAs. Each mitochondrion holds about 5 copies.
facts.fact4: Inherited from the mother: in humans the mitochondria, and their DNA, normally come only from the egg, with rare exceptions.
facts.fact5: Origin: Lynn Margulis's paper "On the Origin of Mitosing Cells" was rejected by about fifteen journals before it appeared in 1967, and her idea that mitochondria were once bacteria was largely ignored for a decade. Today it is the textbook explanation; the ancestor was probably related to the alphaproteobacteria.
facts.fact6: Energy: with oxygen, mitochondria get about 30 ATP from each glucose molecule, against 2 from glycolysis alone. An adult recycles roughly 50 kg of ATP a day — about their own body weight — reusing each molecule 1,000–1,500 times.
facts.fact7: Name: Albert von Kölliker first described them in insect muscle in 1857, and Carl Benda named them mitochondria, "thread-like granules", in 1898. "Powerhouse of the cell" was popularised by Philip Siekevitz in a 1957 Scientific American article.

chankillo.name: Chankillo
chankillo.seoTitle: How Long Is Chankillo? Peru's Thirteen Towers Sun Calendar
chankillo.tagline: Thirteen stone towers strung along a 300-metre ridge in Peru's coastal desert, built more than 2,200 years ago to follow the rising and setting Sun through the whole year.
chankillo.body: Chankillo is an ancient ceremonial centre in the Casma Valley on Peru's desert north coast. UNESCO dates its use to about 250–200 BC; the 2007 study that explained it placed it in the 4th century BC. Its best-known part is the Thirteen Towers: flat-topped stone towers 2–6 metres high, spaced only about 5 metres apart in a line about 300 metres long along a low ridge running roughly north to south. Seen from an observing point in a building about 235 metres to the west, the row forms an artificial toothed horizon that covers almost exactly the stretch where the Sun rises over a year: at the June solstice it comes up just left of the northernmost tower, at the December solstice out of the top of the southernmost one, and on every other day in one of the gaps or behind a tower. A matching observing point on the east side did the same for sunsets, so a trained watcher could tell the date to within a day or two. Travellers had noticed the towers for some 200 years, but only in 2007 did the archaeologist Iván Ghezzi and the archaeoastronomer Clive Ruggles show in the journal Science what they were for; Chankillo is regarded as the oldest known solar observatory in the Americas. A triple-walled hilltop building nearby, long taken for a fort, is now read as a fortified temple, and offerings, feasting debris and tightly controlled access suggest the Sun was worshipped here as well as watched.
chankillo.narrative: At about 300 metres, the line of towers is a little longer than the Titanic (269 m) and nearly as long as the Eiffel Tower is tall (330 m): laid on its side, the tower would stick out past the row by about 30 metres. The Great Pyramid's base (230 m) would fit along it with room to spare, and Stonehenge's sarsen circle (30 m) would fit ten times over. Yet each tower is only 2–6 metres high, no taller than a one- or two-storey house: what made them a calendar was not their height but their even spacing, seen from 235 metres away.
chankillo.funFact: The builders seem to have borrowed one marker from nature. Seen from the western observing point, the June-solstice Sun rose just left of the northernmost tower, right where the slope of a natural hill, Cerro Mucho Malo, meets a more distant hill behind it — so the hill may have served as an extra 'tower' at the end of the row. Almost two thousand years later, the Inca left an offering at that same tower: a small female figurine inside a sea shell, placed in the middle of the first step of its staircase.
chankillo.metaDescription: Chankillo's Thirteen Towers line a 300 m ridge in Peru and track the Sun's rising and setting all year: the oldest known solar observatory in the Americas.

image.alt: The Thirteen Towers of Chankillo as a dark, notched silhouette along the top of a bare desert ridge, with the morning Sun glowing through white clouds in a blue sky above them.

facts.fact1: Line of towers: about 300 m long, running roughly north to south along a low ridge; the gaps between the 13 towers are only 4.7–5.1 m wide.
facts.fact2: Towers: flat-topped stone-and-mortar blocks covering 75–125 m² each and 2–6 m high; the northern ones are taller, apparently to make up for the hill sloping down. Narrow staircases, 1.3–1.5 m wide, climb their north and south sides — some too steep to use.
facts.fact3: Age: UNESCO dates the site's use to about 250–200 BC, late in Peru's Early Horizon period, after which it was destroyed and abandoned; the 2007 Science study described it as a 4th-century BC complex — about 2,300 years old.
facts.fact4: Calendar: from observing points about 235 m to the west and to the east, the row spans the Sun's full yearly range of sunrises and sunsets. The Sun rises in each gap for only one or two days, so dates could be read to within 1–2 days.
facts.fact5: Explained in 2007 by Iván Ghezzi and Clive Ruggles as the oldest known solar observatory in the Americas — almost two thousand years older than the Sun pillars that the Inca later raised at Cusco.
facts.fact6: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021 as the Chankillo Archaeoastronomical Complex, together with the triple-walled Fortified Temple on a nearby hilltop and the natural marker hill Cerro Mucho Malo.

goseck_circle.name: Goseck Circle
goseck_circle.tagline: A ring of ditch, bank and double wooden palisade 75 metres across, built in Germany around 4900 BC with gates facing the midwinter sunrise and sunset.
goseck_circle.body: The Goseck circle is a Neolithic circular enclosure on a plateau above the Saale valley at Goseck in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, built around 4900 BC by farmers of the Stroke-ornamented Pottery culture and used for perhaps two centuries. It is about 75 metres across: a ring-shaped ditch with a low earth bank, and inside it two concentric wooden palisades, all cut by three gateways facing north, south-east and south-west. Seen from the centre, the south-east gate frames the sunrise and the south-west gate the sunset around the winter solstice — to within three or four days in the sky of about 4800 BC — and smaller gaps in the palisade line up with the summer solstice. The ring's outline was spotted from the air in 1991 by the aerial archaeologist Otto Braasch, as marks in a crop field; the site was fully excavated in 2002–2004 and rebuilt in oak in 2005, opening to visitors on the winter solstice, 21 December. Cattle skulls, about 30 cattle horn cores and pits holding burnt remains and human bones point to rituals held there. It is often called one of the oldest known solar observatories, but that label is partly marketing: the clear alignments are with the solstices, and whether the ring was used to follow the Sun through the year or only to mark a few special days is debated. About 150 similar enclosures are known from Neolithic central and eastern Europe, and the Nebra Sky Disc was found only about 25 km away, though it was made more than 3,000 years later.
goseck_circle.narrative: At about 75 metres across, the Goseck circle is a little smaller than Newgrange (85 m) and two and a half times as wide as Stonehenge's sarsen circle (30 m), which was raised some 2,400 years later. Three blue whales nose to tail (3 × 25 m) would just reach across it, and it is a little wider than a football pitch is wide (about 68 m). The rebuilt oak posts are 2.4 metres tall — higher than a doorway, and tall enough to hide most of the horizon from someone standing in the middle, so the low midwinter Sun is seen through the gates.
goseck_circle.funFact: The gateways narrow towards the middle, like the sights of a rifle: the excavators found that the inner palisade's opening was narrower than the outer one, and the outer one narrower than the causeway across the ditch. The only thing the rebuilders had to guess was the height of the posts: they chose 2.40 metres, though the excavator François Bertemes thinks the originals may have been closer to three.
goseck_circle.metaDescription: The Goseck circle in Germany is 75 m across, built around 4900 BC with gates aimed at the midwinter sunrise and sunset. Size, age and the solstice gates.

image.alt: The rebuilt Goseck circle on a summer day: a gravel path crosses a dry grassy field to a gateway in a long, low wall of dark oak posts, with low earth banks on either side, a lone visitor standing in the gap, trees behind and white clouds in a blue sky.

facts.fact1: Size: about 75 m across to the outer edge of the ditch (the ditch ring itself is about 71 m); inside stand two concentric palisades about 56 and 49 m across. The V-shaped ditch was up to 1.8 m deep.
facts.fact2: Age: built around 4900 BC — 40 radiocarbon dates place it in the 49th century BC — and probably in use into the 47th century BC, by people of the Stroke-ornamented Pottery culture.
facts.fact3: Gates: three, facing north, south-east and south-west. From the centre the two southern ones point to the winter-solstice sunrise and sunset of about 4800 BC, to within three or four days; the northern one points almost exactly due north. Further gaps in the palisade match the summer solstice.
facts.fact4: Discovery: spotted in 1991 by Otto Braasch in aerial photographs; excavated by the University of Halle under François Bertemes in 2002–2004.
facts.fact5: Rebuilt in 2005 on the original post holes, with oak palisades 2.4 m high, and opened on 21 December 2005, the winter solstice. It is one stop on the 'Himmelswege' (Sky Paths) tourist route, about 25 km from the find site of the Nebra Sky Disc.
facts.fact6: Finds: fragments of cattle skulls and about 30 cattle horn cores in the ditch, and pits with traces of fire and human bones — signs of ritual, perhaps of special burial rites or even sacrifice, though that is not proven.

abu_simbel.name: Abu Simbel
abu_simbel.seoTitle: How Tall Is Abu Simbel? Size of Ramesses II's Sun Temple
abu_simbel.tagline: A temple cut into a Nubian cliff for Ramesses II, its 33-metre facade guarded by four 20-metre statues of the king — and twice a year the rising Sun reaches the gods in its deepest room.
abu_simbel.body: The Great Temple of Abu Simbel was carved into a sandstone cliff beside the Nile in ancient Nubia, in the far south of Egypt, for Pharaoh Ramesses II, who ruled from about 1279 to 1213 BC; the work is usually dated to about 1264–1244 BC. Its facade is about 33 metres high and 38 metres wide, fronted by four seated colossal statues of the king, each about 20 metres tall, and behind the door a line of halls runs straight into the rock to a small sanctuary about 60 metres in. On its back wall sit four carved gods: Ra-Horakhty, Amun-Ra, Ramesses himself as a god, and Ptah. On the mornings around 22 February and 22 October, the rising Sun shines through the doorway along the whole length of the temple and lights three of the statues, while Ptah, a god linked with the realm of the dead, stays in shadow. A popular story says the two dates were the king's birthday and coronation day, but there is no evidence for it. In 1964–68, as the lake behind the new Aswan High Dam rose, an international campaign led by UNESCO cut the temple into hundreds of blocks and rebuilt it 65 metres higher and about 200 metres further from the river, keeping its orientation so that the sunbeam still reaches the sanctuary; whether the dates shifted, and by how much, is uncertain, though about one day is the figure most often given. Together with the smaller temple Ramesses built next to it for Queen Nefertari and the goddess Hathor, it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae' (1979).
abu_simbel.narrative: The 33-metre facade is about as tall as an 11-storey building and a little taller than El Castillo at Chichén Itzá (30 m). A blue whale (25 m) standing on its tail would reach only about three-quarters of the way up, while the Great Pyramid (139 m) is about four times taller. Each seated colossus, at about 20 metres, is as tall as a six- or seven-storey building. When the temple was moved in the 1960s, the whole thing was lifted 65 metres — about twice the height of its own facade.
abu_simbel.funFact: The colossi's heads were too heavy for the cranes, which could lift at most 30 tonnes. So in October 1965 the most experienced stone-cutters first sawed off the crowns and then cut each face away from behind the ears; the next day the first face, weighing 19 tonnes, was lifted clear. In all the two temples were cut into 1,036 blocks — 807 of them for the Great Temple — and rebuilt inside concrete domes hidden under an artificial hill.
abu_simbel.metaDescription: Abu Simbel's Great Temple has a 33 m facade with four 20 m statues of Ramesses II, and twice a year the Sun lights its inner sanctuary. Size and sunbeam.

image.alt: The facade of the Great Temple at Abu Simbel in bright sunlight: four huge seated statues of Ramesses II carved from pale sandstone, the second one broken off above the waist with its head and torso lying at its feet, flanking a dark doorway, with small standing figures between their legs.

facts.fact1: Facade: about 33 m high and 38 m wide, cut out of the living rock and crowned by a frieze of 22 baboons raising their arms to the rising Sun.
facts.fact2: Colossi: four seated statues of Ramesses II, each about 20 m tall, with smaller figures of his queen Nefertari, his mother and some of his children standing beside their legs.
facts.fact3: Age: made for Ramesses II, who ruled from about 1279 to 1213 BC; the work is usually dated to about 1264–1244 BC, some 20 years.
facts.fact4: Sunbeam: around 22 February and 22 October the sunrise lights the statues of Ra-Horakhty, Amun-Ra and Ramesses at the back of the sanctuary, some 60 m from the entrance, while Ptah stays dark. That the dates mark the king's birthday and coronation is an unproven tradition; Egyptologists usually date his accession to about 31 May 1279 BC.
facts.fact5: Rescue: in 1964–68 the two temples were cut into 1,036 blocks, raised 65 m and moved about 200 m back onto an artificial hill, at a cost of about US$41.7 million shared between Egypt and 48 other countries; the relocated temples were inaugurated on 22 September 1968.
facts.fact6: Rediscovery: almost buried in sand, the temple was found by Johann Ludwig Burckhardt in March 1813, and Giovanni Belzoni dug his way in on 1 August 1817. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'Nubian Monuments from Abu Simbel to Philae' since 1979.

about.title: About Quantumaire
about.tagline: A small, careful map of everything.
about.intro: Quantumaire is an interactive educational tour of scale from the smallest known particles to the largest structures in the observable universe. The premise is simple: most explanations of scale either over-simplify (planets compared to fruit) or over-complicate (raw scientific notation with no anchor). We try for a third way — one reference object, one clear gradient of confidence, and an honest label on every claim.
about.scaleHeading: How we make the numbers graspable
about.scaleBody: Sizes on this site span more than 60 orders of magnitude, so every scale is logarithmic: each step along the track is ten times bigger than the last, which lets a quark and the observable universe share one line. You can switch the explorer between size, distance from Earth and temperature. Long distances also show how long light takes to cross them, from light-seconds to light-years. Every topic page translates its size into everyday terms — hairs, football pitches, the Eiffel Tower — and the classic reference still runs through it all: shrink Earth to a 0.5 mm grain of sand and the Sun becomes a billiard ball six metres away. Units switch between metric and imperial, and temperatures between °C, °F and kelvin.
about.badgesIntro: Not every claim in science carries the same weight. A measurement is not a theory; a theory is not a hunch. Every topic on Quantumaire wears one of four badges so you always know what you are reading.
about.badgeFactBody: Directly measured or directly observed. Atoms exist. The Sun fuses hydrogen. Earth is round. We may refine the precision, but the existence of the thing is not in question.
about.badgeEstablishedBody: A well-tested theoretical framework that fits the evidence we have. Special relativity. The Big Bang. The size of the observable universe. Open to refinement, but supported by enormous, convergent observational data.
about.badgeProbableBody: Our current best explanation for something real that we have not yet fully pinned down. Dark matter is a clear example: we can map it through gravitational lensing, but we don't know what particle it is made of.
about.badgeSpeculativeBody: Ideas worth taking seriously, but not proven. We label them clearly. We will never dress up a speculation as a fact.
about.editorialBody: We would rather be slightly behind the literature than dramatically ahead of the evidence. When we discover a mistake we correct it visibly. Where reasonable people disagree, we say so. We use sources we can defend — peer-reviewed papers, established textbooks, working scientists — over flashy press releases.
about.languagesBody: Every page exists in English and in Serbian (Latin script). The two language versions have their own canonical URLs so they can be discovered, cited, and translated independently — by people and by AI search engines alike.
about.imageAlt: Stylised cosmic diagram showing the spectrum of confidence from fact to speculation.
about.seoTitle: About Quantumaire: How We Measure the Universe

topicsIndex.title: Guides
topicsIndex.tagline: Concept pages that put the individual objects on Quantumaire in context.
topicsIndex.intro: Each topic page covers one object: UY Scuti, the Moon, the black hole at the centre of our galaxy. A guide covers the bigger picture: what stars are, how planets are defined, why black holes have an event horizon. Start with one when you want context for several objects at once.

stars.title: Stars
stars.seoTitle: Stars Explained: How Big, Hot and Far Are They?
stars.tagline: The nuclear furnaces of the universe.
stars.intro: A star is a ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, hot and dense enough in its core to fuse light atomic nuclei into heavier ones — and to release the energy that keeps the rest of it from collapsing. Stars come in a huge range of colours, sizes, and temperatures, but every one is doing the same fundamental thing: burning.
stars.section1Heading: Colours, temperatures, and the OBAFGKM scale
stars.section1Body: Astronomers classify stars by surface temperature, from O (the hottest, brightest blue stars) through B, A, F, G, K, to M (the coolest red dwarfs). The mnemonic "Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me" is about a century old. (Temperatures below are in kelvin. To convert to Celsius, subtract 273 — at these stellar scales the difference is negligible.) O-class stars exceed 30,000 K (≈ 30,000 °C) and are rare and brilliant. B-class are 10,000–30,000 K, blue. A-class (7,500–10,000 K, white) includes Sirius. F-class are yellow-white. G-class (5,200–6,000 K, ≈ 5,000–5,700 °C, yellow) includes our Sun. K-class are orange. M-class (under 3,700 K, ≈ under 3,400 °C, red) are the most common type in the galaxy.
stars.section2Body: A second classification ladder runs from dwarfs to hypergiants. White dwarfs are stellar corpses smaller than Earth. Brown dwarfs straddle the line between large planets and small stars. Main-sequence stars like the Sun sit in the middle. Red giants and supergiants swell as they age.
