Hypergiants like UY Scuti are so puffy that their surface, placed where the Sun is, would reach past Mars — the very largest, perhaps past Jupiter — but they are also among the most short-lived stars in the galaxy.
stars.section3Body: Every star starts as a knot of cold gas inside a molecular cloud, collapsing under its own gravity. As the centre densifies and heats, hydrogen begins fusing into helium and the new star joins the "main sequence" — the steady-burning phase where it spends most of its life. The Sun has been in main-sequence phase for about 4.6 billion years and has roughly another five to go.
stars.section4Body: What a star becomes when it dies depends on how massive it was. Sun-sized stars puff into red giants, shed their outer layers, and leave behind a slow-cooling white dwarf. Larger stars — 8 to 25 solar masses — end in supernova explosions, collapsing their cores into neutron stars. Truly massive stars (above ~25 solar masses) usually leave black holes instead — sometimes after a weaker explosion, sometimes with almost none. Black holes are, in this sense, the graveyards of the most massive stars.
stars.section5Body: There are an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars in the Milky Way alone, and hundreds of billions of galaxies — perhaps up to 2 trillion — in the observable universe. The smallest known stars are about the size of Jupiter — some slightly smaller. The largest red supergiants, placed at the Sun's position, would reach past Mars and possibly beyond Jupiter. The hottest stars exceed 200,000 K (≈ 200,000 °C) at their surfaces; the coolest red dwarfs are around 2,300 K (≈ 2,000 °C) — cooler than a welding torch's flame.
stars.metaDescription: How big, hot and far stars are: from red dwarfs to supergiants, star colours and temperatures, how stars live and die, and how many exist.

planets.title: Planets
planets.seoTitle: The Planets: Sizes, Distances and Facts Compared
planets.intro: A planet is a body massive enough to be rounded by its own gravity, orbiting a star, and clearing the neighbourhood around its orbit. The third clause — added by the International Astronomical Union in 2006 — is what reclassified Pluto. By that definition our Solar System has eight planets; by older definitions it had more.
planets.section1Body: Our Solar System has four small rocky "terrestrial" planets close to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — and four large gaseous outer ones: Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants), Uranus and Neptune (ice giants, with proportionally more water, ammonia and methane). Between the two groups circles the Asteroid Belt, rubble that Jupiter's gravity never let grow into a planet. Beyond Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt and a population of icy bodies, including five recognised dwarf planets.
planets.section2Body: Since the first confirmed exoplanet around a Sun-like star in 1995, more than 6,000 have been catalogued. Many do not resemble anything in our system: "hot Jupiters" that orbit closer than Mercury, "super-Earths" between Earth and Neptune in size with no equivalent here, "rogue planets" wandering free without a star at all. Most stars in the galaxy probably have planets.
planets.section3Heading: Where planet ends and star begins
planets.section3Body: The line between large planet and small star is blurry. Brown dwarfs — failed stars massive enough to fuse deuterium but not hydrogen — occupy that grey zone. Jupiter would need to grow about 80 times more massive to ignite hydrogen fusion and become a true star — so despite the 'failed star' nickname, it never came close.
planets.section4Body: A planet capable of liquid water at its surface needs a stable orbit in the "habitable zone" around its star, a substantial atmosphere, a magnetic field to deflect stellar radiation, and probably plate tectonics to recycle nutrients. Earth has all four. We have so far found no other world that demonstrably does — though several look intriguing.
planets.metaDescription: What makes a planet a planet, why Pluto was reclassified, the eight planets compared by size and distance, and the thousands found beyond.

blackHoles.title: Black holes
blackHoles.seoTitle: Black Holes: How Big Can They Get?
blackHoles.tagline: Regions of spacetime nothing can escape.
blackHoles.intro: A black hole is a region where matter has collapsed into a gravitational well so deep that not even light moving at the cosmic speed limit can climb back out. Once you cross its event horizon, you're committed. We can't see inside one directly — we infer their existence from how they bend light, swallow gas, and tug on the stars around them.
blackHoles.section1Body: Black holes come in three rough size classes. Stellar-mass black holes weigh 3 to a few tens of solar masses and form when massive stars die. Intermediate-mass black holes — hundreds to hundreds of thousands of solar masses — were long theorised and only recently confirmed in a handful of specific systems. Supermassive black holes, millions to tens of billions of solar masses, sit at the centres of almost every large galaxy. How the supermassive ones grew so fast in the early universe is still an open question.
blackHoles.section2Heading: Not every star becomes a black hole
blackHoles.section2Body: What a dying star leaves behind depends on its mass. Sun-sized stars end as cooling white dwarfs. Stars 8 to 25 times the Sun's mass collapse into neutron stars after their supernova. The heaviest stars — those above roughly 25 solar masses — usually collapse into stellar-mass black holes, sometimes with only a weak explosion or none at all. Black holes are, in this sense, the graveyards of the most massive stars.
blackHoles.section3Body: Sagittarius A* weighs about 4.15 million solar masses and sits at the centre of the Milky Way; we got its first direct image in 2022. M87* in the galaxy M87 is much heavier — around 6.5 billion solar masses — and was the very first black hole ever imaged, in 2019. TON 618 and Phoenix-A are contenders for the most massive known, each tens of billions of solar masses. Gaia BH1 is the nearest known black hole of any kind — a much smaller stellar-mass one only 1,560 light-years away.
blackHoles.section4Body: Past the event horizon, our current theories run out. General relativity predicts a "singularity" — a point of infinite density — at the centre of every black hole. But infinities in physics are usually a sign that the theory is incomplete, not a real prediction. A future theory of quantum gravity, when we have one, will probably replace the singularity with something less infinite.
blackHoles.section5Body: Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that black holes are not actually perfectly black — they radiate a tiny amount of thermal energy from just outside their event horizon. Over inconceivably long timescales (at least 10⁶⁷ years even for a black hole of just one solar mass, far longer for heavier ones) they should slowly evaporate. We have never observed this happen — it's far too faint.
blackHoles.metaDescription: Black holes from a few Suns to 66 billion: how big they get, how we photograph them, Hawking radiation, and what is still speculation.

nebulae.title: Nebulae
nebulae.seoTitle: What Is a Nebula? Star Nurseries and Remnants
nebulae.tagline: Where stars are born and where they go to die.
nebulae.intro: A nebula is a vast cloud of gas and dust drifting through interstellar space. Some are nurseries where new stars are condensing under gravity. Others are graveyards — the puffed-out remains of stars that finished burning. They are the loudest, prettiest objects in deep-sky astrophotography, and the slowest-moving cosmic events humans can directly observe.
nebulae.section1Body: Astronomers usually sort nebulae into four kinds. Emission nebulae glow because hot young stars ionise their gas — the Orion Nebula is the classic example, and the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, nearly 1,000 light-years across, is the biggest one near us. Reflection nebulae merely scatter light from nearby stars, with no light of their own. Planetary nebulae are the shed outer layers of dying Sun-like stars — the Ring Nebula and the Cat's Eye are famous examples (the misleading name comes from their round, planet-like appearance through small 18th-century telescopes). Supernova remnants are the violent debris of dying massive stars — the Crab Nebula was created by a supernova observed from Earth in 1054 CE.
nebulae.section2Body: Most stars form inside cold, dense molecular clouds. Gravity collapses pockets of gas into protostars; nearby young stars then heat and ionise the leftover gas, lighting up the region. The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula — that Hubble image you've seen — are a stellar nursery in progress. Our Sun was almost certainly born in a similar nursery; its siblings have long since drifted apart across the galaxy.
nebulae.section3Body: When a Sun-like star runs out of hydrogen fuel, it expands into a red giant, then sheds its outer atmosphere into space. The exposed core — a hot white dwarf — illuminates that shed gas from the inside, producing a planetary nebula. In about five billion years, this is what will happen to the Sun. The phase lasts only tens of thousands of years before the gas dissipates.
nebulae.section4Body: When a star above eight solar masses dies, its outer layers explode at thousands of kilometres per second, leaving a shock wave of hot gas that lights up for tens of thousands of years. The Crab Nebula still expands at about 1,500 km/s, and a rapidly spinning neutron star — the Crab Pulsar — sits at its centre, the collapsed core of the original star.
nebulae.keyNumber1Label: Crab Nebula's supernova seen from Earth
nebulae.keyNumber3Label: Star mass that ends in a supernova

bigBang.title: The Big Bang
bigBang.seoTitle: The Big Bang Explained: 13.8 Billion Years Ago
bigBang.tagline: The hot, dense origin of the universe we can see.
bigBang.intro: Our best current picture of cosmic history says that around 13.8 billion years ago, everything in the observable universe was packed into a state so hot and dense that ordinary matter, light and space behaved in ways our theories can no longer fully describe. From that state — call it the Big Bang — space expanded, cooled, and produced the matter, stars and galaxies we observe today. The Big Bang is not an explosion *inside* space; it is the expansion *of* space itself.
bigBang.section1Body: In the 1920s Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are receding from us, and the further away they are, the faster they recede. This is the strongest direct evidence for cosmic expansion. We are not at any special centre — every galaxy sees this same outward flow from every other galaxy. Run the expansion backwards in time and everything collapses to a single hot dense state.
bigBang.section2Heading: Cosmic microwave background — the universe's baby photo
bigBang.section2Body: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, space cooled enough for atoms to form and light to travel freely for the first time. That ancient light, redshifted into microwaves by 13.8 billion years of expansion, now bathes the entire sky in a faint, almost-uniform glow. Tiny temperature variations across this Cosmic Microwave Background map the seeds of every galaxy that exists today. We have measured it with extraordinary precision — it is among the best-tested predictions in all of physics.
bigBang.section3Body: In 1998, two independent teams measuring distant supernovae found that the universe's expansion isn't slowing down (as gravity would suggest) — it's speeding up. A mysterious form of energy embedded in space itself, called *dark energy*, appears to be pushing space apart faster and faster. Over the next hundred billion years, this acceleration will eventually carry every galaxy outside our local group beyond the cosmic horizon. The acceleration is **established theory**; what dark energy actually *is* remains a deep open question.
bigBang.section4Heading: Before the Big Bang? Speculation only
bigBang.section4Body: Asking "what happened before the Big Bang?" sits at the very edge of physics. Several ideas exist — eternal inflation, where our universe is one of many bubbles in a much larger inflating multiverse; cyclic models, where Big Bangs and Big Crunches repeat; bouncing models from loop quantum gravity. None has been observationally confirmed; some may even be unconfirmable in principle. **This entire area is speculative** — fascinating, but not yet science the way the rest of this page is.
bigBang.metaDescription: What happened 13.8 billion years ago, how we know — expansion, the cosmic microwave background, light elements — and what is still open.

supernova.title: Supernovae
supernova.seoTitle: What Is a Supernova? How Massive Stars Die
supernova.tagline: How massive stars die — and what they leave behind.
supernova.intro: A supernova is the explosive death of a star, which can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. The explosion seeds the universe with heavy elements — much of the matter in your body heavier than helium was forged inside stars and scattered by events like this. Telescopes now catch thousands of supernovae a year in other galaxies, but in our own Milky Way one goes off only about twice a century — and dust has hidden every one since 1604.
supernova.section1Body: Astronomers see two main flavours. **Core-collapse supernovae** (Types II, Ib, Ic) happen when a star above about 8 solar masses runs out of nuclear fuel — its core collapses in a fraction of a second, then rebounds, blowing the outer layers off. **Thermonuclear supernovae** (Type Ia) happen when a white dwarf in a binary system accretes enough matter to ignite runaway carbon fusion, vaporising the entire star. The latter are so consistent in brightness they're used as standard candles to measure cosmic distances.
supernova.section2Body: If the dying star was 8–25 solar masses, its collapsed core remains as a neutron star — a city-sized object as heavy as the Sun. If above ~25 solar masses, the collapse goes further and a stellar-mass black hole is left in the centre. The outer layers expand as a glowing supernova remnant — the Crab Nebula is the most famous, the visible debris of a supernova humans on Earth recorded in 1054 CE.
supernova.section3Body: **SN 1054** — recorded by Chinese, Japanese and Arab astronomers in July 1054 CE — produced the Crab Nebula and its central pulsar. **SN 1572** was observed by Tycho Brahe and broke the medieval belief in an unchanging cosmos. **SN 1987A**, in the Large Magellanic Cloud, was the closest naked-eye supernova in nearly 400 years and the first whose pre-explosion star was identified.
supernova.section4Body: Hydrogen and helium come from the Big Bang. Almost everything else — carbon, oxygen, calcium, iron, gold, uranium — is forged either inside stars or in supernovae and neutron-star mergers. Carl Sagan's line that "we are made of star-stuff" is literally true: every atom in your body heavier than helium was forged inside an ancient star and scattered across space when it died. You are, structurally, recycled supernova.
supernova.keyNumber1Label: Star mass for a core-collapse supernova
supernova.keyNumber3Label: Last one seen in our galaxy

time.title: Time
time.seoTitle: Is Time Relative? Time Dilation Explained
time.tagline: Not as universal as it feels.
time.intro: Newton thought time flowed at the same rate everywhere. Einstein showed otherwise. Time runs slower when you move fast, and slower deep inside a gravitational well. The effects are tiny in everyday life but real, measurable, and built into the satellites in your phone's GPS chip. This page sticks to the parts that are **established theory** — well-tested for over a century.
time.section1Heading: Moving fast slows your clock (special relativity)
time.section1Body: Einstein's 1905 special theory of relativity says that two observers moving relative to each other will disagree about how much time has passed between two events. Specifically: a clock moving past you ticks slower than your own. The effect is real but tiny at everyday speeds. At 1% of the speed of light a clock runs about 0.005% slow. At 99% it runs **seven times** slower. This isn't an illusion — it's been measured directly with atomic clocks on fast aircraft. **Status: established theory, verified repeatedly.**
time.section2Body: Einstein's 1915 general theory of relativity says gravity also slows time. A clock at sea level ticks slightly slower than a clock at the top of Mount Everest. A clock just outside a black hole's event horizon would tick arbitrarily slowly compared to ours. The effect is tiny on Earth but huge near a black hole — and significant enough that GPS satellites have to correct their clocks by 38 microseconds per day, or your phone's location would drift by around ten kilometres a day. **Status: established theory, again verified directly.**
time.section3Body: If one twin stays on Earth and the other accelerates to near light-speed, travels to a distant star, and returns — the travelling twin will be younger. This isn't a paradox: the two twins are not symmetric, because only the traveller switches from an outbound to an inbound frame of reference. Their paths through spacetime differ, and the bent path accumulates less time. The effect has been measured with atomic clocks flown around the world. **Status: real consequence of relativity, observationally confirmed.**
time.section4Body: Why does time only move forwards? Physically, almost every law of physics works the same backwards as forwards — except, in practice, the second law of thermodynamics, which says total entropy — roughly, a measure of how many ways the parts of a system can be arranged — never decreases. That asymmetry is what gives time its direction. Why the universe started in such a low-entropy state, though, is a much harder question — and an open one. **Status: the arrow itself is established; its ultimate origin is speculative.**

distances.title: Distances
distances.seoTitle: Space Distances Explained: Light-Years, AU, Parsecs
distances.tagline: From light-seconds to the cosmic horizon.
distances.intro: Once you leave Earth, conventional units stop being useful. Astronomers measure distance in light-time (how long it took the light to reach us), in astronomical units (the Earth-Sun distance), or in parsecs and light-years. Below is a rough distance ladder, from the closest places we can reach to the edge of what we can ever see.
distances.section1Body: Light takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth from the Moon, 8 minutes from the Sun, and about 5½ hours from Pluto. Voyager 1 — the farthest human-made object — passed one light-day from Earth in November 2026: a full day of signal delay each way. Beyond that lies the Oort Cloud, a faint shell of icy bodies whose outer edge may sit at one full *light-year* or more.
distances.section2Body: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star beyond the Sun, is 4.24 light-years away. Alpha Centauri A and B sit just behind it. Sirius — the brightest star in our night sky — is 8.6 light-years away. The light from Vega, 25 light-years off, left around the time today's 25-year-olds were born. At Voyager 1's speed you'd reach Proxima in about 75,000 years.
distances.section3Body: Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at our galactic centre, is 26,000 light-years from Earth. The far side of the Milky Way is around 80,000 light-years. Andromeda — our nearest large galactic neighbour — is 2.5 million light-years away; its light set out when our genus, Homo, was still in its infancy. The Virgo Cluster, the dense centre of our local cosmic neighbourhood, sits 54 million light-years off.
distances.section4Body: We can only see light that's had time to reach us since the Big Bang, but space has also been expanding the whole time the light was travelling. The most distant light we can see comes from objects that are *now* about 46 billion light-years away — even though their light has been travelling "only" 13.8 billion years. That is our observable horizon. Beyond it almost certainly lies more universe; the limit is on what we can know, not on what exists.

moons.title: Moons
moons.seoTitle: Moons of the Solar System: Sizes and Facts
moons.tagline: The natural satellites of the planets.
moons.intro: A moon — also called a natural satellite — is any body that orbits a planet, dwarf planet, or other small Solar System body. Our Solar System has hundreds of confirmed moons, ranging from boulder-sized objects to worlds larger than Mercury. Some have atmospheres, subsurface oceans, or active volcanism. A few are among the most likely places to find life beyond Earth.
moons.section1Body: Our Moon is large for a moon orbiting a small planet — about a quarter of Earth's diameter. It formed about 4.5 billion years ago, almost certainly when a Mars-sized body collided with the young Earth, and the debris from that impact coalesced. The Moon stabilises Earth's axial tilt and drives our tides; it's slowly drifting away from us at about 3.8 cm per year.
moons.section2Heading: The giants — Ganymede, Titan, Callisto, Io, Europa
moons.section2Body: The four largest moons in the Solar System — Ganymede, Titan, Callisto and Io — are all bigger than Earth's Moon, and Ganymede is even larger than the planet Mercury. Ganymede (a moon of Jupiter) is the biggest moon in the Solar System. Titan (a moon of Saturn) has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and rivers of liquid methane. Europa (Jupiter) hides a vast salty ocean beneath an icy shell — one of the most promising places to search for life elsewhere in the Solar System.
moons.section3Body: Jupiter has 115 known moons and Saturn 293 (as of August 2026), and the numbers keep climbing as large telescopes pick out ever-smaller captured objects. Most of these are bodies a few kilometres across in irregular orbits — almost certainly debris from earlier collisions, not moons that formed alongside the planet.
moons.section4Body: Moons around planets in other star systems — exomoons — are theoretically expected almost everywhere, but none has yet been definitively confirmed. They are far harder to detect than exoplanets: a moon shows up only as a tiny periodic wobble inside another tiny periodic wobble. A handful of candidates exist, including a possible Neptune-sized exomoon around the gas giant Kepler-1625b.
moons.metaDescription: Our Solar System has hundreds of moons. How they form, the biggest ones compared — Ganymede is wider than Mercury — and which may hide oceans.

howBigIsTheUniverse.title: How Big Is the Universe?
howBigIsTheUniverse.seoTitle: How Big Is the Universe? The Observable Universe
howBigIsTheUniverse.tagline: The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across. The universe as a whole may have no edge at all.
howBigIsTheUniverse.intro: Short answer: the part we can see — the observable universe — is a sphere about 93 billion light-years in diameter, centred on us. That is roughly 8.8 × 10²⁶ metres, or about 70 billion billion Earths laid side by side. The universe as a whole is larger than that, possibly far larger, and it may be infinite. Nobody knows, and with current physics we may never be able to find out. Below: why the number is 93 billion and not 13.8 billion, what the cosmic horizon actually is, what might lie beyond it, and how to picture a size this large.
howBigIsTheUniverse.section1Heading: Why 93 billion light-years if the universe is only 13.8 billion years old?
howBigIsTheUniverse.section1Body: This is the most common point of confusion. The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so it seems no light could have travelled more than 13.8 billion light-years — which would make the visible universe 27.6 billion light-years across. But space has been expanding the whole time that light was in flight. The oldest light we can detect, the cosmic microwave background, was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang by hot gas that was then only about 42 million light-years from the matter that would one day become our galaxy. Since then the expansion has stretched that gap roughly 1,100 times: the gas that emitted the light we see today is now about 46 billion light-years away. Double that radius and you get a diameter of about 93 billion light-years. No speed limit was broken. The light always moved at light speed through space; it is the space behind it that kept growing.
howBigIsTheUniverse.section2Heading: The edge is a horizon, not a wall
howBigIsTheUniverse.section2Body: The observable universe has no physical boundary. Its edge is a horizon, like the horizon at sea: a limit set by where you stand and by how long light has had to travel. An observer in a galaxy 10 billion light-years from us has their own observable universe, centred on them and only partly overlapping ours. That is also why we appear to sit at the centre — everyone does. The Big Bang did not happen at one spot we could point to; it happened everywhere at once, and every location sees the expansion the same way. Galaxies more than about 14 billion light-years away are currently receding faster than light, which relativity allows because nothing is moving through space faster than light — the distance between us is growing. And because the expansion is accelerating, light that distant galaxies emit today will never reach us if they are now more than roughly 16 billion light-years away. The part of the cosmos we could ever contact is, in effect, slowly shrinking.
howBigIsTheUniverse.section3Heading: What lies beyond: finite or infinite?
howBigIsTheUniverse.section3Body: Beyond our horizon there is almost certainly more of the same — galaxies, clusters and the cosmic web — because nothing we observe hints at any change near the edge of our view. How much more is unknown. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background by ESA's Planck satellite show that space is flat to within a fraction of a percent (a curvature parameter of 0.0007 ± 0.0019, consistent with zero). A perfectly flat universe with the simplest possible shape would be infinite. A very slightly curved one could close back on itself like the surface of a ball — finite, yet with no edge anywhere. Even in that case, one statistical analysis of the data (Vardanyan, Trotta and Silk, 2011) concluded that the whole universe would have to be several times larger in volume than everything we can observe. Truth-status, honestly labelled: the 93-billion-light-year figure for the observable part is established theory, reliable to within a few percent. The size of everything is an open question — infinite is possible, finite but enormous is possible, and no current experiment can tell the two apart.
howBigIsTheUniverse.section4Body: A single number this big means little on its own, so climb to it in steps. Earth is 12,742 km across. The Sun is about 109 Earths wide and 150 million km away. A light-year is about 9.46 trillion km, and the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 4.24 light-years off. The Milky Way spans roughly 100,000 light-years and holds 100 to 400 billion stars. Andromeda, the nearest large galaxy, lies 2.5 million light-years away. Laniakea, the supercluster we live in, is about 500 million light-years across. The observable universe, at 93 billion light-years, is about 930,000 Milky Ways wide, or nearly 190 Laniakeas, and contains hundreds of billions of galaxies — some estimates run as high as 2 trillion. Now shrink everything by the same factor, using this site's reference scale where Earth is a 0.5 mm grain of sand: the Sun becomes a 5.4 cm ball about 5.9 metres away, the Milky Way stretches about 40 million kilometres, and the entire observable universe is roughly 3.6 light-years across — almost as wide as the real distance from here to Proxima Centauri.
howBigIsTheUniverse.section5Body: "The universe is 13.8 billion light-years across." No — 13.8 billion is its age in years. Because of expansion, the observable part is about 93 billion light-years wide. "The Big Bang was an explosion from a centre." It was not an explosion into pre-existing space; space itself began expanding everywhere, so there is no centre and no point it expanded from. "The universe is expanding into something." Expansion means that distances between widely separated galaxies grow; it doesn't require any outside space to grow into. "Everything is expanding, including us." Gravitationally bound systems — atoms, people, planets, the Solar System, the Milky Way, even our Local Group of galaxies — do not expand. The stretching only wins out on the scales between groups and clusters of galaxies. "Nothing can recede faster than light." Relativity limits motion through space, not the growth of space itself; most galaxies in the observable universe are, today, receding from us faster than light. "We can see the whole universe." We see only what light has had time to bring us. The observable universe is a bubble around us, not the whole thing.

planetSizesCompared.title: Planet Sizes Compared
planetSizesCompared.seoTitle: Planet Sizes Compared: From Mercury to Jupiter
planetSizesCompared.tagline: All eight planets, plus Pluto and the Moon, side by side — diameters, volumes, and a scale model you could walk.
planetSizesCompared.intro: The planets of the Solar System differ in size far more than most illustrations let on. Jupiter is about 29 times wider than Mercury, the Sun is about ten times wider than Jupiter, and the four giant planets hold more than 99% of all planetary mass. Below are the numbers — mean diameters from NASA's planetary fact sheets — in order, followed by the volume comparisons people most often ask about and a scale model that makes the gaps between the planets feel as real as their sizes.
planetSizesCompared.section1Body: Using mean diameters: first, Jupiter, 139,820 km — about 11 Earths across. Second, Saturn, 116,460 km — about 9.1 Earths. Third, Uranus, 50,724 km — about 4 Earths. Fourth, Neptune, 49,244 km — just under 3.9 Earths. Fifth, Earth, 12,742 km. Sixth, Venus, 12,104 km — 95% of Earth's width, almost a twin. Seventh, Mars, 6,779 km — 53% of Earth. Eighth, Mercury, 4,879 km — 38% of Earth. For comparison, our Moon is 3,475 km across (27% of Earth), and the dwarf planet Pluto is 2,377 km (19% of Earth) — smaller than the Moon. And the Sun, at about 1.39 million km, is roughly 109 Earths wide. The giant planets spin so fast that they visibly bulge: Jupiter measures 142,984 km across the equator but 133,708 km from pole to pole, and Saturn 120,536 km against 108,728 km. That is why figures quoted for them vary depending on whether a source gives the equatorial or the mean diameter.
planetSizesCompared.section2Heading: How many Earths fit inside Jupiter — and inside the Sun?
planetSizesCompared.section2Body: Volume grows with the cube of width, so modest differences in diameter become huge differences in volume. Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth, so about 1,300 Earths would fit inside it by volume. Saturn holds about 760 Earths, Uranus about 63 and Neptune about 58. The Sun, 109 times Earth's width, has the volume of about 1.3 million Earths — or about 1,000 Jupiters. Going the other way, roughly 49 Moons would fill Earth, and about three Plutos would fill the Moon. (These are volume ratios. Real spheres leave gaps when packed, so fewer solid balls would actually fit.) Mass tells a different story from size. Jupiter is 318 times Earth's mass, not 1,300 times, because it is mostly hydrogen and helium. Saturn is so light for its size that its average density, about 0.69 grams per cubic centimetre, is lower than that of water. And Neptune, although slightly smaller than Uranus, is the heavier of the two — about 17 Earth masses against Uranus's 14.5.
planetSizesCompared.section3Heading: A scale model: Earth as a grain of sand
planetSizesCompared.section3Body: Quantumaire's reference scale shrinks Earth to a single 0.5 mm grain of sand. At that scale the Sun is a ball about 5.4 cm across — billiard-ball size — and Earth sits about 5.9 metres from it. Mercury is a 0.19 mm speck 2.3 m from the Sun. Venus is 0.47 mm, at 4.2 m. Earth is the 0.5 mm grain, at 5.9 m, with the Moon a 0.14 mm fleck just 1.5 cm away. Mars is 0.27 mm, at 8.9 m. Jupiter is the biggest bead, about 5.5 mm, at 31 m. Saturn is 4.6 mm, at 56 m. Uranus is 2 mm, at 113 m. Neptune is 1.9 mm, at 177 m. Pluto, a 0.09 mm dust mote, circles on average about 230 m out. The whole planetary system fits inside a few city blocks — but the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, would be another small ball about 1,600 kilometres away. That emptiness is the real lesson of any honest scale model: the planets are tiny compared with the distances between them.
planetSizesCompared.section4Body: Line up the seven other planets edge to edge, using their mean diameters, and they add up to about 380,000 km — just under the average Earth–Moon distance of 384,400 km. (It only works on average: when the Moon is at its closest, around 363,000 km, they no longer fit.) Two moons are wider than the planet Mercury — Jupiter's Ganymede at 5,268 km and Saturn's Titan at 5,150 km — although both have less than half of Mercury's mass. Saturn's main rings stretch about 270,000 km from edge to edge, more than twice the planet's own width, yet they are typically only about ten metres thick. Jupiter's Great Red Spot has been shrinking for well over a century; once about three Earths wide, it is today only slightly wider than one. And Earth, it turns out, is the largest of the rocky planets — the biggest solid world orbiting the Sun.
planetSizesCompared.section5Heading: Why most pictures get it wrong
planetSizesCompared.section5Body: Almost every poster of the Solar System cheats, and it has to. Draw Earth as a 1 cm dot and the Sun becomes a disc about 1.1 metres across, about 117 metres away; Neptune would sit 3.5 kilometres off. No page can show both true sizes and true distances, so illustrations squeeze the gaps by factors of thousands and often shrink the Sun too. That leaves a false impression of a crowded system. The opposite is true: the planets together fill a vanishingly small part of the volume inside Neptune's orbit. Pluto, which appears in many older charts as the ninth planet, was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 after astronomers found other bodies of similar size in the Kuiper Belt — one of them, Eris, nearly as wide and slightly more massive.

smallestThingsInTheUniverse.title: The Smallest Things in the Universe
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.seoTitle: The Smallest Things in the Universe
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.tagline: From cells to quarks to the Planck length — what is really small, what is point-like, and how we can possibly know.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.intro: Ask what the smallest thing in the universe is and the answer depends on what you mean. The smallest living cells are bacteria a few hundred nanometres across. The smallest objects with a measured size are protons and neutrons, under two femtometres wide. The truly fundamental particles — quarks and electrons — have no measured size at all: every experiment so far finds them point-like, and only upper limits exist. Below everything sits the Planck length, a theoretical scale where today's physics stops working. Here is the ladder from top to bottom, with an honest label on each rung.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section1Heading: The living world: cells, bacteria and viruses
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section1Body: A human hair is roughly 70 micrometres (µm) thick, close to the smallest detail your eye can make out at reading distance, about 0.1 mm. Below that limit everything is invisible without help. Most pollen grains are 10 to 100 µm, typically about a third of a hair's width. A human red blood cell is about 8 µm across, and a typical animal cell 10 to 30 µm. Most bacteria are 0.5 to 5 µm long, and the smallest are only about 0.2 to 0.3 µm — 200 to 300 nanometres (nm). Viruses are smaller still: most measure 20 to 300 nm, and the smallest known, such as circoviruses, are under 20 nm. There are exceptions in both directions. Giant viruses like Pithovirus reach about 1.5 µm, bigger than many bacteria, while the bacterium Thiomargarita magnifica grows up to about 2 cm long — visible to the naked eye. Smaller than any virus, the DNA double helix inside your cells is about 2 nm wide.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section2Body: Atoms are where chemistry lives, and molecules are what they build: a water molecule, one oxygen and two hydrogens, is about 0.28 nm across. They range from about 0.1 nm across for hydrogen to around half a nanometre for the largest — so somewhere between about 150,000 and 700,000 atoms side by side would span the thickness of a human hair. Almost all of an atom is empty space. Its nucleus is 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than the atom itself: blow an atom up to the size of a football stadium and the nucleus would be about the size of a pea on the centre spot, holding more than 99.9% of the mass. The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons. A proton's charge radius is about 0.84 femtometres (0.84 × 10⁻¹⁵ m), making it about 1.7 fm across. Even that figure took effort: in 2010, measurements using muonic hydrogen gave a value about 4% smaller than the older accepted one, the so-called proton radius puzzle. Later experiments have mostly converged on the smaller value. Note that a proton has no hard surface; its "size" is the extent of its electric charge, which fades out gradually.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section3Heading: Quarks and electrons: as small as we can measure
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section3Body: Protons and neutrons are each made of three quarks, and atoms are completed by electrons. As far as anyone can tell, both quarks and electrons are point particles: they show no internal structure and no measurable size. That is not the same as proving their size is zero — it means every experiment so far has come up empty. At the HERA electron–proton collider in Hamburg, the ZEUS experiment set an upper limit of 0.43 × 10⁻¹⁸ m on the radius of a quark (published 2016), about 2,000 times smaller than a proton's radius. Electrons have been tested to similar or finer levels without any sign of structure. On this site, the quark page's figure of 10⁻¹⁸ m is such an upper bound, not a measured diameter. If you measure smallness by mass instead, the champions are neutrinos: the KATRIN experiment has shown that a neutrino weighs less than 0.45 eV, under a millionth of an electron's mass. Photons and gluons have no mass at all.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section4Heading: The Planck length: a limit of theory, not a pixel
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section4Body: The Planck length, about 1.6 × 10⁻³⁵ m, is built from three constants of nature: the speed of light, the gravitational constant and Planck's constant. It is about 10²⁰ times smaller than a proton — roughly as much smaller than a proton as Earth is smaller than the observable universe. Physicists expect that at around this scale the quantum effects of gravity become important, and that general relativity and quantum mechanics, as we currently write them, stop giving trustworthy answers. It is often described as the "pixel size" of the universe or the smallest length that can exist. That claim goes beyond the evidence. No experiment has shown that space is grainy; some approaches to quantum gravity, such as loop quantum gravity, suggest a discrete structure near this scale, while others do not. Observations of distant gamma-ray bursts have searched for the tiny differences in the speed of light that the simplest grainy-space models predict, and so far have ruled several of them out. Our most powerful colliders probe distances down to roughly 10⁻¹⁹ m — still several million billion times larger than the Planck length.
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section5Heading: How we measure the very small
smallestThingsInTheUniverse.section5Body: Each step down the scale needs a new tool. The naked eye resolves about 0.1 mm. Ordinary light microscopes are limited by the wavelength of light to about 200 nm — enough to see bacteria, but not most viruses — although super-resolution fluorescence methods, honoured with the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, push that to tens of nanometres. Electron microscopes use electrons, whose wavelength is far shorter, and the best modern instruments resolve detail finer than 0.1 nm: individual atoms. The scanning tunnelling microscope, invented in 1981 by Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer, maps single atoms on a surface by feeling them with a sharp tip. Below the atom, nothing can be photographed; sizes are inferred from scattering — firing particles at a target and studying how they bounce. Rutherford found the atomic nucleus this way in 1911 from gold-foil experiments, and Robert Hofstadter used electron scattering in the 1950s to measure the size of the proton. Today's colliders follow the same logic: the higher the energy, the shorter the wavelength, and the finer the detail they can resolve.

largestThingsInTheUniverse.title: The Largest Things in the Universe
largestThingsInTheUniverse.seoTitle: The Largest Things in the Universe
largestThingsInTheUniverse.tagline: The biggest star, black hole, galaxy and cosmic structure — with honest error bars.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.intro: "Largest" is a slippery word in astronomy. Stars have fuzzy edges, black-hole masses are inferred indirectly, galaxies fade gradually into darkness, and some of the biggest claimed structures may be partly patterns in noise. So instead of one confident record per category, here are the leading contenders and how sure we are about each. Climbing from stars to the cosmic web, every step is roughly a thousand to a million times bigger than the one before.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section1Body: The biggest stars are red supergiants and hypergiants — swollen, cool stars near the end of their lives. Their sizes are calculated from brightness and temperature, and brightness depends on distance, so estimates shift a lot. UY Scuti, once listed at about 1,700 times the Sun's radius, was revised down to roughly 900 after the Gaia mission improved its distance; it is the largest star on this site, but no longer a record holder. Current leading candidates include Stephenson 2-18, estimated at around 1,800 solar radii with error bars of several hundred and some doubt about its distance; WOH G64 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, about 1,500; VY Canis Majoris, about 1,400; and RW Cephei, about 1,100. Placed where the Sun is, VY Canis Majoris would swallow the orbit of Jupiter, and even UY Scuti would reach past Mars and the asteroid belt, most of the way to Jupiter. Size is not mass: these puffed-up giants weigh only around 7 to 40 Suns. The most massive star known, R136a1, has roughly 200 solar masses but is only a few dozen times wider than the Sun.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section2Body: A black hole's size — the width of its event horizon — grows in direct proportion to its mass, so the biggest black holes are the heaviest. TON 618, a quasar whose light has travelled about 10.8 billion years, is estimated at around 40 billion solar masses (older estimates said 66 billion), giving an event horizon about 1,600 astronomical units across — some 20 times the width of Pluto's orbit. That mass comes from the speed of gas around the black hole, a method uncertain by a factor of two or three. The black hole in Holmberg 15A, the central galaxy of the cluster Abell 85, was weighed at about 40 billion solar masses from the motions of its stars, a more direct method. Phoenix-A's estimates range from a few billion to about 100 billion solar masses; this site uses about 25 billion. For comparison, M87*, the first black hole ever imaged, is about 6.5 billion solar masses, and Sagittarius A* at the centre of our galaxy about 4 million. Some theorists argue that black holes fed by glowing accretion disks struggle to grow past about 50 billion solar masses, which would put TON 618 near a natural ceiling.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section3Body: Galaxies have no sharp edge — their light simply fades into the dark — so their sizes depend on how deep you look. The Milky Way's starry disk is about 100,000 light-years across. The largest known spiral, the Condor Galaxy (NGC 6872), stretches more than 500,000 light-years from tip to tip, pulled out by a collision with a neighbour. The true giants are elliptical galaxies at the hearts of galaxy clusters. IC 1101 is the classic example: its faint halo of stars has been traced across well over a million light-years, though published figures vary widely with the depth of the images and the definition used. If you count radio jets, the records grow further. Porphyrion, reported in 2024, blasts jets from its central black hole that span about 23 million light-years end to end — the longest known — overtaking Alcyoneus, at about 16 million light-years, found in 2022. Those jets are thin streams of plasma, not stars, so most astronomers do not count them as part of the galaxy's size.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section4Body: Galaxy clusters are the largest things in the universe held together by their own gravity. They span a few million to about 15 million light-years and can contain thousands of galaxies; the nearest big one, the Virgo Cluster, has about 1,500 galaxies and lies about 54 million light-years away. Above that scale, structures are not bound — cosmic expansion is slowly pulling them apart. Superclusters are mapped by how galaxies move. Laniakea, our own, was defined in 2014 by Brent Tully and colleagues from the motions of thousands of galaxies. It spans roughly 500 million light-years and contains about 100,000 galaxies, all flowing toward a gravitational basin called the Great Attractor. Because it is defined by flows, its exact boundaries depend on method. Between the superclusters lie voids: the Boötes Void, for instance, is a nearly empty region about 330 million light-years across.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section5Heading: Walls, rings and arcs: records that may not be real
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section5Body: Beyond superclusters, astronomers have reported a series of giant patterns. The Sloan Great Wall (found in 2003) and the South Pole Wall (2020) each stretch about 1.4 billion light-years. Quipu, described in 2025, is a similar-sized chain of galaxy clusters and has been called the largest known structure in the nearby universe. Further out, the Big Ring (2024) is a ring of galaxies about 1.3 billion light-years in diameter, and the Giant Arc (2021) a crescent about 3.3 billion light-years long. The most extreme claim is the Hercules–Corona Borealis Great Wall, identified in 2013–2014 from an apparent clustering of gamma-ray bursts and estimated at around 10 billion light-years long. It rests on a small number of bursts, and other analyses argue it may be a statistical fluke or a side effect of where telescopes have looked; treat it as contested. Cosmologists expect the universe to look smooth on scales above roughly 1.2 billion light-years. Some of these structures challenge that expectation, but simulations of standard cosmology also produce chance patterns this large, so none has yet overturned it.
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section6Heading: The largest of all: the observable universe
largestThingsInTheUniverse.section6Body: Everything above fits inside the observable universe, a sphere about 93 billion light-years across — the region from which light has had time to reach us in 13.8 billion years of cosmic expansion. It contains hundreds of billions of galaxies, perhaps as many as 2 trillion. It is about 930,000 Milky Ways wide, nearly 190 Laniakeas, and roughly 700 trillion UY Scutis. Whether the whole universe is larger — finite but enormous, or infinite — is an open question. That makes the observable universe the largest thing we can actually measure, rather than the largest thing that exists.

tallestStructures.title: Tallest Buildings and Structures
tallestStructures.seoTitle: Tallest Buildings in the World, Compared by Height
tallestStructures.tagline: From the Great Pyramid to the Burj Khalifa — how the record for the tallest thing people have built kept climbing, and what stops it.
tallestStructures.intro: For nearly four thousand years the tallest thing people had ever built was a pile of limestone in Egypt. Then, in a little over a century, iron and steel took the record from about 170 metres to 828. Here is how the height record climbed, how heights are actually measured, what limits a skyscraper, and how our tallest works compare with the tallest things nature grows — side by side on one scale.
tallestStructures.section1Body: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 2560 BC at about 146.6 m; it has since lost its top and casing and stands about 139 m today. Nothing built by people topped it until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral in England, around 1311, which reached about 160 m before it blew down in 1548. The **Eiffel Tower** of 1889 nearly doubled the record at 300 m — 330 m today with its antennas — and held it until New York's Chrysler Building passed it in 1930. The tallest-building record then raced upward — the Empire State Building (381 m) in 1931, Taipei 101 (508 m) in 2004 and the Burj Khalifa, 828 m, in 2010 — while for a few decades thin guyed radio masts were taller still, such as the 646 m Warsaw Radio Mast (1974–1991).
tallestStructures.section2Heading: How tall is tall? The rules
tallestStructures.section2Body: Heights sound simple until you have to decide where the top is. The Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat measures a building to its architectural top — spires count, but antennas, flagpoles and signs do not. That is why spires are popular: they add height cheaply. The empty spire and top floors of the Burj Khalifa add about 244 m that nobody can live or work in, a so-called vanity height. Statues have their own conventions too: the Statue of Liberty is 46 m from heel to torch, but 93 m from the ground once you include its pedestal and foundation.
tallestStructures.section3Heading: Why buildings can't just keep growing
tallestStructures.section3Body: Above a few hundred metres the problem is less weight than wind. A tall tower is a giant lever, and gusts set it swaying; designers taper the shape, twist it, or hang huge pendulums near the top — Taipei 101's weighs about 660 tonnes — to damp the motion. Lifts are the other limit: steel cables get so heavy that very tall buildings need sky lobbies where you change lifts halfway up. And every extra floor needs more structure below it and more space for lifts, so the floors you can actually rent shrink as the tower climbs. Even so, Jeddah Tower in Saudi Arabia, planned to pass 1,000 m, is under construction.
tallestStructures.section4Body: Living things reach heights that would challenge an engineer. The giraffe, at about 5.5 m, is the tallest animal; the tallest known tree, a coast redwood called Hyperion, stands about 116 m, and the **General Sherman** sequoia, though only 84 m tall, is the largest single tree by volume. Mountains dwarf them all: **Mount Everest** rises 8,849 m above sea level — more than ten Burj Khalifas stacked up. Measured from its base on the ocean floor, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is even taller, at about 10,200 m, though most of it is underwater.

humanBodyBySize.title: The Human Body by Size
humanBodyBySize.seoTitle: The Human Body by Size: From You to Your DNA
humanBodyBySize.tagline: From a 1.7-metre person down through 30 trillion cells to DNA two nanometres wide — and the bacteria and viruses that ride along.
humanBodyBySize.intro: You are the most familiar object on the scale, and also one of the most crowded. A 1.7-metre human is built from about 30 trillion cells, each packed with molecules, and carries roughly as many bacteria again. Here is the body from the outside in — person, cells, molecules — and the microscopic passengers that live on and in us, each with a size you can compare.
humanBodyBySize.section1Body: Quantumaire uses 1.7 m for an adult **human** — a little above the world average across men and women. A typical adult body is around 60% water by mass, and it contains roughly 7 × 10²⁷ atoms, most of them hydrogen. Scale it all up and the numbers stay surprising: laid end to end, the blood vessels in one adult would stretch tens of thousands of kilometres, and the total surface of your lungs' air sacs is about half a tennis court.
humanBodyBySize.section2Body: A 2016 census of the body counted about 30 trillion human cells — and about 84% of them are red blood cells, little discs about 7.5 µm wide that carry oxygen. A typical body cell is around 10 µm across, roughly a tenth of a hair's width. The extremes are far apart: an egg cell is about 0.1 mm, just visible to the naked eye, while some nerve cells run about a metre, from the base of the spine to the toes. Your body replaces billions of cells every day; red blood cells last about four months.
humanBodyBySize.section3Heading: Inside a cell: DNA and molecules
humanBodyBySize.section3Body: Inside the nucleus of every cell that has one sit two full sets of your genome: 46 chromosomes holding about 6 billion base-pair 'letters' of DNA. The double helix is only about 2 nm wide, yet stretched out the DNA in a single cell would be about 2 metres long — packed into a nucleus a few micrometres across. Go smaller and you reach the molecules everything is made of: a water molecule, the most common one in your body, is about 0.28 nm across, and an atom is about 0.1 nm.
humanBodyBySize.section4Body: The same 2016 census estimated about 38 trillion bacteria living in and on us, mostly in the gut — slightly more than our own cells, but together weighing only about 0.2 kg because each is so small, typically 1–2 µm long. Viruses are smaller still, mostly 20–300 nm, below what a light microscope can show; the flu virus is about 100 nm across. Most of these passengers are harmless or helpful, digesting food we can't and crowding out the ones that would make us ill.
